All three are inclined alike.

A short rectangular lug projects radially outward from the outer boundary of the second cam ring segment 24, close to the right joint. Its circumferentially facing end surface, the surface facing away from the right joint, is the ring drive face 36.

The following description of embodiments refers to the accompanying drawings. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout. Terms of direction are used with respect to the frame of the clamp: the axis of the frame is the axis about which the frame is annular in the closed condition and with which the axis of a clamped pipe substantially coincides, "inward" and "radially inward" mean toward that axis, "outward" and "radially outward" mean away from it, and "circumferential" means about that axis. These terms describe relationships within the clamp and do not require the clamp to be used in any particular attitude.

Overall arrangement

FIG. 1 shows a split pipe clamp 100 in the closed condition around a pipe 90. The clamp 100 has a first frame half 10 and a second frame half 12. Each of the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 is semicircular, and the two frame halves together surround the pipe 90. The first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are joined at one end, referred to as the hinge end, by a hinge 14, and are releasably joined at the other end, referred to as the latch end, by a releasable latch 16. The hinge 14 permits the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 to be swung apart far enough for the clamp 100 to be passed sideways onto a pipe 90 that is already installed, so that the clamp 100 need not be threaded over a free end of the pipe 90. When the frame halves are brought together and the latch 16 is engaged, the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 define a frame that is annular about the axis of the clamp 100.

Three jaw carriages 30 are distributed around the frame in the closed condition, so that the three jaw carriages 30 approach the pipe 90 from three different directions. Each jaw carriage 30 moves radially with respect to the frame and bears on the pipe 90 through a jaw pad 40 described below. The three jaw carriages 30 are the only members of the clamp 100 that touch the pipe 90 when the clamp 100 is clamped, and the position of the frame on the pipe 90 is established by them rather than by contact between the pipe 90 and a bore of the frame. The clamp 100 accordingly does not require a frame bore, liner, or insert dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter, and the same clamp 100 serves pipes of different diameters within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

The frame may carry a mounting boss 70 outside the annular guide described below. The mounting boss 70 supports a sensor, a tool, a bracket, a length of conduit, or other equipment that is to be held on the pipe 90 by the clamp 100. The mounting boss 70 is connected neither to the segmented cam ring nor to any jaw carriage 30 and does not participate in the synchronization of the jaw carriages 30. Equipment carried at the mounting boss 70 therefore lies outside the drive path by which the jaws are advanced, and the mounting boss 70 may be placed on either frame half at whatever circumferential position suits the equipment to be carried. The mounting boss 70 is an optional feature of the clamp 100 and may be omitted.

The segmented cam ring

FIG. 2 shows the segmented cam ring 20 of the clamp 100, drawn removed from the frame with its segments in the coupled condition. The segmented cam ring 20 comprises a first cam ring segment 22 and a second cam ring segment 24. The first cam ring segment 22 is carried by the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 is carried by the second frame half 12, so that each frame half carries one segment of the ring and each segment travels with its own frame half when the clamp 100 is opened.

The first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 meet at two places, one at the hinge end and one at the latch end. At the hinge end the two segments have complementary coupling faces 26, and at the latch end they have complementary coupling faces 28. The complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are circumferentially facing drive faces, each pair being shaped so that one segment can transmit circumferential force to the other through the joint. The faces are brought into engagement by the same motion that closes the frame halves: as the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are swung together about the hinge 14 and the latch 16 is engaged, the complementary coupling faces 26 close on one another at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 close on one another at the latch end.

Coupling the segments in this way solves a problem created by splitting the clamp. A clamp that must open from the side cannot carry a continuous drive ring across the split, and a divided drive must otherwise be operated separately in each half, with the result that the two halves advance their jaws by amounts that are not fixed relative to one another. Here the division of the ring is undone by the act of closing the clamp. In the closed condition the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 are coupled at both ends and rotate together in the annular guide as a coupled ring, and a circumferential input applied to either segment is carried around the whole ring. One input, applied at one point on one frame half, therefore reaches every jaw carriage 30 through a single kinematic element, and the relationship between the jaw carriages 30 is set by the geometry of the ring rather than by the way the clamp is operated. When the latch 16 is released and the frame halves are swung apart, the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 separate and each segment stays with its own frame half, so that the coupling is made and broken automatically with each use and requires no separate assembly step.

The segmented cam ring 20 has three oblique slots 34, one for each jaw carriage 30. Each oblique slot 34 passes through the segmented cam ring 20 and is inclined to the radial direction of the frame at the circumferential position of that slot, so that circumferential movement of the ring produces a radial displacement of anything constrained to follow the slot. The three oblique slots 34 have the same inclination, so that a given rotation of the coupled ring advances each jaw carriage 30 by the same radial increment. The inclination of the oblique slots 34 sets the ratio between the circumferential stroke of the coupled ring and the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30, and is selected so that the available stroke of the coupled ring produces the radial travel required to span the intended range of pipe diameters, and so that the mechanical advantage at the jaw pads 40 is sufficient for the clamping force to be developed by hand at the latch 16. A shallower inclination gives greater mechanical advantage and less radial travel for a given stroke, and a steeper inclination gives more radial travel and less mechanical advantage.

The segmented cam ring 20 further has a ring drive face 36, shown in FIG. 2 at the latch end of the ring, against which the latch acts as described below. The ring drive face 36 faces circumferentially and is presented at a position on the ring where the latch can reach it, in the illustrated embodiment on the segment adjacent the latch end.

The jaw carriages

FIG. 3 is a fragmentary sectional view through one jaw carriage 30. The frame is channeled to form an annular guide 18 that receives the segmented cam ring 20 and retains it against radial and axial displacement while permitting it to move circumferentially. The annular guide 18 is formed in both frame halves, one arcuate portion of the annular guide 18 in each frame half, and the two arcuate portions register with one another in the closed condition to form a continuous annular path in which the coupled ring turns.

The frame is further formed with a radial guide 38 at the position of each jaw carriage 30. Each jaw carriage 30 is received in a respective radial guide 38 and is constrained by the radial guide 38 to move radially with respect to the frame. Each jaw carriage 30 carries a follower 32 that projects from the jaw carriage 30 into a respective one of the oblique slots 34 of the segmented cam ring 20. The follower 32 may be a pin, a post, a roller, or a like projection able to bear against the sides of the oblique slot 34.

The follower 32 is constrained in two ways at once. The radial guide 38 prevents the jaw carriage 30, and therefore the follower 32, from moving circumferentially, while the oblique slot 34 confines the follower 32 to a path that is inclined to the radial direction. When the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the side of each oblique slot 34 bears on the corresponding follower 32 and drives it, and with it the jaw carriage 30, radially inward along the radial guide 38. Because all three followers 32 are engaged in slots of the same inclination in one coupled ring, the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism, by equal radial increments, for as long as the ring turns. The jaw pads therefore close on the pipe together and the frame takes up a position centered on the pipe.

At its inner end each jaw carriage 30 carries a jaw pad 40. The jaw pad 40 is pivotally mounted on the jaw carriage 30 and has a concave bearing face directed inwardly of the frame. Because the jaw pad 40 is free to pivot on the jaw carriage 30, the concave bearing face aligns itself with the outer surface of the pipe as it lands, and the contact is distributed along the face instead of being taken at one edge of it. The same concave bearing face therefore seats on pipes of different diameters, and no insert dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter is required. The bearing face may be faced or lined with a material chosen for the pipe to be gripped, for example a material softer than the pipe surface where a coated or thin walled pipe is to be clamped.

A carriage return spring 44 acts on each jaw carriage 30 and biases the jaw carriage 30 radially outward. In the illustrated embodiment the carriage return spring 44 is a compression spring seated between an abutment of the radial guide 38 and a shoulder of the jaw carriage 30. When the latch 16 is released and the drive from the latch to the ring drive face 36 is removed, the carriage return springs 44 push the jaw carriages 30 outward, the followers 32 bear on the opposite sides of their oblique slots 34, and the coupled ring is turned back through its stroke. The jaws are thus retracted from the pipe by the same synchronized path, and the clamp 100 is left with its jaw carriages 30 retracted and ready for the next installation. Retraction of the jaw carriages 30 also clears the jaw pads 40 from the pipe before the frame halves are swung apart, so that the pipe surface is not scraped by a jaw pad 40 that is still bearing on it.

The latch and the force-limiting drive train

FIG. 4 shows the latch 16 in fragmentary section. The latch 16 includes a latch housing 58 mounted on the frame at the latch end, a latch handle 50 pivotally mounted on the latch housing 58, a wedge 52 movable in the latch housing 58, and a force-limiting spring stack 54 in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52. The wedge 52 is positioned so that its inclined face bears on the ring drive face 36 of the segmented cam ring 20.

The latch 16 has two engaged positions. In a first position, the latch 16 holds the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 closed around the pipe 90 but does not clamp it: the frame is captive on the pipe 90 and cannot fall away, while the jaw carriages 30 remain retracted under their carriage return springs 44 and the clamp 100 can still be slid or turned along the pipe 90 to its intended position. In a second, over-center position, the latch handle 50 has been carried past the point of maximum resistance, and the reaction transmitted back from the wedge 52 through the force-limiting spring stack 54 acts to hold the latch handle 50 in the second position rather than to open it, so that the latch 16 stays closed without a separate securing element. Movement of the latch handle 50 from the first position to the second position advances the wedge 52 against the ring drive face 36. The inclined face of the wedge 52 converts that advance into circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the coupled ring turns through its limited stroke, the extent of the stroke being set by the travel of the wedge 52 between the first and second positions of the latch 16.

The force-limiting spring stack 54 answers the problem of what becomes of the operator's remaining handle travel. The jaw pads 40 land on the pipe 90 at some point in the stroke that depends on the diameter of the pipe 90, and the latch handle 50 has still to be carried into its over-center position. If the drive train from the latch handle 50 to the wedge 52 were rigid, that remaining travel would be taken up by whatever part of the assembly yielded first, in practice by driving one jaw farther into the pipe 90 than the others and loading it far more heavily. Here the force-limiting spring stack 54 is the most compliant element of the drive train once the jaw pads 40 are seated. Additional travel of the latch handle 50 after all three jaw pads 40 have contacted the pipe 90 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than forcing one jaw carriage 30 farther inward than the others, and the clamping force delivered at the jaw pads 40 is accordingly determined by the compression of the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than by how hard the operator pulls the latch handle 50. The force-limiting spring stack 54 comprises one or more resilient elements arranged in a stack whose combined rate and travel are chosen so that the stack is stiff enough to carry the load required to advance the jaw carriages 30 to the pipe 90, and yielding enough to absorb the remaining travel of the latch handle 50 over the intended range of pipe diameters.

An indicator pin 56 is coupled to the force-limiting spring stack 54 and projects from the latch housing 58. As the force-limiting spring stack 54 compresses, the indicator pin 56 moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing 58, and the position of the indicator pin 56 with respect to that fixed edge shows the operator when the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered a predetermined compression range. The predetermined compression range is the range of stack compression that corresponds to the clamping force for which the clamp 100 is intended. The indicator pin 56 therefore reports clamp loading mechanically, at the clamp itself and without any separate instrument, and what it reports is the state of the force-limiting spring stack 54. It is not a measurement of the diameter of the pipe 90 and is not derived from the position of the jaw carriages 30: a large pipe and a small pipe seat the jaw pads 40 at different points in the stroke of the coupled ring, but the indicator pin 56 shows the same predetermined compression range in each case when the same clamping force has been reached.

Operation

To install the clamp 100 on a pipe 90, the operator opens the latch 16 and swings the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 apart about the hinge 14. The first cam ring segment 22 stays with the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 stays with the second frame half 12, and the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are separated. The operator places the frame halves around the pipe 90 from the side and closes them about the hinge 14. Closing the frame halves brings the complementary coupling faces 26 into engagement at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 into engagement at the latch end, coupling the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 into the coupled ring within the annular guide 18.

The operator then moves the latch 16 to its first position, in which the frame is held around the pipe 90 without clamping and can still be positioned along the pipe 90. When the clamp 100 is where it is wanted, the operator moves the latch handle 50 to the second, over-center position. The wedge 52 is driven against the ring drive face 36, the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the sides of the three oblique slots 34 drive the three followers 32, and the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism until the pivoting jaw pads 40 seat on the pipe 90. The remaining travel of the latch handle 50 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54, and the operator watches the indicator pin 56 move relative to the fixed edge of the latch housing 58 and so sees that the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered the predetermined compression range. The latch 16 is left in the over-center position and the clamp 100 is loaded on the pipe 90.

To remove the clamp 100, the operator releases the latch 16. The latch handle 50 comes back over center, the wedge 52 retreats from the ring drive face 36, and the force-limiting spring stack 54 is unloaded. The carriage return springs 44 then push the jaw carriages 30 radially outward, turning the coupled ring back through its stroke by way of the followers 32 in the oblique slots 34, so that all three jaw pads 40 lift from the pipe 90 together. Only then are the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 swung apart about the hinge 14 and the clamp 100 taken off the pipe 90. The clamp 100 is undamaged by the cycle and may be installed again on the same pipe or on a pipe of a different diameter within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

Variations

The frame halves, the segmented cam ring 20, the jaw carriages 30, and the latch 16 may be made of any materials having the strength and stiffness required for the loads to be carried, and the parts that slide on one another, in particular the segmented cam ring 20 in the annular guide 18 and each jaw carriage 30 in its radial guide 38, may be surfaced or lubricated to reduce friction in the drive path. The hinge 14 may be any joint that allows the frame halves to swing apart about a fixed axis at the hinge end while holding the complementary coupling faces 26 in register when the halves are closed. The complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 may take any complementary shapes that transmit circumferential force between the segments and that come into engagement as the frame halves close and separate as they open. The wedge 52 may act on the ring drive face 36 directly or through an intermediate sliding member, provided that the force-limiting spring stack 54 remains in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52. The carriage return spring 44 of each jaw carriage 30 may act between the jaw carriage 30 and its radial guide 38 as illustrated, or elsewhere on the jaw carriage 30, provided that it biases the jaw carriage 30 outward when the drive from the latch 16 is removed.

Features described above in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another, except where the context makes the combination impossible. The embodiments described are illustrative of the disclosed clamp and are not exhaustive of it, and the scope of protection is defined by the claims that follow rather than by any particular embodiment described here.

input.summary: Wrote the complete first draft of "Self-Centering Split Pipe Clamp With Synchronized Radial Jaws" from the inventor's disclosure: all ten draft/ sections, draft/numerals.md (25 numerals), and four figure specifications (overall clamp on a pipe, the segmented cam ring alone, a sectional detail through one jaw carriage, and a sectional detail of the latch drive train). Claim 1 is an apparatus claim built on the disclosed core relationship (segments coupled by the act of closing the frame, one coupled ring driving all three carriages through oblique slots), with a 12-claim dependent ladder, an independent system claim for the equipment-carrying assembly, and an independent method claim with three dependents. Important caveat for the user, as the brief instructed: prior_art/INDEX.md is empty, no search was run, and the art available to this draft may therefore be incomplete; nothing here is a statement about patentability.
reasoning: Claim 1 carries the one relationship the inventor called essential and that a searcher would have to find as a combination: a cam ring that is divided with the split body, one segment per frame half, whose complementary coupling faces at the hinge end and at the latch end engage as the halves close so that the two segments then rotate as a single coupled ring, plus followers in oblique slots that turn that one rotation into synchronized inward travel of all three carriages. The self-restoring drive across the split is the feature doing the technical work, and the Background states the problem it solves (a split body cannot carry a continuous drive ring; separately driven halves lose the fixed relation between their jaws) so the argument exists in the specification before it is needed.

Deliberately left out of claim 1: the force-limiting spring stack, the indicator pin, the two-position over-center latch, the mounting boss, the word semicircular, and the equal inclination of the slots. Each is a real and separately arguable limitation, so each became a dependent (2, 3, 5, 12, 13, 8) rather than scope surrendered up front. Claim 1 keeps only what makes the mechanism work: hinge and latch, three carriages in radial guides, pivoting concave pads, the segmented ring with its coupling faces, the oblique slots and followers, the wedge on the ring drive face, and outward biasing springs.

Kept 'three' rather than 'a plurality of' jaw carriages in claim 1. The disclosure only ever describes three; a plurality claim would rest on written-description support the source does not give. The scope cost is small because the synchronizing ring, not the count, is what distinguishes the mechanism.

Dependent ladder is graduated rather than decorative: 2 and 3 are the next-narrowest fallback (spring stack, then indicator); 4 pins the indicator to spring-stack compression and away from carriage position, which is the difference between reporting load and reporting pipe size; 5 and 6 cover the two-position over-center latch; 7 covers the reverse path, where the return springs turn the ring back through the followers; 8 covers equal-inclination slots and self-centering; 9 covers diameter tolerance without a size-specific insert; 10 and 11 cover the split annular guide and the automatic making and breaking of the coupling on each use, which is the fallback if the coupling faces alone are attacked.

Wrote a system claim (14) as well as apparatus and method because the assembler who fits a sensor, tool, or conduit to the mounting boss is a different party from the clamp maker, and the method claims (17 to 20) are infringed by the installer. The method independent recites the coupling step explicitly, so it is not a bare use of the apparatus.

Description was written to support every claim term verbatim, including 'ring drive face', 'complementary coupling faces at the hinge end', 'carriage return spring', 'predetermined compression range', and 'without an insert dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter'. Where the disclosure gave a function but no implementation, the text uses functional language and stated selection criteria (slot inclination trades mechanical advantage against radial travel; spring stack rate chosen to be stiff enough to advance the carriages and yielding enough to absorb remaining handle travel) rather than inventing dimensions, angles, forces, or materials.

The disclosure's phrase 'complementary drive faces' was used for two different things (the segment joints and the face the wedge strikes). I named the joint features 'complementary coupling faces' and the wedge target the 'ring drive face' so that antecedent basis stays clean, and the description states the coupling faces are circumferentially facing drive faces so the source vocabulary is not lost.

Four figures, split so that no sheet is overcrowded and so each numeral group is coherent: FIG. 1 carries the assembly-level numerals (8), FIG. 2 isolates the ring so the two coupling joints, the oblique slots, and the ring drive face can be read without frame structure competing for space (7), FIG. 3 is a radial section carrying the guide, carriage, follower, slot, pad, and return spring (8), FIG. 4 is the latch train with handle, wedge, spring stack, indicator pin, housing, and the ring fragment it acts on (8). Parts that appear on a sheet without their own numeral (the frame body in FIG. 3, the supporting body in FIG. 4, the pad pivot) are described generically in those briefs and never named with a canonical part name there.
Background is written as an unattributed statement of the field's problems because prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references. No citation key exists, so none is used; no document is characterized.

input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so there was nothing to read, cite, or write around from the file set, and the Background therefore contains no citation keys and characterizes no document. In place of reference-by-reference differentiation, the draft was shaped so that its point of novelty is stated as a combination rather than as a component: claim 1 requires that the drive ring be divided between the frame halves and be re-coupled at both the hinge end and the latch end by the closing motion itself, so that a single latch input reaches every jaw carriage through one kinematic element. Common alternatives in this field, band or saddle clamps that pull the split body onto the pipe, bore-and-insert clamps sized to a nominal diameter, and clamps whose halves are tightened separately, are described in the Background as problems to be solved and are excluded by the claim language, which requires jaw-established positioning rather than bore-established positioning. Terminology was chosen to be accurate for this mechanism and not to borrow a chuck or band-clamp vocabulary: 'segmented cam ring', 'coupled ring', 'complementary coupling faces', 'ring drive face', 'jaw carriage', and 'force-limiting spring stack'. The second distinguishing thread, the force-limiting spring stack that absorbs latch travel after all pads land and an indicator pin that reports stack compression rather than jaw position or pipe size, is claimed in dependent and method claims and its technical rationale is set out in the description, so it is available as a fallback if a search later turns up art on synchronized jaw advancement. Because no search was run, the user should treat the available art as incomplete and have the claims re-checked against a real search before filing.

- Claim 14 is a system claim to the clamp plus equipment carried on the mounting boss; claims 17 to 20 are the method of installing, force-limiting, reading the indicator, and releasing.

Claim 1 is an apparatus claim built on the disclosed core relationship (segments coupled by the act of closing the frame, one coupled ring driving all three carriages through oblique slots), with a 12-claim dependent ladder, an independent system claim for the equipment-carrying assembly, and an independent method claim with three dependents. reasoning: Claim 1 carries the one relationship the inventor called essential and that a searcher would have to find as a combination: a cam ring that is divided with the split body, one segment per frame half, whose complementary coupling faces at the hinge end and at the latch end engage as the halves close so that the two segments then rotate as a single coupled ring, plus followers in oblique slots that turn that one rotation into synchronized inward travel of all three carriages. The self-restoring drive across the split is the feature doing the technical work, and the Background states the problem it solves (a split body cannot carry a continuous drive ring; separately driven halves lose the fixed relation between their jaws) so the argument exists in the specification before it is needed.

Deliberately left out of claim 1: the force-limiting spring stack, the indicator pin, the two-position over-center latch, the mounting boss, the word semicircular, and the equal inclination of the slots. Each is a real and separately arguable limitation, so each became a dependent (2, 3, 5, 12, 13, 8) rather than scope surrendered up front. Claim 1 keeps only what makes the mechanism work: hinge and latch, three carriages in radial guides, pivoting concave pads, the segmented ring with its coupling faces, the oblique slots and followers, the wedge on the ring drive face, and outward biasing springs.

Kept 'three' rather than 'a plurality of' jaw carriages in claim 1. The disclosure only ever describes three; a plurality claim would rest on written-description support the source does not give. The scope cost is small because the synchronizing ring, not the count, is what distinguishes the mechanism.

1	The following description of embodiments refers to the accompanying drawings. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout. Terms of direction are used with respect to the frame of the clamp: the axis of the frame is the axis about which the frame is annular in the closed condition and with which the axis of a clamped pipe substantially coincides, "inward" and "radially inward" mean toward that axis, "outward" and "radially outward" mean away from it, and "circumferential" means about that axis. These terms describe relationships within the clamp and do not require the clamp to be used in any particular attitude.
2	
3	Overall arrangement
4	
5	FIG. 1 shows a split pipe clamp 100 in the closed condition around a pipe 90. The clamp 100 has a first frame half 10 and a second frame half 12. Each of the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 is semicircular, and the two frame halves together surround the pipe 90. The first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are joined at one end, referred to as the hinge end, by a hinge 14, and are releasably joined at the other end, referred to as the latch end, by a releasable latch 16. The hinge 14 permits the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 to be swung apart far enough for the clamp 100 to be passed sideways onto a pipe 90 that is already installed, so that the clamp 100 need not be threaded over a free end of the pipe 90. When the frame halves are brought together and the latch 16 is engaged, the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 define a frame that is annular about the axis of the clamp 100.
6	
7	Three jaw carriages 30 are distributed around the frame in the closed condition, so that the three jaw carriages 30 approach the pipe 90 from three different directions. Each jaw carriage 30 moves radially with respect to the frame and presents a concave pad face at its inner end, the pad being described below in connection with FIG. 3. The three jaw carriages 30 are the only members of the clamp 100 that touch the pipe 90 when the clamp 100 is clamped, and the position of the frame on the pipe 90 is established by them rather than by contact between the pipe 90 and a bore of the frame. The clamp 100 accordingly does not require a frame bore, liner, or insert dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter, and the same clamp 100 serves pipes of different diameters within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.
8	
9	The frame may carry a mounting boss 70 outside the annular guide described below. The mounting boss 70 supports a sensor, a tool, a bracket, a length of conduit, or other equipment that is to be held on the pipe 90 by the clamp 100. The mounting boss 70 is connected neither to the segmented cam ring nor to any jaw carriage 30 and does not participate in the synchronization of the jaw carriages 30. Equipment carried at the mounting boss 70 therefore lies outside the drive path by which the jaws are advanced, and the mounting boss 70 may be placed on either frame half at whatever circumferential position suits the equipment to be carried. The mounting boss 70 is an optional feature of the clamp 100 and may be omitted.
10	
11	The segmented cam ring
12	
13	FIG. 2 shows the segmented cam ring 20 of the clamp 100, drawn removed from the frame with its segments in the coupled condition. The segmented cam ring 20 comprises a first cam ring segment 22 and a second cam ring segment 24. The first cam ring segment 22 is carried by the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 is carried by the second frame half 12, so that each frame half carries one segment of the ring and each segment travels with its own frame half when the clamp 100 is opened.
14	
15	The first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 meet at two places, one at the hinge end and one at the latch end. At the hinge end the two segments have complementary coupling faces 26, and at the latch end they have complementary coupling faces 28. The complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are circumferentially facing drive faces, each pair being shaped so that one segment can transmit circumferential force to the other through the joint. The faces are brought into engagement by the same motion that closes the frame halves: as the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are swung together about the hinge 14 and the latch 16 is engaged, the complementary coupling faces 26 close on one another at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 close on one another at the latch end.
16	
17	Coupling the segments in this way solves a problem created by splitting the clamp. A clamp that must open from the side cannot carry a continuous drive ring across the split, and a divided drive must otherwise be operated separately in each half, with the result that the two halves advance their jaws by amounts that are not fixed relative to one another. Here the division of the ring is undone by the act of closing the clamp. In the closed condition the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 are coupled at both ends and rotate together in the annular guide as a coupled ring, and a circumferential input applied to either segment is carried around the whole ring. One input, applied at one point on one frame half, therefore reaches every jaw carriage 30 through a single kinematic element, and the relationship between the jaw carriages 30 is set by the geometry of the ring rather than by the way the clamp is operated. When the latch 16 is released and the frame halves are swung apart, the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 separate and each segment stays with its own frame half, so that the coupling is made and broken automatically with each use and requires no separate assembly step.
18	
19	The segmented cam ring 20 has three oblique slots 34, one for each jaw carriage 30. Each oblique slot 34 passes through the segmented cam ring 20 and is inclined to the radial direction of the frame at the circumferential position of that slot, so that circumferential movement of the ring produces a radial displacement of anything constrained to follow the slot. The three oblique slots 34 have the same inclination, so that a given rotation of the coupled ring advances each jaw carriage 30 by the same radial increment. The inclination of the oblique slots 34 sets the ratio between the circumferential stroke of the coupled ring and the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30, and is selected so that the available stroke of the coupled ring produces the radial travel required to span the intended range of pipe diameters, and so that the mechanical advantage at the jaw pads 40 is sufficient for the clamping force to be developed by hand at the latch 16. A shallower inclination gives greater mechanical advantage and less radial travel for a given stroke, and a steeper inclination gives more radial travel and less mechanical advantage.
20	
21	The segmented cam ring 20 further has a ring drive face 36, shown in FIG. 2 at the latch end of the ring, against which the latch acts as described below. The ring drive face 36 faces circumferentially and is presented at a position on the ring where the latch can reach it, in the illustrated embodiment on the segment adjacent the latch end.
22	
23	The jaw carriages
24	
25	FIG. 3 is a fragmentary sectional view through one jaw carriage 30. The frame is channeled to form an annular guide 18 that receives the segmented cam ring 20 and retains it against radial and axial displacement while permitting it to move circumferentially. The annular guide 18 is formed in both frame halves, one arcuate portion of the annular guide 18 in each frame half, and the two arcuate portions register with one another in the closed condition to form a continuous annular path in which the coupled ring turns.
26	
27	The frame is further formed with a radial guide 38 at the position of each jaw carriage 30. Each jaw carriage 30 is received in a respective radial guide 38 and is constrained by the radial guide 38 to move radially with respect to the frame. Each jaw carriage 30 carries a follower 32 that projects from the jaw carriage 30 into a respective one of the oblique slots 34 of the segmented cam ring 20. The follower 32 may be a pin, a post, a roller, or a like projection able to bear against the sides of the oblique slot 34.
28	
29	The follower 32 is constrained in two ways at once. The radial guide 38 prevents the jaw carriage 30, and therefore the follower 32, from moving circumferentially, while the oblique slot 34 confines the follower 32 to a path that is inclined to the radial direction. When the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the side of each oblique slot 34 bears on the corresponding follower 32 and drives it, and with it the jaw carriage 30, radially inward along the radial guide 38. Because all three followers 32 are engaged in slots of the same inclination in one coupled ring, the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism, by equal radial increments, for as long as the ring turns. The jaw pads therefore close on the pipe together and the frame takes up a position centered on the pipe.
30	
31	At its inner end each jaw carriage 30 carries a jaw pad 40. The jaw pad 40 is pivotally mounted on the jaw carriage 30 and has a concave bearing face directed inwardly of the frame. Because the jaw pad 40 is free to pivot on the jaw carriage 30, the concave bearing face aligns itself with the outer surface of the pipe as it lands, and the contact is distributed along the face instead of being taken at one edge of it. The same concave bearing face therefore seats on pipes of different diameters, and no insert dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter is required. The bearing face may be faced or lined with a material chosen for the pipe to be gripped, for example a material softer than the pipe surface where a coated or thin walled pipe is to be clamped.
32	
33	A carriage return spring 44 acts on each jaw carriage 30 and biases the jaw carriage 30 radially outward. In the illustrated embodiment the carriage return spring 44 is a compression spring seated between an abutment of the radial guide 38 and a shoulder of the jaw carriage 30. When the latch 16 is released and the drive from the latch to the ring drive face 36 is removed, the carriage return springs 44 push the jaw carriages 30 outward, the followers 32 bear on the opposite sides of their oblique slots 34, and the coupled ring is turned back through its stroke. The jaws are thus retracted from the pipe by the same synchronized path, and the clamp 100 is left with its jaw carriages 30 retracted and ready for the next installation. Retraction of the jaw carriages 30 also clears the jaw pads 40 from the pipe before the frame halves are swung apart, so that the pipe surface is not scraped by a jaw pad 40 that is still bearing on it.
34	
35	The latch and the force-limiting drive train
36	
37	FIG. 4 shows the latch 16 in fragmentary section. The latch 16 includes a latch housing 58 mounted on the frame at the latch end, a latch handle 50 pivotally mounted on the latch housing 58, a wedge 52 movable in the latch housing 58, and a force-limiting spring stack 54 in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52. The wedge 52 is positioned so that its inclined face bears on the ring drive face 36 of the segmented cam ring 20.
38	
39	The latch 16 has two engaged positions. In a first position, the latch 16 holds the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 closed around the pipe 90 but does not clamp it: the frame is captive on the pipe 90 and cannot fall away, while the jaw carriages 30 remain retracted under their carriage return springs 44 and the clamp 100 can still be slid or turned along the pipe 90 to its intended position. In a second, over-center position, the latch handle 50 has been carried past the point of maximum resistance, and the reaction transmitted back from the wedge 52 through the force-limiting spring stack 54 acts to hold the latch handle 50 in the second position rather than to open it, so that the latch 16 stays closed without a separate securing element. Movement of the latch handle 50 from the first position to the second position advances the wedge 52 against the ring drive face 36. The inclined face of the wedge 52 converts that advance into circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the coupled ring turns through its limited stroke, the extent of the stroke being set by the travel of the wedge 52 between the first and second positions of the latch 16.
40	
41	The force-limiting spring stack 54 answers the problem of what becomes of the operator's remaining handle travel. The jaw pads 40 land on the pipe 90 at some point in the stroke that depends on the diameter of the pipe 90, and the latch handle 50 has still to be carried into its over-center position. If the drive train from the latch handle 50 to the wedge 52 were rigid, that remaining travel would be taken up by whatever part of the assembly yielded first, in practice by driving one jaw farther into the pipe 90 than the others and loading it far more heavily. Here the force-limiting spring stack 54 is the most compliant element of the drive train once the jaw pads 40 are seated. Additional travel of the latch handle 50 after all three jaw pads 40 have contacted the pipe 90 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than forcing one jaw carriage 30 farther inward than the others, and the clamping force delivered at the jaw pads 40 is accordingly determined by the compression of the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than by how hard the operator pulls the latch handle 50. The force-limiting spring stack 54 comprises one or more resilient elements arranged in a stack whose combined rate and travel are chosen so that the stack is stiff enough to carry the load required to advance the jaw carriages 30 to the pipe 90, and yielding enough to absorb the remaining travel of the latch handle 50 over the intended range of pipe diameters.
42	
43	An indicator pin 56 is coupled to the force-limiting spring stack 54 and projects from the latch housing 58. As the force-limiting spring stack 54 compresses, the indicator pin 56 moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing 58, and the position of the indicator pin 56 with respect to that fixed edge shows the operator when the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered a predetermined compression range. The predetermined compression range is the range of stack compression that corresponds to the clamping force for which the clamp 100 is intended. The indicator pin 56 therefore reports clamp loading mechanically, at the clamp itself and without any separate instrument, and what it reports is the state of the force-limiting spring stack 54. It is not a measurement of the diameter of the pipe 90 and is not derived from the position of the jaw carriages 30: a large pipe and a small pipe seat the jaw pads 40 at different points in the stroke of the coupled ring, but the indicator pin 56 shows the same predetermined compression range in each case when the same clamping force has been reached.
44	
45	Operation
46	
47	To install the clamp 100 on a pipe 90, the operator opens the latch 16 and swings the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 apart about the hinge 14. The first cam ring segment 22 stays with the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 stays with the second frame half 12, and the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are separated. The operator places the frame halves around the pipe 90 from the side and closes them about the hinge 14. Closing the frame halves brings the complementary coupling faces 26 into engagement at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 into engagement at the latch end, coupling the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 into the coupled ring within the annular guide 18.
48	
49	The operator then moves the latch 16 to its first position, in which the frame is held around the pipe 90 without clamping and can still be positioned along the pipe 90. When the clamp 100 is where it is wanted, the operator moves the latch handle 50 to the second, over-center position. The wedge 52 is driven against the ring drive face 36, the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the sides of the three oblique slots 34 drive the three followers 32, and the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism until the pivoting jaw pads 40 seat on the pipe 90. The remaining travel of the latch handle 50 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54, and the operator watches the indicator pin 56 move relative to the fixed edge of the latch housing 58 and so sees that the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered the predetermined compression range. The latch 16 is left in the over-center position and the clamp 100 is loaded on the pipe 90.
50	
51	To remove the clamp 100, the operator releases the latch 16. The latch handle 50 comes back over center, the wedge 52 retreats from the ring drive face 36, and the force-limiting spring stack 54 is unloaded. The carriage return springs 44 then push the jaw carriages 30 radially outward, turning the coupled ring back through its stroke by way of the followers 32 in the oblique slots 34, so that all three jaw pads 40 lift from the pipe 90 together. Only then are the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 swung apart about the hinge 14 and the clamp 100 taken off the pipe 90. The clamp 100 is undamaged by the cycle and may be installed again on the same pipe or on a pipe of a different diameter within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.
52	
53	Variations
54	
55	The frame halves, the segmented cam ring 20, the jaw carriages 30, and the latch 16 may be made of any materials having the strength and stiffness required for the loads to be carried, and the parts that slide on one another, in particular the segmented cam ring 20 in the annular guide 18 and each jaw carriage 30 in its radial guide 38, may be surfaced or lubricated to reduce friction in the drive path. The hinge 14 may be any joint that allows the frame halves to swing apart about a fixed axis at the hinge end while holding the complementary coupling faces 26 in register when the halves are closed. The complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 may take any complementary shapes that transmit circumferential force between the segments and that come into engagement as the frame halves close and separate as they open. The wedge 52 may act on the ring drive face 36 directly or through an intermediate sliding member, provided that the force-limiting spring stack 54 remains in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52. The carriage return spring 44 of each jaw carriage 30 may act between the jaw carriage 30 and its radial guide 38 as illustrated, or elsewhere on the jaw carriage 30, provided that it biases the jaw carriage 30 outward when the drive from the latch 16 is removed.
56	
57	Features described above in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another, except where the context makes the combination impossible. The embodiments described are illustrative of the disclosed clamp and are not exhaustive of it, and the scope of protection is defined by the claims that follow rather than by any particular embodiment described here.
58

The following description of embodiments refers to the accompanying drawings. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout. Terms of direction are used with respect to the frame of the clamp: the axis of the frame is the axis about which the frame is annular in the closed condition and with which the axis of a clamped pipe substantially coincides, "inward" and "radially inward" mean toward that axis, "outward" and "radially outward" mean away from it, and "circumferential" means about that axis. These terms describe relationships within the clamp and do not require the clamp to be used in any particular attitude.

Overall arrangement

FIG. 1 shows a split pipe clamp 100 in the closed condition around a pipe 90. The clamp 100 has a first frame half 10 and a second frame half 12. Each of the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 is semicircular, and the two frame halves together surround the pipe 90. The first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are joined at one end, referred to as the hinge end, by a hinge 14, and are releasably joined at the other end, referred to as the latch end, by a releasable latch 16. The hinge 14 permits the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 to be swung apart far enough for the clamp 100 to be passed sideways onto a pipe 90 that is already installed, so that the clamp 100 need not be threaded over a free end of the pipe 90. When the frame halves are brought together and the latch 16 is engaged, the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 define a frame that is annular about the axis of the clamp 100.

Three jaw carriages 30 are distributed around the frame in the closed condition, so that the three jaw carriages 30 approach the pipe 90 from three different directions. Each jaw carriage 30 moves radially with respect to the frame and presents a concave pad face at its inner end, the pad being described below in connection with FIG. 3. The three jaw carriages 30 are the only members of the clamp 100 that touch the pipe 90 when the clamp 100 is clamped, and the position of the frame on the pipe 90 is established by them rather than by contact between the pipe 90 and a bore of the frame. The clamp 100 accordingly does not require a frame bore, liner, or insert dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter, and the same clamp 100 serves pipes of different diameters within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

The frame may carry a mounting boss 70 outside the annular guide described below. The mounting boss 70 supports a sensor, a tool, a bracket, a length of conduit, or other equipment that is to be held on the pipe 90 by the clamp 100. The mounting boss 70 is connected neither to the segmented cam ring nor to any jaw carriage 30 and does not participate in the synchronization of the jaw carriages 30. Equipment carried at the mounting boss 70 therefore lies outside the drive path by which the jaws are advanced, and the mounting boss 70 may be placed on either frame half at whatever circumferential position suits the equipment to be carried. The mounting boss 70 is an optional feature of the clamp 100 and may be omitted.

The segmented cam ring

FIG. 2 shows the segmented cam ring 20 of the clamp 100, drawn removed from the frame with its segments in the coupled condition. The segmented cam ring 20 comprises a first cam ring segment 22 and a second cam ring segment 24. The first cam ring segment 22 is carried by the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 is carried by the second frame half 12, so that each frame half carries one segment of the ring and each segment travels with its own frame half when the clamp 100 is opened.

The first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 meet at two places, one at the hinge end and one at the latch end. At the hinge end the two segments have complementary coupling faces 26, and at the latch end they have complementary coupling faces 28. The complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are circumferentially facing drive faces, each pair being shaped so that one segment can transmit circumferential force to the other through the joint. The faces are brought into engagement by the same motion that closes the frame halves: as the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are swung together about the hinge 14 and the latch 16 is engaged, the complementary coupling faces 26 close on one another at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 close on one another at the latch end.

Coupling the segments in this way solves a problem created by splitting the clamp. A clamp that must open from the side cannot carry a continuous drive ring across the split, and a divided drive must otherwise be operated separately in each half, with the result that the two halves advance their jaws by amounts that are not fixed relative to one another. Here the division of the ring is undone by the act of closing the clamp. In the closed condition the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 are coupled at both ends and rotate together in the annular guide as a coupled ring, and a circumferential input applied to either segment is carried around the whole ring. One input, applied at one point on one frame half, therefore reaches every jaw carriage 30 through a single kinematic element, and the relationship between the jaw carriages 30 is set by the geometry of the ring rather than by the way the clamp is operated. When the latch 16 is released and the frame halves are swung apart, the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 separate and each segment stays with its own frame half, so that the coupling is made and broken automatically with each use and requires no separate assembly step.

The segmented cam ring 20 has three oblique slots 34, one for each jaw carriage 30. Each oblique slot 34 passes through the segmented cam ring 20 and is inclined to the radial direction of the frame at the circumferential position of that slot, so that circumferential movement of the ring produces a radial displacement of anything constrained to follow the slot. The three oblique slots 34 have the same inclination, so that a given rotation of the coupled ring advances each jaw carriage 30 by the same radial increment. The inclination of the oblique slots 34 sets the ratio between the circumferential stroke of the coupled ring and the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30, and is selected so that the available stroke of the coupled ring produces the radial travel required to span the intended range of pipe diameters, and so that the mechanical advantage at the jaw pads 40 is sufficient for the clamping force to be developed by hand at the latch 16. A shallower inclination gives greater mechanical advantage and less radial travel for a given stroke, and a steeper inclination gives more radial travel and less mechanical advantage.

The segmented cam ring 20 further has a ring drive face 36, shown in FIG. 2 at the latch end of the ring, against which the latch acts as described below. The ring drive face 36 faces circumferentially and is presented at a position on the ring where the latch can reach it, in the illustrated embodiment on the segment adjacent the latch end.

The jaw carriages

FIG. 3 is a fragmentary sectional view through one jaw carriage 30. The frame is channeled to form an annular guide 18 that receives the segmented cam ring 20 and retains it against radial and axial displacement while permitting it to move circumferentially. The annular guide 18 is formed in both frame halves, one arcuate portion of the annular guide 18 in each frame half, and the two arcuate portions register with one another in the closed condition to form a continuous annular path in which the coupled ring turns.

The frame is further formed with a radial guide 38 at the position of each jaw carriage 30. Each jaw carriage 30 is received in a respective radial guide 38 and is constrained by the radial guide 38 to move radially with respect to the frame. Each jaw carriage 30 carries a follower 32 that projects from the jaw carriage 30 into a respective one of the oblique slots 34 of the segmented cam ring 20. The follower 32 may be a pin, a post, a roller, or a like projection able to bear against the sides of the oblique slot 34.

The follower 32 is constrained in two ways at once. The radial guide 38 prevents the jaw carriage 30, and therefore the follower 32, from moving circumferentially, while the oblique slot 34 confines the follower 32 to a path that is inclined to the radial direction. When the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the side of each oblique slot 34 bears on the corresponding follower 32 and drives it, and with it the jaw carriage 30, radially inward along the radial guide 38. Because all three followers 32 are engaged in slots of the same inclination in one coupled ring, the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism, by equal radial increments, for as long as the ring turns. The jaw pads therefore close on the pipe together and the frame takes up a position centered on the pipe.

At its inner end each jaw carriage 30 carries a jaw pad 40. The jaw pad 40 is pivotally mounted on the jaw carriage 30 and has a concave bearing face directed inwardly of the frame. Because the jaw pad 40 is free to pivot on the jaw carriage 30, the concave bearing face aligns itself with the outer surface of the pipe as it lands, and the contact is distributed along the face instead of being taken at one edge of it. The same concave bearing face therefore seats on pipes of different diameters, and no insert dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter is required. The bearing face may be faced or lined with a material chosen for the pipe to be gripped, for example a material softer than the pipe surface where a coated or thin walled pipe is to be clamped.

A carriage return spring 44 acts on each jaw carriage 30 and biases the jaw carriage 30 radially outward. In the illustrated embodiment the carriage return spring 44 is a compression spring seated between an abutment of the radial guide 38 and a shoulder of the jaw carriage 30. When the latch 16 is released and the drive from the latch to the ring drive face 36 is removed, the carriage return springs 44 push the jaw carriages 30 outward, the followers 32 bear on the opposite sides of their oblique slots 34, and the coupled ring is turned back through its stroke. The jaws are thus retracted from the pipe by the same synchronized path, and the clamp 100 is left with its jaw carriages 30 retracted and ready for the next installation. Retraction of the jaw carriages 30 also clears the jaw pads 40 from the pipe before the frame halves are swung apart, so that the pipe surface is not scraped by a jaw pad 40 that is still bearing on it.

The latch and the force-limiting drive train

FIG. 4 shows the latch 16 in fragmentary section. The latch 16 includes a latch housing 58 mounted on the frame at the latch end, a latch handle 50 pivotally mounted on the latch housing 58, a wedge 52 movable in the latch housing 58, and a force-limiting spring stack 54 in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52. The wedge 52 is positioned so that its inclined face bears on the ring drive face 36 of the segmented cam ring 20.

The latch 16 has two engaged positions. In a first position, the latch 16 holds the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 closed around the pipe 90 but does not clamp it: the frame is captive on the pipe 90 and cannot fall away, while the jaw carriages 30 remain retracted under their carriage return springs 44 and the clamp 100 can still be slid or turned along the pipe 90 to its intended position. In a second, over-center position, the latch handle 50 has been carried past the point of maximum resistance, and the reaction transmitted back from the wedge 52 through the force-limiting spring stack 54 acts to hold the latch handle 50 in the second position rather than to open it, so that the latch 16 stays closed without a separate securing element. Movement of the latch handle 50 from the first position to the second position advances the wedge 52 against the ring drive face 36. The inclined face of the wedge 52 converts that advance into circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the coupled ring turns through its limited stroke, the extent of the stroke being set by the travel of the wedge 52 between the first and second positions of the latch 16.

The force-limiting spring stack 54 answers the problem of what becomes of the operator's remaining handle travel. The jaw pads 40 land on the pipe 90 at some point in the stroke that depends on the diameter of the pipe 90, and the latch handle 50 has still to be carried into its over-center position. If the drive train from the latch handle 50 to the wedge 52 were rigid, that remaining travel would be taken up by whatever part of the assembly yielded first, in practice by driving one jaw farther into the pipe 90 than the others and loading it far more heavily. Here the force-limiting spring stack 54 is the most compliant element of the drive train once the jaw pads 40 are seated. Additional travel of the latch handle 50 after all three jaw pads 40 have contacted the pipe 90 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than forcing one jaw carriage 30 farther inward than the others, and the clamping force delivered at the jaw pads 40 is accordingly determined by the compression of the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than by how hard the operator pulls the latch handle 50. The force-limiting spring stack 54 comprises one or more resilient elements arranged in a stack whose combined rate and travel are chosen so that the stack is stiff enough to carry the load required to advance the jaw carriages 30 to the pipe 90, and yielding enough to absorb the remaining travel of the latch handle 50 over the intended range of pipe diameters.

An indicator pin 56 is coupled to the force-limiting spring stack 54 and projects from the latch housing 58. As the force-limiting spring stack 54 compresses, the indicator pin 56 moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing 58, and the position of the indicator pin 56 with respect to that fixed edge shows the operator when the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered a predetermined compression range. The predetermined compression range is the range of stack compression that corresponds to the clamping force for which the clamp 100 is intended. The indicator pin 56 therefore reports clamp loading mechanically, at the clamp itself and without any separate instrument, and what it reports is the state of the force-limiting spring stack 54. It is not a measurement of the diameter of the pipe 90 and is not derived from the position of the jaw carriages 30: a large pipe and a small pipe seat the jaw pads 40 at different points in the stroke of the coupled ring, but the indicator pin 56 shows the same predetermined compression range in each case when the same clamping force has been reached.

The first cam ring segment 22 stays with the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 stays with the second frame half 12, and the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are separated. The wedge 52 is driven against the ring drive face 36, the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the sides of the three oblique slots 34 drive the three followers 32, and the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism until the pivoting jaw pads 40 seat on the pipe 90. The remaining travel of the latch handle 50 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54, and the operator watches the indicator pin 56 move relative to the fixed edge of the latch housing 58 and so sees that the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered the predetermined compression range. The latch 16 is left in the over-center position and the clamp 100 is loaded on the pipe 90.

To remove the clamp 100, the operator releases the latch 16. The latch handle 50 comes back over center, the wedge 52 retreats from the ring drive face 36, and the force-limiting spring stack 54 is unloaded. The carriage return springs 44 then push the jaw carriages 30 radially outward, turning the coupled ring back through its stroke by way of the followers 32 in the oblique slots 34, so that all three jaw pads 40 lift from the pipe 90 together. Only then are the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 swung apart about the hinge 14 and the clamp 100 taken off the pipe 90. The clamp 100 is undamaged by the cycle and may be installed again on the same pipe or on a pipe of a different diameter within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

Variations

The frame halves, the segmented cam ring 20, the jaw carriages 30, and the latch 16 may be made of any materials having the strength and stiffness required for the loads to be carried, and the parts that slide on one another, in particular the segmented cam ring 20 in the annular guide 18 and each jaw carriage 30 in its radial guide 38, may be surfaced or lubricated to reduce friction in the drive path. The hinge 14 may be any joint that allows the frame halves to swing apart about a fixed axis at the hinge end while holding the complementary coupling faces 26 in register when the halves are closed. The complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 may take any complementary shapes that transmit circumferential force between the segments and that come into engagement as the frame halves close and separate as they open. The wedge 52 may act on the ring drive face 36 directly or through an intermediate sliding member, provided that the force-limiting spring stack 54 remains in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52. The three oblique slots 34 have the same inclination, so that a given rotation of the coupled ring advances each jaw carriage 30 by the same radial increment. The inclination of the oblique slots 34 sets the ratio between the circumferential stroke of the coupled ring and the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30, and is selected so that the available stroke of the coupled ring produces the radial travel required to span the intended range of pipe diameters, and so that the mechanical advantage at the jaw pads 40 is sufficient for the clamping force to be developed by hand at the latch 16. A shallower inclination gives greater mechanical advantage and less radial travel for a given stroke, and a steeper inclination gives more radial travel and less mechanical advantage.

The segmented cam ring 20 further has a ring drive face 36, shown in FIG. 2 at the latch end of the ring, against which the latch acts as described below. The ring drive face 36 faces circumferentially and is presented at a position on the ring where the latch can reach it, in the illustrated embodiment on the segment adjacent the latch end.

The jaw carriages

FIG. 3 is a fragmentary sectional view through one jaw carriage 30. The frame is channeled to form an annular guide 18 that receives the segmented cam ring 20 and retains it against radial and axial displacement while permitting it to move circumferentially. The annular guide 18 is formed in both frame halves, one arcuate portion of the annular guide 18 in each frame half, and the two arcuate portions register with one another in the closed condition to form a continuous annular path in which the coupled ring turns.

The frame is further formed with a radial guide 38 at the position of each jaw carriage 30. Each jaw carriage 30 is received in a respective radial guide 38 and is constrained by the radial guide 38 to move radially with respect to the frame. Each jaw carriage 30 carries a follower 32 that projects from the jaw carriage 30 into a respective one of the oblique slots 34 of the segmented cam ring 20. The follower 32 may be a pin, a post, a roller, or a like projection able to bear against the sides of the oblique slot 34.

The follower 32 is constrained in two ways at once. The radial guide 38 prevents the jaw carriage 30, and therefore the follower 32, from moving circumferentially, while the oblique slot 34 confines the follower 32 to a path that is inclined to the radial direction. When the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the side of each oblique slot 34 bears on the corresponding follower 32 and drives it, and with it the jaw carriage 30, radially inward along the radial guide 38. Because all three followers 32 are engaged in slots of the same inclination in one coupled ring, the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism, by equal radial increments, for as long as the ring turns. The jaw pads therefore close on the pipe together and the frame takes up a position centered on the pipe.

At its inner end each jaw carriage 30 carries a jaw pad 40. The jaw pad 40 is pivotally mounted on the jaw carriage 30 and has a concave bearing face directed inwardly of the frame. Because the jaw pad 40 is free to pivot on the jaw carriage 30, the concave bearing face aligns itself with the outer surface of the pipe as it lands, and the contact is distributed along the face instead of being taken at one edge of it. The same concave bearing face therefore seats on pipes of different diameters, and no insert dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter is required. The bearing face may be faced or lined with a material chosen for the pipe to be gripped, for example a material softer than the pipe surface where a coated or thin walled pipe is to be clamped.

A carriage return spring 44 acts on each jaw carriage 30 and biases the jaw carriage 30 radially outward. In the illustrated embodiment the carriage return spring 44 is a compression spring seated between an abutment of the radial guide 38 and a shoulder of the jaw carriage 30. When the latch 16 is released and the drive from the latch to the ring drive face 36 is removed, the carriage return springs 44 push the jaw carriages 30 outward, the followers 32 bear on the opposite sides of their oblique slots 34, and the coupled ring is turned back through its stroke. FIG. 4 shows the latch 16 in fragmentary section. The latch 16 includes a latch housing 58 mounted on the frame at the latch end, a latch handle 50 pivotally mounted on the latch housing 58, a wedge 52 movable in the latch housing 58, and a force-limiting spring stack 54 in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52. The wedge 52 is positioned so that its inclined face bears on the ring drive face 36 of the segmented cam ring 20.

The latch 16 has two engaged positions. In a first position, the latch 16 holds the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 closed around the pipe 90 but does not clamp it: the frame is captive on the pipe 90 and cannot fall away, while the jaw carriages 30 remain retracted under their carriage return springs 44 and the clamp 100 can still be slid or turned along the pipe 90 to its intended position. In a second, over-center position, the latch handle 50 has been carried past the point of maximum resistance, and the reaction transmitted back from the wedge 52 through the force-limiting spring stack 54 acts to hold the latch handle 50 in the second position rather than to open it, so that the latch 16 stays closed without a separate securing element. Movement of the latch handle 50 from the first position to the second position advances the wedge 52 against the ring drive face 36. The inclined face of the wedge 52 converts that advance into circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the coupled ring turns through its limited stroke, the extent of the stroke being set by the travel of the wedge 52 between the first and second positions of the latch 16.

The force-limiting spring stack 54 answers the problem of what becomes of the operator's remaining handle travel. The jaw pads 40 land on the pipe 90 at some point in the stroke that depends on the diameter of the pipe 90, and the latch handle 50 has still to be carried into its over-center position. If the drive train from the latch handle 50 to the wedge 52 were rigid, that remaining travel would be taken up by whatever part of the assembly yielded first, in practice by driving one jaw farther into the pipe 90 than the others and loading it far more heavily. Here the force-limiting spring stack 54 is the most compliant element of the drive train once the jaw pads 40 are seated. Additional travel of the latch handle 50 after all three jaw pads 40 have contacted the pipe 90 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than forcing one jaw carriage 30 farther inward than the others, and the clamping force delivered at the jaw pads 40 is accordingly determined by the compression of the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than by how hard the operator pulls the latch handle 50. The force-limiting spring stack 54 comprises one or more resilient elements arranged in a stack whose combined rate and travel are chosen so that the stack is stiff enough to carry the load required to advance the jaw carriages 30 to the pipe 90, and yielding enough to absorb the remaining travel of the latch handle 50 over the intended range of pipe diameters.

An indicator pin 56 is coupled to the force-limiting spring stack 54 and projects from the latch housing 58. As the force-limiting spring stack 54 compresses, the indicator pin 56 moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing 58, and the position of the indicator pin 56 with respect to that fixed edge shows the operator when the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered a predetermined compression range. The predetermined compression range is the range of stack compression that corresponds to the clamping force for which the clamp 100 is intended. The indicator pin 56 therefore reports clamp loading mechanically, at the clamp itself and without any separate instrument, and what it reports is the state of the force-limiting spring stack 54. It is not a measurement of the diameter of the pipe 90 and is not derived from the position of the jaw carriages 30: a large pipe and a small pipe seat the jaw pads 40 at different points in the stroke of the coupled ring, but the indicator pin 56 shows the same predetermined compression range in each case when the same clamping force has been reached.

Operation

To install the clamp 100 on a pipe 90, the operator opens the latch 16 and swings the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 apart about the hinge 14. The first cam ring segment 22 stays with the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 stays with the second frame half 12, and the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are separated. The operator places the frame halves around the pipe 90 from the side and closes them about the hinge 14. Closing the frame halves brings the complementary coupling faces 26 into engagement at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 into engagement at the latch end, coupling the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 into the coupled ring within the annular guide 18.

The operator then moves the latch 16 to its first position, in which the frame is held around the pipe 90 without clamping and can still be positioned along the pipe 90. When the clamp 100 is where it is wanted, the operator moves the latch handle 50 to the second, over-center position. The wedge 52 is driven against the ring drive face 36, the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the sides of the three oblique slots 34 drive the three followers 32, and the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism until the pivoting jaw pads 40 seat on the pipe 90. The remaining travel of the latch handle 50 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54, and the operator watches the indicator pin 56 move relative to the fixed edge of the latch housing 58 and so sees that the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered the predetermined compression range. To remove the clamp 100, the operator releases the latch 16. The latch handle 50 comes back over center, the wedge 52 retreats from the ring drive face 36, and the force-limiting spring stack 54 is unloaded. The frame halves, the segmented cam ring 20, the jaw carriages 30, and the latch 16 may be made of any materials having the strength and stiffness required for the loads to be carried, and the parts that slide on one another, in particular the segmented cam ring 20 in the annular guide 18 and each jaw carriage 30 in its radial guide 38, may be surfaced or lubricated to reduce friction in the drive path.
