The following description of embodiments refers to the accompanying drawings. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout. Terms of direction are used with respect to the frame of the clamp: the axis of the frame is the axis about which the frame is annular in the closed condition and with which the axis of a clamped pipe substantially coincides, "inward" and "radially inward" mean toward that axis, "outward" and "radially outward" mean away from it, and "circumferential" means about that axis. These terms describe relationships within the clamp and do not require the clamp to be used in any particular attitude.

Overall arrangement

FIG. 1 shows a split pipe clamp 100 in the closed condition around a pipe 90. The clamp 100 has a first frame half 10 and a second frame half 12. Each of the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 is semicircular, and the two frame halves together surround the pipe 90. The first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are joined at one end, referred to as the hinge end, by a hinge 14, and are releasably joined at the other end, referred to as the latch end, by a releasable latch 16. The hinge 14 permits the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 to be swung apart far enough for the clamp 100 to be passed sideways onto a pipe 90 that is already installed, so that the clamp 100 need not be threaded over a free end of the pipe 90. When the frame halves are brought together and the latch 16 is engaged, the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 define a frame that is annular about the axis of the clamp 100.

Three jaw carriages 30 are distributed around the frame in the closed condition, so that the three jaw carriages 30 approach the pipe 90 from three different directions. Each jaw carriage 30 moves radially with respect to the frame and carries at its inner end a jaw pad 40, which is described below in connection with FIG. 3. The jaw pads 40 carried at the inner ends of the three jaw carriages 30 bear on the pipe 90 when the clamp 100 is clamped. The clamp 100 does not require an insert dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter, and the same clamp 100 serves pipes of different diameters within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

The frame may carry a mounting boss 70 outside the annular guide 18 described below, as shown in FIG. 5. The mounting boss 70 supports a sensor, a tool, or a conduit that is to be held on the pipe 90 by the clamp 100. The mounting boss 70 is connected neither to the segmented cam ring 20 nor to any jaw carriage 30 and does not participate in the synchronization of the jaw carriages 30. Equipment carried at the mounting boss 70 therefore lies outside the drive path by which the jaws are advanced. The mounting boss 70 is an optional feature of the clamp 100 and may be omitted.

The segmented cam ring

FIG. 2 shows the segmented cam ring 20 of the clamp 100, drawn removed from the frame with its segments in the coupled condition. The segmented cam ring 20 comprises a first cam ring segment 22 and a second cam ring segment 24. The first cam ring segment 22 is carried by the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 is carried by the second frame half 12, so that each frame half carries one segment of the ring and each segment travels with its own frame half when the clamp 100 is opened.

The first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 meet at two places, one at the hinge end and one at the latch end. At the hinge end the two segments have complementary coupling faces 26, and at the latch end they have complementary coupling faces 28. The complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are circumferentially facing drive faces, each pair being shaped so that one segment can transmit circumferential force to the other through the joint. The faces are brought into engagement by the same motion that closes the frame halves: as the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are swung together about the hinge 14 and the latch 16 is engaged, the complementary coupling faces 26 close on one another at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 close on one another at the latch end.

Coupling the segments in this way solves a problem created by splitting the clamp. A clamp that must open from the side cannot carry a continuous drive ring across the split, and a divided drive must otherwise be operated separately in each half, with the result that the two halves advance their jaws by amounts that are not fixed relative to one another. Here the division of the ring is undone by the act of closing the clamp. In the closed condition the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 are coupled at both ends and rotate together in the annular guide as a coupled ring, and a circumferential input applied to either segment is carried around the whole ring. One input, applied at one point on one frame half, therefore reaches every jaw carriage 30 through a single kinematic element, and the relationship between the jaw carriages 30 is set by the geometry of the ring rather than by the way the clamp is operated. When the latch 16 is released and the frame halves are swung apart, the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 separate and each segment stays with its own frame half, so that the coupling is made and broken automatically with each use and requires no separate assembly step.

The segmented cam ring 20 has three oblique slots 34, one for each jaw carriage 30. Each oblique slot 34 passes through the segmented cam ring 20 and is inclined to the radial direction of the frame at the circumferential position of that slot, so that circumferential movement of the ring produces a radial displacement of anything constrained to follow the slot. The three oblique slots 34 have the same inclination, so that a given rotation of the coupled ring advances each jaw carriage 30 by the same radial increment. The inclination of the oblique slots 34 sets the ratio between the circumferential stroke of the coupled ring and the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

The segmented cam ring 20 further has a ring drive face 36, shown in FIG. 2 at the latch end of the ring, against which the latch acts as described below. The ring drive face 36 is presented at a position on the ring that the wedge of the latch can reach, in the illustrated embodiment on the segment adjacent the latch end, and it lies at an inclination to the direction in which that wedge advances, so that advance of the wedge moves the segmented cam ring 20 circumferentially.

The jaw carriages

FIG. 3 is a fragmentary sectional view through one jaw carriage 30. The frame is channeled to form the annular guide 18, which receives the segmented cam ring 20 and retains it against radial and axial displacement while permitting it to move circumferentially. The annular guide 18 is formed in both frame halves, one arcuate portion of the annular guide 18 in each frame half, and the two arcuate portions register with one another in the closed condition to form a continuous annular path in which the coupled ring turns.

The frame is further formed with a radial guide 38 at the position of each jaw carriage 30. Each jaw carriage 30 is received in a respective radial guide 38 and is constrained by the radial guide 38 to move radially with respect to the frame. Each jaw carriage 30 carries a follower 32 that projects from the jaw carriage 30 into a respective one of the oblique slots 34 of the segmented cam ring 20. The follower 32 bears against the sides of the oblique slot 34.

The follower 32 is constrained in two ways at once. The radial guide 38 prevents the jaw carriage 30, and therefore the follower 32, from moving circumferentially, while the oblique slot 34 confines the follower 32 to a path that is inclined to the radial direction. When the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the side of each oblique slot 34 bears on the corresponding follower 32 and drives it, and with it the jaw carriage 30, radially inward along the radial guide 38. Because all three followers 32 are engaged in slots of the same inclination in one coupled ring, the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism, by equal radial increments, for as long as the ring turns. The jaw pads therefore close on the pipe together.

At its inner end each jaw carriage 30 carries a jaw pad 40. The jaw pad 40 is pivotally mounted on the jaw carriage 30 and has a concave bearing face directed inwardly of the frame. Because the jaw pad 40 is free to pivot on the jaw carriage 30, the concave bearing face aligns itself with the outer surface of the pipe as it lands, and the contact is distributed along the face instead of being taken at one edge of it. The same concave bearing face therefore seats on pipes of different diameters, and no insert dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter is required.

A carriage return spring 44 acts between each jaw carriage 30 and the frame so as to urge that jaw carriage 30 radially outward. When the latch 16 is released and the drive from the latch to the ring drive face 36 is removed, the carriage return springs 44 push the jaw carriages 30 outward, the followers 32 bear on the opposite sides of their oblique slots 34, and the coupled ring is turned back through its stroke. The jaws are thus retracted from the pipe by the same synchronized path, and the clamp 100 is left with its jaw carriages 30 retracted and ready for the next installation. Retraction of the jaw carriages 30 also clears the jaw pads 40 from the pipe before the frame halves are swung apart, so that the pipe surface is not scraped by a jaw pad 40 that is still bearing on it.

The latch and the force-limiting drive train

FIG. 4 shows the latch 16 in fragmentary section. The latch 16 includes a latch housing 58 mounted on the frame at the latch end, a latch handle 50 pivotally mounted on the latch housing 58, a wedge 52 movable in the latch housing 58, and a force-limiting spring stack 54 in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52. The wedge 52 is positioned so that its inclined face bears on the ring drive face 36 of the segmented cam ring 20.

The latch 16 has two engaged positions. In a first position, the latch 16 holds the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 closed around the pipe 90 but does not clamp it: the frame is captive on the pipe 90 and cannot fall away, while the jaw carriages 30 remain retracted under their carriage return springs 44 and the clamp 100 can still be slid or turned along the pipe 90 to its intended position. In a second, over-center position, the latch handle 50 has been carried past the point of maximum resistance, and the reaction transmitted back from the wedge 52 through the force-limiting spring stack 54 acts to hold the latch handle 50 in the second position rather than to open it, so that the latch 16 stays closed without a separate securing element. Movement of the latch handle 50 from the first position to the second position advances the wedge 52 against the ring drive face 36. The inclined face of the wedge 52 converts that advance into circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the coupled ring turns through its limited stroke, the extent of the stroke being set by the travel of the wedge 52 between the first and second positions of the latch 16.

The force-limiting spring stack 54 answers the problem of what becomes of the operator's remaining handle travel. The jaw pads 40 land on the pipe 90 at some point in the stroke that depends on the diameter of the pipe 90, and the latch handle 50 has still to be carried into its over-center position. If the drive train from the latch handle 50 to the wedge 52 were rigid, that remaining travel would be taken up by whatever part of the assembly yielded first, in practice by driving one jaw farther into the pipe 90 than the others and loading it far more heavily. Here the force-limiting spring stack 54 is the most compliant element of the drive train once the jaw pads 40 are seated. Additional travel of the latch handle 50 after all three jaw pads 40 have contacted the pipe 90 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than forcing one jaw carriage 30 farther inward than the others, and the clamping force delivered at the jaw pads 40 is accordingly determined by the compression of the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than by how hard the operator pulls the latch handle 50. The force-limiting spring stack 54 comprises one or more resilient elements arranged in a stack whose combined rate and travel are chosen so that the stack is stiff enough to carry the load required to advance the jaw carriages 30 to the pipe 90, and yielding enough to absorb the remaining travel of the latch handle 50 over the intended range of pipe diameters.

An indicator pin 56 is coupled to the force-limiting spring stack 54 and projects from the latch housing 58. As the force-limiting spring stack 54 compresses, the indicator pin 56 moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing 58, and the position of the indicator pin 56 with respect to that fixed edge shows the operator when the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered a predetermined compression range. The predetermined compression range is the range of stack compression that corresponds to the clamping force for which the clamp 100 is intended. The indicator pin 56 therefore reports clamp loading mechanically, at the clamp itself and without any separate instrument, and what it reports is the state of the force-limiting spring stack 54. It is not a measurement of the diameter of the pipe 90 and is not derived from the position of the jaw carriages 30: a large pipe and a small pipe seat the jaw pads 40 at different points in the stroke of the coupled ring, but the indicator pin 56 shows the same predetermined compression range in each case when the same clamping force has been reached.

Operation

To install the clamp 100 on a pipe 90, the operator opens the latch 16 and swings the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 apart about the hinge 14. The first cam ring segment 22 stays with the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 stays with the second frame half 12, and the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are separated. The operator places the frame halves around the pipe 90 from the side and closes them about the hinge 14. Closing the frame halves brings the complementary coupling faces 26 into engagement at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 into engagement at the latch end, coupling the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 into the coupled ring within the annular guide 18.

The operator then moves the latch 16 to its first position, in which the frame is held around the pipe 90 without clamping and can still be positioned along the pipe 90. When the clamp 100 is where it is wanted, the operator moves the latch handle 50 to the second, over-center position. The wedge 52 is driven against the ring drive face 36, the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the sides of the three oblique slots 34 drive the three followers 32, and the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism until the pivoting jaw pads 40 seat on the pipe 90. The remaining travel of the latch handle 50 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54, and the operator watches the indicator pin 56 move relative to the fixed edge of the latch housing 58 and so sees that the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered the predetermined compression range. The latch 16 is left in the over-center position and the clamp 100 is loaded on the pipe 90.

To remove the clamp 100, the operator releases the latch 16. The latch handle 50 comes back over center, the wedge 52 retreats from the ring drive face 36, and the force-limiting spring stack 54 is unloaded. The carriage return springs 44 then push the jaw carriages 30 radially outward, turning the coupled ring back through its stroke by way of the followers 32 in the oblique slots 34, so that all three jaw pads 40 lift from the pipe 90 together. Only then are the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 swung apart about the hinge 14 and the clamp 100 taken off the pipe 90. The clamp 100 is undamaged by the cycle and may be installed again on the same pipe or on a pipe of a different diameter within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

Variations

The frame halves, the segmented cam ring 20, the jaw carriages 30, and the latch 16 may be made of any materials having the strength and stiffness required for the loads to be carried, and the parts that slide on one another, in particular the segmented cam ring 20 in the annular guide 18 and each jaw carriage 30 in its radial guide 38, may be surfaced or lubricated to reduce friction in the drive path. The hinge 14 may be any joint that allows the frame halves to swing apart about a fixed axis at the hinge end while holding the complementary coupling faces 26 in register when the halves are closed. The complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 may take any complementary shapes that transmit circumferential force between the segments and that come into engagement as the frame halves close and separate as they open. The wedge 52 may act on the ring drive face 36 directly or through an intermediate sliding member, provided that the force-limiting spring stack 54 remains in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52. The carriage return spring 44 of each jaw carriage 30 may act between the jaw carriage 30 and its radial guide 38 as illustrated, or elsewhere on the jaw carriage 30, provided that it biases the jaw carriage 30 outward when the drive from the latch 16 is removed.

Features described above in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another, except where the context makes the combination impossible. The embodiments described are illustrative of the disclosed clamp and are not exhaustive of it, and the scope of protection is defined by the claims that follow rather than by any particular embodiment described here.

The jaw pads therefore close on the pipe together.

At its inner end each jaw carriage 30 carries a jaw pad 40. The jaw pad 40 is pivotally mounted on the jaw carriage 30 and has a concave bearing face directed inwardly of the frame. Because the jaw pad 40 is free to pivot on the jaw carriage 30, the concave bearing face aligns itself with the outer surface of the pipe as it lands, and the contact is distributed along the face instead of being taken at one edge of it. The same concave bearing face therefore seats on pipes of different diameters, and no insert dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter is required.

A carriage return spring 44 acts between each jaw carriage 30 and the frame so as to urge that jaw carriage 30 radially outward. When the latch 16 is released and the drive from the latch to the ring drive face 36 is removed, the carriage return springs 44 push the jaw carriages 30 outward, the followers 32 bear on the opposite sides of their oblique slots 34, and the coupled ring is turned back through its stroke. The jaws are thus retracted from the pipe by the same synchronized path, and the clamp 100 is left with its jaw carriages 30 retracted and ready for the next installation. Retraction of the jaw carriages 30 also clears the jaw pads 40 from the pipe before the frame halves are swung apart, so that the pipe surface is not scraped by a jaw pad 40 that is still bearing on it.

The latch and the force-limiting drive train

FIG. 4 shows the latch 16 in fragmentary section. The latch 16 includes a latch housing 58 mounted on the frame at the latch end, a latch handle 50 pivotally mounted on the latch housing 58, a wedge 52 movable in the latch housing 58, and a force-limiting spring stack 54 in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52. The wedge 52 is positioned so that its inclined face bears on the ring drive face 36 of the segmented cam ring 20.

The latch 16 has two engaged positions. In a first position, the latch 16 holds the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 closed around the pipe 90 but does not clamp it: the frame is captive on the pipe 90 and cannot fall away, while the jaw carriages 30 remain retracted under their carriage return springs 44. In a second, over-center position, the latch handle 50 has been carried past the point of maximum resistance, and the reaction transmitted back from the wedge 52 through the force-limiting spring stack 54 acts to hold the latch handle 50 in the second position rather than to open it. Movement of the latch handle 50 from the first position to the second position advances the wedge 52 against the ring drive face 36. The inclined face of the wedge 52 converts that advance into circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the coupled ring turns through its limited stroke, the extent of the stroke being set by the travel of the wedge 52 between the first and second positions of the latch 16.

The force-limiting spring stack 54 answers the problem of what becomes of the operator's remaining handle travel. The jaw pads 40 land on the pipe 90 at some point in the stroke that depends on the diameter of the pipe 90, and the latch handle 50 has still to be carried into its over-center position. If the drive train from the latch handle 50 to the wedge 52 were rigid, that remaining travel would be taken up by whatever part of the assembly yielded first, in practice by driving one jaw farther into the pipe 90 than the others and loading it far more heavily. Here the force-limiting spring stack 54 is the most compliant element of the drive train once the jaw pads 40 are seated. Additional travel of the latch handle 50 after all three jaw pads 40 have contacted the pipe 90 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than forcing one jaw carriage 30 farther inward than the others, and the clamping force delivered at the jaw pads 40 is accordingly determined by the compression of the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than by how hard the operator pulls the latch handle 50. The force-limiting spring stack 54 comprises one or more resilient elements arranged in a stack whose combined rate and travel are chosen so that the stack is stiff enough to carry the load required to advance the jaw carriages 30 to the pipe 90, and yielding enough to absorb the remaining travel of the latch handle 50 over the intended range of pipe diameters.

An indicator pin 56 is coupled to the force-limiting spring stack 54 and projects from the latch housing 58. As the force-limiting spring stack 54 compresses, the indicator pin 56 moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing 58, and the position of the indicator pin 56 with respect to that fixed edge shows the operator when the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered a predetermined compression range. The predetermined compression range is the range of stack compression that corresponds to the clamping force for which the clamp 100 is intended. The indicator pin 56 therefore reports clamp loading mechanically, at the clamp itself and without any separate instrument, and what it reports is the state of the force-limiting spring stack 54. It is not a measurement of the diameter of the pipe 90 and is not derived from the position of the jaw carriages 30: a large pipe and a small pipe seat the jaw pads 40 at different points in the stroke of the coupled ring, but the indicator pin 56 shows the same predetermined compression range in each case when the same clamping force has been reached.

Operation

To install the clamp 100 on a pipe 90, the operator opens the latch 16 and swings the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 apart about the hinge 14. The first cam ring segment 22 stays with the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 stays with the second frame half 12, and the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are separated. The operator places the frame halves around the pipe 90 from the side and closes them about the hinge 14. Closing the frame halves brings the complementary coupling faces 26 into engagement at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 into engagement at the latch end, coupling the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 into the coupled ring within the annular guide 18.

The operator then moves the latch 16 to its first position, in which the frame is held around the pipe 90 without clamping and can still be positioned along the pipe 90. When the clamp 100 is where it is wanted, the operator moves the latch handle 50 to the second, over-center position. The wedge 52 is driven against the ring drive face 36, the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the sides of the three oblique slots 34 drive the three followers 32, and the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism until the pivoting jaw pads 40 seat on the pipe 90. The remaining travel of the latch handle 50 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54, and the operator watches the indicator pin 56 move relative to the fixed edge of the latch housing 58 and so sees that the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered the predetermined compression range. The latch 16 is left in the over-center position and the clamp 100 is loaded on the pipe 90.

To remove the clamp 100, the operator releases the latch 16. The latch handle 50 comes back over center, the wedge 52 retreats from the ring drive face 36, and the force-limiting spring stack 54 is unloaded. The carriage return springs 44 then push the jaw carriages 30 radially outward, turning the coupled ring back through its stroke by way of the followers 32 in the oblique slots 34, so that all three jaw pads 40 lift from the pipe 90 together. Only then are the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 swung apart about the hinge 14 and the clamp 100 taken off the pipe 90. The clamp 100 is undamaged by the cycle and may be installed again on the same pipe or on a pipe of a different diameter within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

Variations

The frame halves, the segmented cam ring 20, the jaw carriages 30, and the latch 16 may be made of any materials having the strength and stiffness required for the loads to be carried, and the parts that slide on one another, in particular the segmented cam ring 20 in the annular guide 18 and each jaw carriage 30 in its radial guide 38, may be surfaced or lubricated to reduce friction in the drive path. The hinge 14 may be any joint that allows the frame halves to swing apart about a fixed axis at the hinge end while holding the complementary coupling faces 26 in register when the halves are closed. The complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 may take any complementary shapes that transmit circumferential force between the segments and that come into engagement as the frame halves close and separate as they open. The wedge 52 may act on the ring drive face 36 directly or through an intermediate sliding member, provided that the force-limiting spring stack 54 remains in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52. The carriage return spring 44 of each jaw carriage 30 may act between the jaw carriage 30 and its radial guide 38 as illustrated, or elsewhere on the jaw carriage 30, provided that it biases the jaw carriage 30 outward when the drive from the latch 16 is removed.

Features described above in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another, except where the context makes the combination impossible. The embodiments described are illustrative of the disclosed clamp and are not exhaustive of it, and the scope of protection is defined by the claims that follow rather than by any particular embodiment described here.

The following description of embodiments refers to the accompanying drawings. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout. Terms of direction are used with respect to the frame of the clamp: the axis of the frame is the axis about which the frame is annular in the closed condition and with which the axis of a clamped pipe substantially coincides, "inward" and "radially inward" mean toward that axis, "outward" and "radially outward" mean away from it, and "circumferential" means about that axis. These terms describe relationships within the clamp and do not require the clamp to be used in any particular attitude.

Overall arrangement

FIG. 1 shows a split pipe clamp 100 in the closed condition around a pipe 90. The clamp 100 has a first frame half 10 and a second frame half 12. Each of the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 is semicircular, and the two frame halves together surround the pipe 90. The first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are joined at one end, referred to as the hinge end, by a hinge 14, and are releasably joined at the other end, referred to as the latch end, by a releasable latch 16. The hinge 14 permits the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 to be swung apart far enough for the clamp 100 to be passed sideways onto a pipe 90 that is already installed, so that the clamp 100 need not be threaded over a free end of the pipe 90. When the frame halves are brought together and the latch 16 is engaged, the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 define a frame that is annular about the axis of the clamp 100.

Three jaw carriages 30 are distributed around the frame in the closed condition, so that the three jaw carriages 30 approach the pipe 90 from three different directions. Each jaw carriage 30 moves radially with respect to the frame and carries at its inner end a jaw pad 40, which is described below in connection with FIG. 3. The jaw pads 40 carried at the inner ends of the three jaw carriages 30 bear on the pipe 90 when the clamp 100 is clamped. The clamp 100 does not require an insert dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter, and the same clamp 100 serves pipes of different diameters within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

The frame may carry a mounting boss 70 outside the annular guide 18 described below, as shown in FIG. 5. The mounting boss 70 supports a sensor, a tool, or a conduit that is to be held on the pipe 90 by the clamp 100. The mounting boss 70 is connected neither to the segmented cam ring 20 nor to any jaw carriage 30 and does not participate in the synchronization of the jaw carriages 30. Equipment carried at the mounting boss 70 therefore lies outside the drive path by which the jaws are advanced. The mounting boss 70 is an optional feature of the clamp 100 and may be omitted.

The segmented cam ring

FIG. 2 shows the segmented cam ring 20 of the clamp 100, drawn removed from the frame with its segments in the coupled condition. The segmented cam ring 20 comprises a first cam ring segment 22 and a second cam ring segment 24. The first cam ring segment 22 is carried by the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 is carried by the second frame half 12, so that each frame half carries one segment of the ring and each segment travels with its own frame half when the clamp 100 is opened.

The first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 meet at two places, one at the hinge end and one at the latch end. At the hinge end the two segments have complementary coupling faces 26, and at the latch end they have complementary coupling faces 28. The complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are circumferentially facing drive faces, each pair being shaped so that one segment can transmit circumferential force to the other through the joint. The faces are brought into engagement by the same motion that closes the frame halves: as the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are swung together about the hinge 14 and the latch 16 is engaged, the complementary coupling faces 26 close on one another at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 close on one another at the latch end.

Coupling the segments in this way solves a problem created by splitting the clamp. A clamp that must open from the side cannot carry a continuous drive ring across the split, and a divided drive must otherwise be operated separately in each half, with the result that the two halves advance their jaws by amounts that are not fixed relative to one another. Here the division of the ring is undone by the act of closing the clamp. In the closed condition the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 are coupled at both ends and rotate together in the annular guide as a coupled ring, and a circumferential input applied to either segment is carried around the whole ring. One input, applied at one point on one frame half, therefore reaches every jaw carriage 30 through a single kinematic element, and the relationship between the jaw carriages 30 is set by the geometry of the ring rather than by the way the clamp is operated. When the latch 16 is released and the frame halves are swung apart, the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 separate and each segment stays with its own frame half, so that the coupling is made and broken automatically with each use and requires no separate assembly step.

The segmented cam ring 20 has three oblique slots 34, one for each jaw carriage 30. Each oblique slot 34 passes through the segmented cam ring 20 and is inclined to the radial direction of the frame at the circumferential position of that slot, so that circumferential movement of the ring produces a radial displacement of anything constrained to follow the slot. The three oblique slots 34 have the same inclination, so that a given rotation of the coupled ring advances each jaw carriage 30 by the same radial increment. The inclination of the oblique slots 34 sets the ratio between the circumferential stroke of the coupled ring and the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

The segmented cam ring 20 further has a ring drive face 36, shown in FIG. 2 at the latch end of the ring, against which the latch acts as described below. The ring drive face 36 is presented at a position on the ring that the wedge of the latch can reach, in the illustrated embodiment on the segment adjacent the latch end, and it lies at an inclination to the direction in which that wedge advances, so that advance of the wedge moves the segmented cam ring 20 circumferentially.

The jaw carriages

FIG. 3 is a fragmentary sectional view through one jaw carriage 30. The frame is channeled to form the annular guide 18, which receives the segmented cam ring 20 and retains it against radial and axial displacement while permitting it to move circumferentially. The annular guide 18 is formed in both frame halves, one arcuate portion of the annular guide 18 in each frame half, and the two arcuate portions register with one another in the closed condition to form a continuous annular path in which the coupled ring turns.

The frame is further formed with a radial guide 38 at the position of each jaw carriage 30. Each jaw carriage 30 is received in a respective radial guide 38 and is constrained by the radial guide 38 to move radially with respect to the frame. Each jaw carriage 30 carries a follower 32 that projects from the jaw carriage 30 into a respective one of the oblique slots 34 of the segmented cam ring 20. The follower 32 bears against the sides of the oblique slot 34.

The follower 32 is constrained in two ways at once. The radial guide 38 prevents the jaw carriage 30, and therefore the follower 32, from moving circumferentially, while the oblique slot 34 confines the follower 32 to a path that is inclined to the radial direction. When the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the side of each oblique slot 34 bears on the corresponding follower 32 and drives it, and with it the jaw carriage 30, radially inward along the radial guide 38. Because all three followers 32 are engaged in slots of the same inclination in one coupled ring, the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism, by equal radial increments, for as long as the ring turns. The jaw pads therefore close on the pipe together.

At its inner end each jaw carriage 30 carries a jaw pad 40. The jaw pad 40 is pivotally mounted on the jaw carriage 30 and has a concave bearing face directed inwardly of the frame. Because the jaw pad 40 is free to pivot on the jaw carriage 30, the concave bearing face aligns itself with the outer surface of the pipe as it lands, and the contact is distributed along the face instead of being taken at one edge of it. The same concave bearing face therefore seats on pipes of different diameters, and no insert dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter is required.

A carriage return spring 44 acts between each jaw carriage 30 and the frame so as to urge that jaw carriage 30 radially outward. When the latch 16 is released and the drive from the latch to the ring drive face 36 is removed, the carriage return springs 44 push the jaw carriages 30 outward, the followers 32 bear on the opposite sides of their oblique slots 34, and the coupled ring is turned back through its stroke. The jaws are thus retracted from the pipe by the same synchronized path, and the clamp 100 is left with its jaw carriages 30 retracted and ready for the next installation. Retraction of the jaw carriages 30 also clears the jaw pads 40 from the pipe before the frame halves are swung apart, so that the pipe surface is not scraped by a jaw pad 40 that is still bearing on it.

The latch and the force-limiting drive train

FIG. 4 shows the latch 16 in fragmentary section. The latch 16 includes a latch housing 58 mounted on the frame at the latch end, a latch handle 50 pivotally mounted on the latch housing 58, a wedge 52 movable in the latch housing 58, and a force-limiting spring stack 54 in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52. The wedge 52 is positioned so that its inclined face bears on the ring drive face 36 of the segmented cam ring 20.

The latch 16 has two engaged positions. In a first position, the latch 16 holds the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 closed around the pipe 90 but does not clamp it: the frame is captive on the pipe 90 and cannot fall away, while the jaw carriages 30 remain retracted under their carriage return springs 44. In a second, over-center position, the latch handle 50 has been carried past the point of maximum resistance, and the reaction transmitted back from the wedge 52 through the force-limiting spring stack 54 acts to hold the latch handle 50 in the second position rather than to open it. Movement of the latch handle 50 from the first position to the second position advances the wedge 52 against the ring drive face 36. The inclined face of the wedge 52 converts that advance into circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the coupled ring turns through its limited stroke, the extent of the stroke being set by the travel of the wedge 52 between the first and second positions of the latch 16.

The force-limiting spring stack 54 answers the problem of what becomes of the operator's remaining handle travel. The jaw pads 40 land on the pipe 90 at some point in the stroke that depends on the diameter of the pipe 90, and the latch handle 50 has still to be carried into its over-center position. If the drive train from the latch handle 50 to the wedge 52 were rigid, that remaining travel would be taken up by whatever part of the assembly yielded first, in practice by driving one jaw farther into the pipe 90 than the others and loading it far more heavily. Here the force-limiting spring stack 54 is the most compliant element of the drive train once the jaw pads 40 are seated. Additional travel of the latch handle 50 after all three jaw pads 40 have contacted the pipe 90 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than forcing one jaw carriage 30 farther inward than the others, and the clamping force delivered at the jaw pads 40 is accordingly determined by the compression of the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than by how hard the operator pulls the latch handle 50. The force-limiting spring stack 54 comprises one or more resilient elements arranged in a stack whose combined rate and travel are chosen so that the stack is stiff enough to carry the load required to advance the jaw carriages 30 to the pipe 90, and yielding enough to absorb the remaining travel of the latch handle 50 over the intended range of pipe diameters.

An indicator pin 56 is coupled to the force-limiting spring stack 54 and projects from the latch housing 58. As the force-limiting spring stack 54 compresses, the indicator pin 56 moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing 58, and the position of the indicator pin 56 with respect to that fixed edge shows the operator when the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered a predetermined compression range. The predetermined compression range is the range of stack compression that corresponds to the clamping force for which the clamp 100 is intended. The indicator pin 56 therefore reports clamp loading mechanically, at the clamp itself and without any separate instrument, and what it reports is the state of the force-limiting spring stack 54. It is not a measurement of the diameter of the pipe 90 and is not derived from the position of the jaw carriages 30: a large pipe and a small pipe seat the jaw pads 40 at different points in the stroke of the coupled ring, but the indicator pin 56 shows the same predetermined compression range in each case when the same clamping force has been reached.

Operation

To install the clamp 100 on a pipe 90, the operator opens the latch 16 and swings the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 apart about the hinge 14. The first cam ring segment 22 stays with the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 stays with the second frame half 12, and the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are separated. The operator places the frame halves around the pipe 90 from the side and closes them about the hinge 14. Closing the frame halves brings the complementary coupling faces 26 into engagement at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 into engagement at the latch end, coupling the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 into the coupled ring within the annular guide 18.

The operator then moves the latch 16 to its first position, in which the frame is held around the pipe 90 without clamping. The operator moves the latch handle 50 to the second, over-center position. The wedge 52 is driven against the ring drive face 36, the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the sides of the three oblique slots 34 drive the three followers 32, and the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism until the pivoting jaw pads 40 seat on the pipe 90. The remaining travel of the latch handle 50 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54, and the operator watches the indicator pin 56 move relative to the fixed edge of the latch housing 58 and so sees that the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered the predetermined compression range. The latch 16 is left in the over-center position and the clamp 100 is loaded on the pipe 90.

To remove the clamp 100, the operator releases the latch 16. The latch handle 50 comes back over center, the wedge 52 retreats from the ring drive face 36, and the force-limiting spring stack 54 is unloaded. The carriage return springs 44 then push the jaw carriages 30 radially outward, turning the coupled ring back through its stroke by way of the followers 32 in the oblique slots 34, so that all three jaw pads 40 lift from the pipe 90 together. Only then are the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 swung apart about the hinge 14 and the clamp 100 taken off the pipe 90. The clamp 100 is undamaged by the cycle and may be installed again on the same pipe or on a pipe of a different diameter within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

Variations

The frame halves, the segmented cam ring 20, the jaw carriages 30, and the latch 16 may be made of any materials having the strength and stiffness required for the loads to be carried, and the parts that slide on one another, in particular the segmented cam ring 20 in the annular guide 18 and each jaw carriage 30 in its radial guide 38, may be surfaced or lubricated to reduce friction in the drive path. The hinge 14 may be any joint that allows the frame halves to swing apart about a fixed axis at the hinge end while holding the complementary coupling faces 26 in register when the halves are closed. The complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 may take any complementary shapes that transmit circumferential force between the segments and that come into engagement as the frame halves close and separate as they open. The wedge 52 may act on the ring drive face 36 directly or through an intermediate sliding member, provided that the force-limiting spring stack 54 remains in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52. The carriage return spring 44 of each jaw carriage 30 may act between the jaw carriage 30 and its radial guide 38 as illustrated, or elsewhere on the jaw carriage 30, provided that it biases the jaw carriage 30 outward when the drive from the latch 16 is removed.

The embodiments described are illustrative of the disclosed clamp and are not exhaustive of it, and the scope of protection is defined by the claims that follow rather than by any particular embodiment described here.

The first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are joined at one end, referred to as the hinge end, by a hinge 14, and are releasably joined at the other end, referred to as the latch end, by a releasable latch 16. The hinge 14 permits the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 to be swung apart far enough for the clamp 100 to be passed sideways onto a pipe 90 that is already installed, so that the clamp 100 need not be threaded over a free end of the pipe 90. When the frame halves are brought together and the latch 16 is engaged, the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 define a frame that is annular about the axis of the clamp 100.

Three jaw carriages 30 are distributed around the frame in the closed condition, so that the three jaw carriages 30 approach the pipe 90 from three different directions. Each jaw carriage 30 moves radially with respect to the frame and carries at its inner end a jaw pad 40, which is described below in connection with FIG. 3. The jaw pads 40 carried at the inner ends of the three jaw carriages 30 bear on the pipe 90 when the clamp 100 is clamped. The clamp 100 does not require an insert dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter, and the same clamp 100 serves pipes of different diameters within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

The frame may carry a mounting boss 70 outside the annular guide 18 described below, as shown in FIG. 5. The mounting boss 70 supports a sensor, a tool, or a conduit that is to be held on the pipe 90 by the clamp 100. The mounting boss 70 is connected neither to the segmented cam ring 20 nor to any jaw carriage 30 and does not participate in the synchronization of the jaw carriages 30. Equipment carried at the mounting boss 70 therefore lies outside the drive path by which the jaws are advanced. The mounting boss 70 is an optional feature of the clamp 100 and may be omitted.

The segmented cam ring

FIG. 2 shows the segmented cam ring 20 of the clamp 100, drawn removed from the frame with its segments in the coupled condition. The segmented cam ring 20 comprises a first cam ring segment 22 and a second cam ring segment 24. The first cam ring segment 22 is carried by the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 is carried by the second frame half 12, so that each frame half carries one segment of the ring and each segment travels with its own frame half when the clamp 100 is opened.

The first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 meet at two places, one at the hinge end and one at the latch end. At the hinge end the two segments have complementary coupling faces 26, and at the latch end they have complementary coupling faces 28. The complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are circumferentially facing drive faces, each pair being shaped so that one segment can transmit circumferential force to the other through the joint. The faces are brought into engagement by the same motion that closes the frame halves: as the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are swung together about the hinge 14 and the latch 16 is engaged, the complementary coupling faces 26 close on one another at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 close on one another at the latch end.

Coupling the segments in this way solves a problem created by splitting the clamp. A clamp that must open from the side cannot carry a continuous drive ring across the split, and a divided drive must otherwise be operated separately in each half, with the result that the two halves advance their jaws by amounts that are not fixed relative to one another. Here the division of the ring is undone by the act of closing the clamp. In the closed condition the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 are coupled at both ends and rotate together in the annular guide as a coupled ring, and a circumferential input applied to either segment is carried around the whole ring. One input, applied at one point on one frame half, therefore reaches every jaw carriage 30 through a single kinematic element, and the relationship between the jaw carriages 30 is set by the geometry of the ring rather than by the way the clamp is operated. When the latch 16 is released and the frame halves are swung apart, the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 separate and each segment stays with its own frame half, so that the coupling is made and broken automatically with each use and requires no separate assembly step.

The segmented cam ring 20 has three oblique slots 34, one for each jaw carriage 30. Each oblique slot 34 passes through the segmented cam ring 20 and is inclined to the radial direction of the frame at the circumferential position of that slot, so that circumferential movement of the ring produces a radial displacement of anything constrained to follow the slot. The three oblique slots 34 have the same inclination, so that a given rotation of the coupled ring advances each jaw carriage 30 by the same radial increment. The inclination of the oblique slots 34 sets the ratio between the circumferential stroke of the coupled ring and the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

The segmented cam ring 20 further has a ring drive face 36, shown in FIG. 2 at the latch end of the ring, against which the latch acts as described below. The ring drive face 36 is presented at a position on the ring that the wedge of the latch can reach, in the illustrated embodiment on the segment adjacent the latch end, and it lies at an inclination to the direction in which that wedge advances, so that advance of the wedge moves the segmented cam ring 20 circumferentially.

The jaw carriages

FIG. 3 is a fragmentary sectional view through one jaw carriage 30. The frame is channeled to form the annular guide 18, which receives the segmented cam ring 20 and retains it against radial and axial displacement while permitting it to move circumferentially. The annular guide 18 is formed in both frame halves, one arcuate portion of the annular guide 18 in each frame half, and the two arcuate portions register with one another in the closed condition to form a continuous annular path in which the coupled ring turns.

The frame is further formed with a radial guide 38 at the position of each jaw carriage 30. Each jaw carriage 30 is received in a respective radial guide 38 and is constrained by the radial guide 38 to move radially with respect to the frame. Each jaw carriage 30 carries a follower 32 that projects from the jaw carriage 30 into a respective one of the oblique slots 34 of the segmented cam ring 20. The follower 32 bears against the sides of the oblique slot 34.

The follower 32 is constrained in two ways at once. The radial guide 38 prevents the jaw carriage 30, and therefore the follower 32, from moving circumferentially, while the oblique slot 34 confines the follower 32 to a path that is inclined to the radial direction. When the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the side of each oblique slot 34 bears on the corresponding follower 32 and drives it, and with it the jaw carriage 30, radially inward along the radial guide 38. Because all three followers 32 are engaged in slots of the same inclination in one coupled ring, the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism, by equal radial increments, for as long as the ring turns. The jaw pads therefore close on the pipe together.

At its inner end each jaw carriage 30 carries a jaw pad 40. The jaw pad 40 is pivotally mounted on the jaw carriage 30 and has a concave bearing face directed inwardly of the frame. Because the jaw pad 40 is free to pivot on the jaw carriage 30, the concave bearing face aligns itself with the outer surface of the pipe as it lands, and the contact is distributed along the face instead of being taken at one edge of it. The same concave bearing face therefore seats on pipes of different diameters, and no insert dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter is required.

A carriage return spring 44 acts between each jaw carriage 30 and the frame so as to urge that jaw carriage 30 radially outward. When the latch 16 is released and the drive from the latch to the ring drive face 36 is removed, the carriage return springs 44 push the jaw carriages 30 outward, the followers 32 bear on the opposite sides of their oblique slots 34, and the coupled ring is turned back through its stroke. The jaws are thus retracted from the pipe by the same synchronized path, and the clamp 100 is left with its jaw carriages 30 retracted and ready for the next installation. Retraction of the jaw carriages 30 also clears the jaw pads 40 from the pipe before the frame halves are swung apart, so that the pipe surface is not scraped by a jaw pad 40 that is still bearing on it.

The latch and the force-limiting drive train

FIG. 4 shows the latch 16 in fragmentary section. The latch 16 includes a latch housing 58 mounted on the frame at the latch end, a latch handle 50 pivotally mounted on the latch housing 58, a wedge 52 movable in the latch housing 58, and a force-limiting spring stack 54 in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52. The wedge 52 is positioned so that its inclined face bears on the ring drive face 36 of the segmented cam ring 20.

The latch 16 has two engaged positions. In a first position, the latch 16 holds the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 closed around the pipe 90 but does not clamp it: the frame is captive on the pipe 90 and cannot fall away, while the jaw carriages 30 remain retracted under their carriage return springs 44. In a second, over-center position, the latch handle 50 has been carried past the point of maximum resistance, and the reaction transmitted back from the wedge 52 through the force-limiting spring stack 54 acts to hold the latch handle 50 in the second position rather than to open it. Movement of the latch handle 50 from the first position to the second position advances the wedge 52 against the ring drive face 36. The inclined face of the wedge 52 converts that advance into circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the coupled ring turns through its limited stroke, the extent of the stroke being set by the travel of the wedge 52 between the first and second positions of the latch 16.

The force-limiting spring stack 54 answers the problem of what becomes of the operator's remaining handle travel. The jaw pads 40 land on the pipe 90 at some point in the stroke that depends on the diameter of the pipe 90, and the latch handle 50 has still to be carried into its over-center position. If the drive train from the latch handle 50 to the wedge 52 were rigid, that remaining travel would be taken up by whatever part of the assembly yielded first, in practice by driving one jaw farther into the pipe 90 than the others and loading it far more heavily. Here the force-limiting spring stack 54 is the most compliant element of the drive train once the jaw pads 40 are seated. Additional travel of the latch handle 50 after all three jaw pads 40 have contacted the pipe 90 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than forcing one jaw carriage 30 farther inward than the others, and the clamping force delivered at the jaw pads 40 is accordingly determined by the compression of the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than by how hard the operator pulls the latch handle 50. The force-limiting spring stack 54 comprises one or more resilient elements arranged in a stack whose combined rate and travel are chosen so that the stack is stiff enough to carry the load required to advance the jaw carriages 30 to the pipe 90, and yielding enough to absorb the remaining travel of the latch handle 50 over the intended range of pipe diameters.

An indicator pin 56 is coupled to the force-limiting spring stack 54 and projects from the latch housing 58. As the force-limiting spring stack 54 compresses, the indicator pin 56 moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing 58, and the position of the indicator pin 56 with respect to that fixed edge shows the operator when the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered a predetermined compression range. The predetermined compression range is the range of stack compression that corresponds to the clamping force for which the clamp 100 is intended. The indicator pin 56 therefore reports clamp loading mechanically, at the clamp itself and without any separate instrument, and what it reports is the state of the force-limiting spring stack 54. It is not a measurement of the diameter of the pipe 90 and is not derived from the position of the jaw carriages 30: a large pipe and a small pipe seat the jaw pads 40 at different points in the stroke of the coupled ring, but the indicator pin 56 shows the same predetermined compression range in each case when the same clamping force has been reached.

Operation

To install the clamp 100 on a pipe 90, the operator opens the latch 16 and swings the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 apart about the hinge 14. The first cam ring segment 22 stays with the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 stays with the second frame half 12, and the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are separated. The operator places the frame halves around the pipe 90 from the side and closes them about the hinge 14. Closing the frame halves brings the complementary coupling faces 26 into engagement at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 into engagement at the latch end, coupling the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 into the coupled ring within the annular guide 18.

The operator then moves the latch 16 to its first position, in which the frame is held around the pipe 90 without clamping. The operator moves the latch handle 50 to the second, over-center position. The wedge 52 is driven against the ring drive face 36, the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the sides of the three oblique slots 34 drive the three followers 32, and the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism until the pivoting jaw pads 40 seat on the pipe 90. The remaining travel of the latch handle 50 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54, and the operator watches the indicator pin 56 move relative to the fixed edge of the latch housing 58 and so sees that the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered the predetermined compression range. The latch 16 is left in the over-center position and the clamp 100 is loaded on the pipe 90.

To remove the clamp 100, the operator releases the latch 16. The latch handle 50 comes back over center, the wedge 52 retreats from the ring drive face 36, and the force-limiting spring stack 54 is unloaded. The carriage return springs 44 then push the jaw carriages 30 radially outward, turning the coupled ring back through its stroke by way of the followers 32 in the oblique slots 34, so that all three jaw pads 40 lift from the pipe 90 together. Only then are the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 swung apart about the hinge 14 and the clamp 100 taken off the pipe 90. The clamp 100 is undamaged by the cycle and may be installed again on the same pipe or on a pipe of a different diameter within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

Variations

The frame halves, the segmented cam ring 20, the jaw carriages 30, and the latch 16 may be made of any materials having the strength and stiffness required for the loads to be carried. The hinge 14 may be any joint that allows the frame halves to swing apart about a fixed axis at the hinge end while holding the complementary coupling faces 26 in register when the halves are closed. The complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 may take any complementary shapes that transmit circumferential force between the segments and that come into engagement as the frame halves close and separate as they open. The wedge 52 may act on the ring drive face 36 directly or through an intermediate sliding member, provided that the force-limiting spring stack 54 remains in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52. The carriage return spring 44 of each jaw carriage 30 may act between the jaw carriage 30 and its radial guide 38 as illustrated, or elsewhere on the jaw carriage 30, provided that it biases the jaw carriage 30 outward when the drive from the latch 16 is removed.

Features described above in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another, except where the context makes the combination impossible. The embodiments described are illustrative of the disclosed clamp and are not exhaustive of it, and the scope of protection is defined by the claims that follow rather than by any particular embodiment described here.

A split pipe clamp is disclosed in which the element that advances the gripping jaws is divided with the clamp body but is made continuous again by the act of closing the clamp, so that one latch motion advances every jaw together.

In one aspect, a split pipe clamp comprises a first frame half and a second frame half joined at a hinge end by a hinge and releasably joined at a latch end by a latch. In a closed condition the two frame halves define a frame having an annular guide and three radial guides. Three jaw carriages are each slidable radially in a respective one of the radial guides, and each jaw carriage carries a jaw pad that is pivotally mounted on the jaw carriage and has a concave bearing face directed inwardly of the frame. A segmented cam ring is received in the annular guide and comprises a first cam ring segment carried by the first frame half and a second cam ring segment carried by the second frame half. The cam ring segments have complementary coupling faces at the hinge end and complementary coupling faces at the latch end, and those faces engage one another as the frame halves are closed, so that in the closed condition the two segments move in the annular guide as a coupled ring. Each jaw carriage has a follower received in a respective oblique slot of the segmented cam ring, each oblique slot being inclined to a radial direction of the frame so that rotation of the coupled ring through a stroke advances the three jaw carriages inwardly in synchronism. A wedge movable by the latch bears on a ring drive face of the segmented cam ring, so that movement of the latch toward a closed position rotates the coupled ring through the stroke, and a carriage return spring biases each jaw carriage outwardly so that releasing the latch retracts the jaws.

Because the coupled ring is a single kinematic element spanning both frame halves, the three jaw carriages are not driven independently. One latch motion, applied at one point on one frame half, is distributed by the coupled ring to every jaw carriage, and the jaw pads close on the pipe together. The frame therefore takes up its position on the pipe from the jaws rather than from a bore matched to a nominal pipe size, and the pivoting concave jaw pads seat on the pipe without an insert dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter.

In a further aspect, the latch has a first position in which the frame halves are held around the pipe without clamping and a second, over-center position in which the wedge drives the cam ring and the pipe is clamped, and a force-limiting spring stack lies in the drive train between a latch handle and the wedge. Travel of the handle that remains after all three jaw pads have contacted the pipe compresses the force-limiting spring stack instead of advancing one jaw carriage farther than the others. An indicator pin moves relative to a fixed edge of a latch housing when the force-limiting spring stack enters a predetermined compression range, giving the operator a mechanical report of clamp loading that is produced by the state of the spring stack and not by the diameter of the pipe.

In a further aspect, the frame carries a mounting boss outside the annular guide for supporting a sensor, a tool, or a conduit, the mounting boss being connected neither to the segmented cam ring nor to any jaw carriage, so that equipment carried on the frame is outside the path by which the jaws are synchronized.

In a further aspect, a method of clamping a pipe comprises opening the latch, swinging the frame halves apart about the hinge, placing the frame halves around a pipe, closing the frame halves so that the complementary coupling faces engage and couple the cam ring segments, moving the latch to the first position, and moving the latch to the second, over-center position so that the wedge rotates the coupled ring and the followers advance the three jaw carriages inwardly in synchronism until the jaw pads seat on the pipe. Releasing the latch unloads the force-limiting spring stack and the carriage return springs retract the jaw carriages before the frame halves are opened.

tool_use_result.originalFile:
Equipment is frequently attached to the outside of a pipe after the pipe has been installed. Sensors, small tools, brackets, and lengths of conduit all have to be carried on a pipe that cannot be taken out of service, cannot be lifted, and has no free end over which a closed ring could be threaded. A clamp intended for that duty therefore has to open from the side, close around the pipe, and grip it firmly enough that the carried equipment keeps its position, while remaining removable so that the same clamp can be taken off and used again elsewhere.

A clamp that opens from the side is split into parts, and the split is what makes the gripping problem difficult. Once the clamp body is divided, any drive element that runs around the body is divided with it. Gripping arrangements that answer this by driving the gripping surfaces of each part separately give up the fixed relationship between the two parts of the drive: the two sides of the clamp advance by amounts that depend on how each side is operated, so the clamp tends to settle off center on the pipe, and the load is shared unevenly between the gripping surfaces. Arrangements that instead pull the split body closed on the pipe, in the manner of a band or a two-bolt saddle, transfer the closing force through the joint at the split and rely on the pipe itself to react the closing motion, so the grip depends on how nearly the bore of the clamp matches the outside diameter of the pipe. Such an arrangement is commonly supplied with liners or inserts machined for one nominal pipe size, and a different pipe size calls for a different insert or a different clamp.

Reusable clamping also has to deal with the force the operator applies. A hand lever gives the operator no measure of what has been done to the pipe. When the gripping elements have reached the pipe, further travel of the lever has to go somewhere, and in a rigid drive train it goes into whichever gripping element happens to touch first, so that one gripping surface is loaded far more than the others. Thin walled tube, coated pipe, and lined pipe are all damaged by that kind of concentrated loading, and the operator has no indication that it has occurred. Torque tools and gauges can be added to the installation, but they add a separate instrument to the task and, when they respond to the position of the gripping elements, they report the size of the pipe rather than the force in the grip.

What has been lacking is a split clamp in which the drive that advances the gripping elements is itself restored to a single, continuous element by the act of closing the clamp, in which every gripping element is advanced from that one drive so that the clamp finds the center of the pipe by itself over a range of pipe sizes, and in which the travel remaining in the operator's lever after the gripping elements have landed on the pipe is absorbed within the clamp and reported to the operator as a loading condition rather than as a dimension.
