The following description of embodiments refers to the accompanying drawings. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout. Terms of direction are used with respect to the frame of the clamp: the axis of the frame is the axis about which the frame is annular in the closed condition and with which the axis of a clamped pipe substantially coincides, "inward" and "radially inward" mean toward that axis, "outward" and "radially outward" mean away from it, and "circumferential" means about that axis. These terms describe relationships within the clamp and do not require the clamp to be used in any particular attitude.

Overall arrangement

FIG. 1 shows a split pipe clamp 100 in the closed condition around a pipe 90. The clamp 100 has a first frame half 10 and a second frame half 12. Each of the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 is semicircular, and the two frame halves together surround the pipe 90. The first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are joined at one end, referred to as the hinge end, by a hinge 14, and are releasably joined at the other end, referred to as the latch end, by a releasable latch 16. The hinge 14 permits the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 to be swung apart far enough for the clamp 100 to be passed sideways onto a pipe 90 that is already installed, so that the clamp 100 need not be threaded over a free end of the pipe 90. When the frame halves are brought together and the latch 16 is engaged, the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 define a frame that is annular about the axis of the clamp 100.

Three jaw carriages 30 are distributed around the frame in the closed condition, so that the three jaw carriages 30 approach the pipe 90 from three different directions. Each jaw carriage 30 moves radially with respect to the frame and carries at its inner end a jaw pad 40, which is described below in connection with FIG. 3. The jaw pads 40 carried at the inner ends of the three jaw carriages 30 bear on the pipe 90 when the clamp 100 is clamped. The clamp 100 does not require an insert dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter, and the same clamp 100 serves pipes of different diameters within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

The frame may carry a mounting boss 70 outside the annular guide 18 described below, as shown in FIG. 5. The mounting boss 70 supports a sensor, a tool, or a conduit that is to be held on the pipe 90 by the clamp 100. The mounting boss 70 is connected neither to the segmented cam ring 20 nor to any jaw carriage 30 and does not participate in the synchronization of the jaw carriages 30. Equipment carried at the mounting boss 70 therefore lies outside the drive path by which the jaws are advanced. The mounting boss 70 is an optional feature of the clamp 100 and may be omitted.

The segmented cam ring

FIG. 2 shows the segmented cam ring 20 of the clamp 100, drawn removed from the frame with its segments in the coupled condition. The segmented cam ring 20 comprises a first cam ring segment 22 and a second cam ring segment 24. The first cam ring segment 22 is carried by the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 is carried by the second frame half 12, so that each frame half carries one segment of the ring and each segment travels with its own frame half when the clamp 100 is opened.

The first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 meet at two places, one at the hinge end and one at the latch end. At the hinge end the two segments have complementary coupling faces 26, and at the latch end they have complementary coupling faces 28. The complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are circumferentially facing drive faces, each pair being shaped so that one segment can transmit circumferential force to the other through the joint. The faces are brought into engagement by the same motion that closes the frame halves: as the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are swung together about the hinge 14 and the latch 16 is engaged, the complementary coupling faces 26 close on one another at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 close on one another at the latch end.

Coupling the segments in this way solves a problem created by splitting the clamp. A clamp that must open from the side cannot carry a continuous drive ring across the split, and a divided drive must otherwise be operated separately in each half, with the result that the two halves advance their jaws by amounts that are not fixed relative to one another. Here the division of the ring is undone by the act of closing the clamp. In the closed condition the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 are coupled at both ends and rotate together in the annular guide as a coupled ring, and a circumferential input applied to either segment is carried around the whole ring. One input, applied at one point on one frame half, therefore reaches every jaw carriage 30 through a single kinematic element, and the relationship between the jaw carriages 30 is set by the geometry of the ring rather than by the way the clamp is operated. When the latch 16 is released and the frame halves are swung apart, the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 separate and each segment stays with its own frame half, so that the coupling is made and broken by the closing and opening of the frame halves.

The segmented cam ring 20 has three oblique slots 34, one for each jaw carriage 30. Each oblique slot 34 is inclined to the radial direction of the frame at the circumferential position of that slot, so that rotation of the coupled ring produces inward travel of its jaw carriage 30, the three oblique slots 34 being arranged so that the three jaw carriages 30 travel inwardly in synchronism. The inclination of the oblique slots 34 sets the ratio between the circumferential stroke of the coupled ring and the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

The segmented cam ring 20 further has a ring drive face 36, shown in FIG. 2 at the latch end of the ring, against which the latch acts as described below. The ring drive face 36 is presented at a position on the ring that the wedge of the latch can reach, and it lies at an inclination to the direction in which that wedge advances, so that advance of the wedge moves the segmented cam ring 20 circumferentially.

The jaw carriages

FIG. 3 is a fragmentary sectional view through one jaw carriage 30. The frame is channeled to form the annular guide 18, which receives the segmented cam ring 20. The annular guide 18 retains the first cam ring segment 22 on the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 on the second frame half 12, and permits the coupled ring to move circumferentially.

The frame is further formed with a radial guide 38 at the position of each jaw carriage 30. Each jaw carriage 30 is received in a respective radial guide 38 and is constrained by the radial guide 38 to move radially with respect to the frame. Each jaw carriage 30 carries a follower 32 that projects from the jaw carriage 30 into a respective one of the oblique slots 34 of the segmented cam ring 20. The follower 32 bears against the sides of the oblique slot 34.

The follower 32 is constrained in two ways at once. The radial guide 38 prevents the jaw carriage 30, and therefore the follower 32, from moving circumferentially, while the oblique slot 34 confines the follower 32 to a path that is inclined to the radial direction. When the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the side of each oblique slot 34 bears on the corresponding follower 32 and drives it, and with it the jaw carriage 30, radially inward along the radial guide 38. Because all three followers 32 are engaged in oblique slots 34 of one coupled ring, the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism for as long as the ring turns. The jaw pads 40 therefore close on the pipe together.

At its inner end each jaw carriage 30 carries a jaw pad 40. The jaw pad 40 is pivotally mounted on the jaw carriage 30 and has a concave bearing face directed inwardly of the frame. Because the jaw pad 40 is free to pivot on the jaw carriage 30, the concave bearing face aligns itself with the outer surface of the pipe as it lands. The same concave bearing face therefore seats on pipes of different diameters, and no insert dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter is required.

A carriage return spring 44 acts between each jaw carriage 30 and the frame so as to urge that jaw carriage 30 radially outward. When the latch 16 is released and the drive from the latch to the ring drive face 36 is removed, the carriage return springs 44 push the jaw carriages 30 outward and the jaw pads 40 are retracted from the pipe, and the clamp 100 is left with its jaw carriages 30 retracted and ready for the next installation. Retraction of the jaw carriages 30 clears the jaw pads 40 from the pipe before the frame halves are swung apart.

The latch and the force-limiting drive train

FIG. 4 shows the latch 16 in fragmentary section. The latch 16 includes a latch housing 58 mounted on the frame at the latch end, a latch handle 50 pivotally mounted on the latch housing 58, a wedge 52 movable in the latch housing 58, and a force-limiting spring stack 54 in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52. The wedge 52 is positioned so that its inclined face bears on the ring drive face 36 of the segmented cam ring 20.

The latch 16 has two engaged positions. In a first position, the latch 16 holds the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 closed around the pipe 90 but does not clamp it: the frame is captive on the pipe 90 and cannot fall away, while the jaw carriages 30 remain retracted under their carriage return springs 44. In a second, over-center position, the wedge 52 drives the segmented cam ring 20 and the pipe 90 is clamped. Movement of the latch handle 50 from the first position to the second position advances the wedge 52 against the ring drive face 36. The inclined face of the wedge 52 converts that advance into circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the coupled ring turns through its limited stroke.

The force-limiting spring stack 54 answers the problem of what becomes of the operator's remaining handle travel. The jaw pads 40 land on the pipe 90 at some point in the stroke that depends on the diameter of the pipe 90, and the latch handle 50 has still to be carried into its over-center position. If the drive train from the latch handle 50 to the wedge 52 were rigid, that remaining travel would be taken up by whatever part of the assembly yielded first, in practice by driving one jaw farther into the pipe 90 than the others and loading it far more heavily. Additional travel of the latch handle 50 after all three jaw pads 40 have contacted the pipe 90 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than forcing one jaw carriage 30 farther inward than the others.

An indicator pin 56 is coupled to the force-limiting spring stack 54 and projects from the latch housing 58. As the force-limiting spring stack 54 compresses, the indicator pin 56 moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing 58, and the position of the indicator pin 56 with respect to that fixed edge shows the operator when the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered a predetermined compression range. The predetermined compression range is the range of stack compression that corresponds to the clamping force for which the clamp 100 is intended. The indicator pin 56 therefore reports clamp loading mechanically, and what it reports is the state of the force-limiting spring stack 54. It is not a measurement of the diameter of the pipe 90.

Operation

To install the clamp 100 on a pipe 90, the operator opens the latch 16 and swings the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 apart about the hinge 14. The first cam ring segment 22 stays with the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 stays with the second frame half 12, and the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are separated. The operator places the frame halves around the pipe 90 from the side and closes them about the hinge 14. Closing the frame halves brings the complementary coupling faces 26 into engagement at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 into engagement at the latch end, coupling the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 into the coupled ring within the annular guide 18.

The operator then moves the latch 16 to its first position, in which the frame is held around the pipe 90 without clamping. The operator moves the latch handle 50 to the second, over-center position. The wedge 52 is driven against the ring drive face 36, the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the sides of the three oblique slots 34 drive the three followers 32, and the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism until the pivoting jaw pads 40 seat on the pipe 90. The remaining travel of the latch handle 50 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54, and the operator watches the indicator pin 56 move relative to the fixed edge of the latch housing 58 and so sees that the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered the predetermined compression range. The latch 16 is left in the over-center position and the clamp 100 is loaded on the pipe 90.

To remove the clamp 100, the operator releases the latch 16. The latch handle 50 comes back over center, the wedge 52 retreats from the ring drive face 36, and the force-limiting spring stack 54 is unloaded. The carriage return springs 44 then push the jaw carriages 30 radially outward, so that the jaw pads 40 lift from the pipe 90. Only then are the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 swung apart about the hinge 14 and the clamp 100 taken off the pipe 90. The clamp 100 is undamaged by the cycle and may be installed again on the same pipe or on a pipe of a different diameter within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

Features described above in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another, except where the context makes the combination impossible. The embodiments described are illustrative of the disclosed clamp and are not exhaustive of it, and the scope of protection is defined by the claims that follow rather than by any particular embodiment described here.

input.summary: The application body, claims, numeral table and five figure briefs were already drafted in full, so this turn resolved the three defects the reviewer raised and one truncated line found alongside them. Removed the sentence clause that told the reader what limits the cam-ring stroke (the inventor says only "a limited stroke" and never names a limiting element, and the added clause fought with the force-limiting-stack paragraph that follows). Rewrote the follower-constraint sentence, which had said in one breath that the follower cannot move circumferentially and that it follows a path inclined to the radial direction; it now states that the slot holds the follower at a position along the slot so that circumferential ring movement displaces the follower radially, which is what the rest of the description and claim 1 say. In the FIG. 4 brief, the latch housing and its cavity are now marked as shown schematically and the walls no longer "guide" the wedge, so no undisclosed housing/wedge connection is asserted; the wedge's up-and-down movement is likewise marked schematic. Also completed the FIG. 4 numeral instruction for numeral 16, whose line ended mid-word ("does not designate the wal"), and made "over-centre" read "over-center" to match the specification. No claim, no numeral, no other section was touched. One caution the brief asked me to state plainly: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, and per input/brief.md no prior-art search was run, so the art available to this draft is empty and may well be incomplete. The Background is written from the disclosed problem alone and contains no citations, since there is no key that could honestly be cited; if a search is later run, the Background and the claim ladder should be revisited against whatever it returns.
reasoning: Claim 1 carries its weight on one relationship the inventor calls essential: the cam ring is split with the body, one segment per frame half, and the complementary coupling faces at the hinge end and at the latch end engage as the halves close, so the two segments thereafter rotate as one coupled ring and a single latch input reaches all three followers. That is the coupling-by-closure limitation, and it is what a band clamp, a two-bolt saddle, or a split clamp with independently driven halves does not have. With prior_art/ empty I could not name a reference the feature clears, so I put the technical problem it solves into the Background and into the specification section 'The segmented cam ring' expressly: a side-opening clamp cannot carry a continuous drive ring across the split, and separately driven halves lose the fixed relationship between the two sides. That explanation is now on the page ahead of any argument that needs it.

Claim 1 also recites the force-limiting spring stack in the drive train between latch handle and wedge, doing real work: after all three pads land, remaining handle travel goes into the stack instead of driving one jaw farther than its neighbours. I kept it in claim 1 rather than pushing it to a dependent because the disclosure names it as part of the essential relationship, and it is a second independent point of distinction if the coupling feature is ever met.

Deliberately left out of claim 1: the indicator pin and its predetermined compression range (claims 2, 3, 11, 14), the two latch positions including the over-center position (claims 4, 12), the mounting boss (claim 8 and independent claim 10), the semicircular frame halves and the three-directions distribution (claim 9), and any statement of what bounds the stroke. Claim 1 says only 'a stroke' and 'the stroke'. Each of those is disclosed and each is a fallback worth having, but none is needed to make the clamp work or to state the invention at its broadest.

The reviewer's first two findings are correct and I applied them as written. The stroke-limiting clause was an invented mechanism: the inventor never says what bounds the stroke, and the clause implied the ring always turns the full stroke, which contradicts the very next paragraph where the stack takes up whatever travel remains once the pads land on a given pipe. Nothing in claim 1 or claim 4 depended on it, so deleting it cost no support.

The follower sentence was a genuine kinematic misstatement rather than loose wording. A path inclined to the radial direction has a circumferential component, which the radial guide forbids in the same sentence. What the oblique slot actually constrains is the follower's position along the slot; the ring's circumferential movement is what converts to radial displacement. The corrected sentence now agrees with the following sentence, with claim 1, and with FIG. 3, where the post's upper and lower sides face the sides of the opening.

The third finding is also right, on a narrower ground: the disclosure names the latch housing only as the part carrying the fixed edge against which the indicator pin is read. A three-walled cavity whose walls guide the wedge is a functional connection, not a bare outline, and every other conventional element in the five briefs (hinge, latch block, pivots, spring seats, mounting boss) is marked schematic. I marked the housing and cavity schematic and dropped the guiding function rather than deleting the cavity, because the wedge still needs somewhere to be drawn and the depiction convention must stay confined to the figure brief. The description's neutral 'a wedge 52 movable in the latch housing 58' was left untouched, and nothing was added to the text or claims to match the drawing.

I found one further defect the review did not list: the FIG. 4 numeral instruction for 16 ended mid-word. Left as it stood it would have reached the renderer as an unfinished instruction. I completed it in the sense the fragment was heading, pointing the callout at the latch assembly as a whole rather than at any single wall, which keeps it distinct from numeral 58 on the top wall of the same enclosure.

Independent claims sit in three statutory frames that different parties infringe: the clamp itself (claim 1), the pipe-mounted equipment assembly with a sensor, tool or conduit on the mounting boss (claim 10), which reaches the integrator who ships equipment already on a clamp, and the method of clamping (claim 13), which reaches the operator's sequence. All three trace to disclosed passages; claim 13's final step, continuing the handle into the over-center position after the pads seat, is the method-side statement of the same force-limiting relationship.

figures/FIG-4.md: added 'The latch housing and its cavity are shown schematically.' to the view paragraph

figures/FIG-4.md: completed the truncated numeral instruction for 16 latch, which previously ended mid-word

Because a later argument has to be built from what is already in the specification, I made sure the two features that carry the independent claims are explained there as solutions to stated technical problems, not merely recited: the section 'The segmented cam ring' explains that a side-opening clamp cannot carry a continuous drive ring across the split and that the division of the ring is undone by the act of closing the clamp, and the latch section explains where the operator's remaining handle travel goes and why a rigid train would overload whichever jaw touches first. structured_output.summary: The application body, claims, numeral table and five figure briefs were already drafted in full, so this turn resolved the three defects the reviewer raised and one truncated line found alongside them. Removed the sentence clause that told the reader what limits the cam-ring stroke (the inventor says only "a limited stroke" and never names a limiting element, and the added clause fought with the force-limiting-stack paragraph that follows). Rewrote the follower-constraint sentence, which had said in one breath that the follower cannot move circumferentially and that it follows a path inclined to the radial direction; it now states that the slot holds the follower at a position along the slot so that circumferential ring movement displaces the follower radially, which is what the rest of the description and claim 1 say. In the FIG. 4 brief, the latch housing and its cavity are now marked as shown schematically and the walls no longer "guide" the wedge, so no undisclosed housing/wedge connection is asserted; the wedge's up-and-down movement is likewise marked schematic. Also completed the FIG. 4 numeral instruction for numeral 16, whose line ended mid-word ("does not designate the wal"), and made "over-centre" read "over-center" to match the specification. No claim, no numeral, no other section was touched. One caution the brief asked me to state plainly: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, and per input/brief.md no prior-art search was run, so the art available to this draft is empty and may well be incomplete. The Background is written from the disclosed problem alone and contains no citations, since there is no key that could honestly be cited; if a search is later run, the Background and the claim ladder should be revisited against whatever it returns.
reasoning: Claim 1 carries its weight on one relationship the inventor calls essential: the cam ring is split with the body, one segment per frame half, and the complementary coupling faces at the hinge end and at the latch end engage as the halves close, so the two segments thereafter rotate as one coupled ring and a single latch input reaches all three followers. That is the coupling-by-closure limitation, and it is what a band clamp, a two-bolt saddle, or a split clamp with independently driven halves does not have. With prior_art/ empty I could not name a reference the feature clears, so I put the technical problem it solves into the Background and into the specification section 'The segmented cam ring' expressly: a side-opening clamp cannot carry a continuous drive ring across the split, and separately driven halves lose the fixed relationship between the two sides. That explanation is now on the page ahead of any argument that needs it.

Claim 1 also recites the force-limiting spring stack in the drive train between latch handle and wedge, doing real work: after all three pads land, remaining handle travel goes into the stack instead of driving one jaw farther than its neighbours. I kept it in claim 1 rather than pushing it to a dependent because the disclosure names it as part of the essential relationship, and it is a second independent point of distinction if the coupling feature is ever met.

Deliberately left out of claim 1: the indicator pin and its predetermined compression range (claims 2, 3, 11, 14), the two latch positions including the over-center position (claims 4, 12), the mounting boss (claim 8 and independent claim 10), the semicircular frame halves and the three-directions distribution (claim 9), and any statement of what bounds the stroke. Claim 1 says only 'a stroke' and 'the stroke'. Each of those is disclosed and each is a fallback worth having, but none is needed to make the clamp work or to state the invention at its broadest.

The reviewer's first two findings are correct and I applied them as written. The stroke-limiting clause was an invented mechanism: the inventor never says what bounds the stroke, and the clause implied the ring always turns the full stroke, which contradicts the very next paragraph where the stack takes up whatever travel remains once the pads land on a given pipe. Nothing in claim 1 or claim 4 depended on it, so deleting it cost no support.

The follower sentence was a genuine kinematic misstatement rather than loose wording. A path inclined to the radial direction has a circumferential component, which the radial guide forbids in the same sentence. What the oblique slot actually constrains is the follower's position along the slot; the ring's circumferential movement is what converts to radial displacement. The corrected sentence now agrees with the following sentence, with claim 1, and with FIG. 3, where the post's upper and lower sides face the sides of the opening.

The third finding is also right, on a narrower ground: the disclosure names the latch housing only as the part carrying the fixed edge against which the indicator pin is read. A three-walled cavity whose walls guide the wedge is a functional connection, not a bare outline, and every other conventional element in the five briefs (hinge, latch block, pivots, spring seats, mounting boss) is marked schematic. I marked the housing and cavity schematic and dropped the guiding function rather than deleting the cavity, because the wedge still needs somewhere to be drawn and the depiction convention must stay confined to the figure brief. The description's neutral 'a wedge 52 movable in the latch housing 58' was left untouched, and nothing was added to the text or claims to match the drawing.

I found one further defect the review did not list: the FIG. 4 numeral instruction for 16 ended mid-word. Left as it stood it would have reached the renderer as an unfinished instruction. I completed it in the sense the fragment was heading, pointing the callout at the latch assembly as a whole rather than at any single wall, which keeps it distinct from numeral 58 on the top wall of the same enclosure.

Independent claims sit in three statutory frames that different parties infringe: the clamp itself (claim 1), the pipe-mounted equipment assembly with a sensor, tool or conduit on the mounting boss (claim 10), which reaches the integrator who ships equipment already on a clamp, and the method of clamping (claim 13), which reaches the operator's sequence. All three trace to disclosed passages; claim 13's final step, continuing the handle into the over-center position after the pads seat, is the method-side statement of the same force-limiting relationship.

The topmost jaw carriage lies on the first frame half 10; the other two lie on the second frame half 12. The circumferential positions of the three jaw carriages 30, and their apportionment between the two frame halves, are shown schematically.

-Each jaw carriage 30 carries at its inner end a separate member, joined to the jaw carriage 30 at a small circle that is a pivot shown schematically. The inner face of that member is a shallow concave arc that meets the outer surface of the pipe 90. That member is the jaw pad 40.

+Each jaw carriage 30 carries at its inner end a separate member, joined to it at a small circle that is a pivot shown schematically. The inner face of that member is a shallow concave arc that meets the outer surface of the pipe 90. That member is the jaw pad 40.

A broken cutting-plane line runs along the radial centre line of the topmost jaw carriage 30, extending past the outer boundary of the ring at one end and past the jaw pad 40 at the other, with a short arrow at each end pointing to the same side, the viewing direction of FIG. 3. It carries no drawing text.

13. A method of clamping a pipe, comprising:

opening a latch of a split pipe clamp and swinging a first frame half and a second frame half of the split pipe clamp apart about a hinge at a hinge end of the split pipe clamp, a first cam ring segment being carried by the first frame half and a second cam ring segment being carried by the second frame half;

placing the first frame half and the second frame half around the pipe;

closing the first frame half and the second frame half about the hinge so that complementary coupling faces at the hinge end and complementary coupling faces at a latch end engage one another and couple the first cam ring segment and the second cam ring segment into a coupled ring received in an annular guide of the split pipe clamp;

moving the latch to a first position in which the first frame half and the second frame half are held around the pipe with three jaw carriages of the split pipe clamp retracted;

moving the latch toward a second, over-center position, thereby driving a wedge against a ring drive face of the coupled ring and rotating the coupled ring through a stroke;

advancing the three jaw carriages inwardly in synchronism by movement of a follower of each jaw carriage in a respective oblique slot of the coupled ring, until a jaw pad pivotally mounted on each jaw carriage seats on the pipe; and

continuing to move a latch handle of the latch into the second, over-center position after all three jaw pads have seated on the pipe, thereby compressing a force-limiting spring stack in a drive train between the latch handle and the wedge rather than advancing one of the jaw carriages farther inwardly than the others.

14. The method of claim 13, further comprising observing displacement of an indicator pin relative to a fixed edge of a latch housing of the latch, the displacement indicating that the force-limiting spring stack has entered a predetermined compression range.

15. The method of claim 13, further comprising releasing the latch to unload the force-limiting spring stack, retracting the three jaw carriages outwardly under carriage return springs so that the three jaw pads lift from the pipe, and thereafter swinging the first frame half and the second frame half apart about the hinge and removing the split pipe clamp from the pipe.
FIG. 1 is a plan view of a split pipe clamp according to one embodiment, shown in the closed condition around a pipe and viewed along the axis of the pipe.

FIG. 2 is a plan view of the segmented cam ring of the clamp of FIG. 1, shown removed from the frame with the cam ring segments in the coupled condition.

FIG. 3 is an enlarged fragmentary sectional view through one jaw carriage of the clamp of FIG. 1, taken along the cutting plane indicated by the cutting-plane line in FIG. 1, which plane contains the radial direction of that jaw carriage and the axis of the frame.

FIG. 4 is an enlarged fragmentary sectional view of the latch of the clamp of FIG. 1, taken in a plane transverse to the axis of the frame at the latch end and viewed from the side of that plane opposite to the side from which FIG. 1 is viewed, showing the drive train between the latch handle and the segmented cam ring.

FIG. 5 is an enlarged fragmentary sectional view through the frame of the clamp of FIG. 1 provided with the optional mounting boss, taken at the mounting boss in a plane containing a radial direction of the frame and the axis of the frame.

input.summary: Fixed all three verified findings. (1) The Brief Description for FIG. 5 now reads as a section through the frame of the clamp of FIG. 1 provided with the optional mounting boss, taken at the mounting boss, so it no longer directs the reader to a feature that FIG. 1 does not depict; FIG-1.md and FIG-5.md were left alone, and the boss remains the optional embodiment the disclosure supports. (2) Claim 13 now recites moving the latch toward the second, over-center position for the wedge-driving step and continuing to move the latch handle into the second, over-center position after all three pads seat, which matches the described operation in which the pads land partway through the travel and the remainder compresses the spring stack; claims 14 and 15 are untouched and the antecedent for the over-center position is still established in the earlier step. (3) FIG-1.md now specifies a broken cutting-plane line along the radial centre line of the topmost jaw carriage 30, running past the outer boundary of the ring at one end and past the jaw pad 40 at the other, with a short arrow at each end pointing to the same side, that being the viewing direction of FIG. 3; the FIG. 3 caption now locates the view by that cutting-plane line. The line is specified to carry no drawing text, because the geometry image never renders text; the caption therefore refers to the cutting-plane line rather than to a rendered "3-3" designation, which keeps the cross-reference complete without asking the renderer to draw characters. Adding the line pushed FIG-1.md over the 2800-character limit, so I removed invented rendering constraints instead of disclosed geometry: the redundant "leaving a visible gap between them" phrasing, the "so that it stands as it does in FIG. 4" instruction on the latch lever, and three over-specified numeral endpoints (100, 10, 12) that now name broad interior or boundary targets. FIG-1.md is 2768 characters and every brief is under the limit. No numeral was added, removed, or redefined; the numeral table, drawings section, detailed description, claims, and all five figure briefs remain in step.
reasoning: The FIG. 5 caption defect was a cross-reference problem, not a source problem, so the cure belonged in the caption. The alternative, drawing the boss into FIG. 1, would have put an expressly optional feature into the view that establishes the base embodiment, and the disclosure says the boss may be carried, not that it is present. Naming it 'provided with the optional mounting boss' keeps FIG. 5 an embodiment of the FIG. 1 clamp while telling the reader why the boss is absent from FIG. 1.

Claim 13's sequence error mattered because the whole force-limiting relationship depends on the pads seating before the handle finishes its travel. Reciting completed arrival at over-center and then continuing into it made the claim recite a sequence the specification contradicts, which is the kind of internal conflict that costs support later. 'Toward' in the fifth step and 'into the second, over-center position' in the last step restore the disclosed order without adding any limitation: the ring still turns through the stroke while the latch travels, and the stack still takes only the travel remaining after all three pads contact.

For the cutting-plane line I departed from the reviewer's exact suggested wording on one point, and the substance of the finding is fully cured. The suggestion called for a line labelled 3-3, but the image pipeline draws only geometry and then places the listed numerals deterministically, so a brief must never ask it to render characters. I specified the line, its extent, and the arrow direction as geometry, stated that it carries no drawing text, and wrote the FIG. 3 caption to locate the view by that cutting-plane line rather than by a 3-3 designation. The reader gets the indication the finding asked for and the caption and the sheet agree.

The arrows are specified as both pointing to the same side of the line, that side being the viewing direction of FIG. 3. That is the physically correct indication for a plane containing the carriage's radial direction and the frame axis: the viewing direction is perpendicular to that plane, so both arrows point circumferentially to one side, and stating it once avoids an arrow pair that contradicts the section it labels.

To make room under the character limit I cut only renderer instructions, never geometry or relationships. 'Leaving a visible gap between them' restated the spacing already given by 'spaced outward from the pipe 90'. 'So that it stands as it does in FIG. 4' told the renderer to match another sheet rather than describing the lever, and the lever's position is already fixed by the side of the block it extends from. The three numeral endpoints lost narrowing modifiers such as 'right of the topmost jaw carriage' and 'at the bottom of the ring' and now name broad interior targets, which is what the endpoint guidance asks for; the endpoints that must stay discriminating, notably 30 and 40 on the topmost carriage and 16 on the latch block, kept the wording that distinguishes them from neighbouring parts.

Nothing in the claims, description, numeral table, or disclosed embodiments was changed to accommodate anything a renderer produced. The only claim edit was the sequence correction, which flows from the specification and the disclosure, and the only figure edits were the cutting-plane line and the removal of invented rendering constraints.

input.prior_art_strategy: Unchanged this turn, and no citation was added or altered. prior_art/INDEX.md still lists no references, and input/brief.md records that no prior-art search was run, so the Background continues to state the problem from the disclosure alone with no citations, since there is no key that could be cited honestly. The features that carry the independent claims remain explained in the specification as answers to stated technical problems, ready for any later argument: the coupling of the two cam ring segments by the act of closing the frame, which restores a single drive element across the split that a side-opening clamp cannot otherwise carry, and the force-limiting spring stack between latch handle and wedge, which absorbs the handle travel that a rigid train would dump into whichever jaw touched first. The claim 13 sequence correction strengthens that second point by making the method recite the order in which the stack actually does its work. The art behind this draft is empty and may be incomplete; the claims should be retested against any search later run, with the dependent ladder, the indicator pin and compression range, the two latch positions, the pivoting pads without a size-specific insert, the segments that separate with their own halves, and the mounting boss outside the drive path, as the retreat order.

The following description of embodiments refers to the accompanying drawings. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout. Terms of direction are used with respect to the frame of the clamp: the axis of the frame is the axis about which the frame is annular in the closed condition and with which the axis of a clamped pipe substantially coincides, "inward" and "radially inward" mean toward that axis, "outward" and "radially outward" mean away from it, and "circumferential" means about that axis. These terms describe relationships within the clamp and do not require the clamp to be used in any particular attitude.

Overall arrangement

FIG. 1 shows a split pipe clamp 100 in the closed condition around a pipe 90. The clamp 100 has a first frame half 10 and a second frame half 12. Each of the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 is semicircular, and the two frame halves together surround the pipe 90. The first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are joined at one end, referred to as the hinge end, by a hinge 14, and are releasably joined at the other end, referred to as the latch end, by a releasable latch 16. The hinge 14 permits the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 to be swung apart far enough for the clamp 100 to be passed sideways onto a pipe 90 that is already installed, so that the clamp 100 need not be threaded over a free end of the pipe 90. When the frame halves are brought together and the latch 16 is engaged, the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 define a frame that is annular about the axis of the clamp 100.

Three jaw carriages 30 are distributed around the frame in the closed condition, so that the three jaw carriages 30 approach the pipe 90 from three different directions. Each jaw carriage 30 moves radially with respect to the frame and carries at its inner end a jaw pad 40, which is described below in connection with FIG. 3. The jaw pads 40 carried at the inner ends of the three jaw carriages 30 bear on the pipe 90 when the clamp 100 is clamped. The clamp 100 does not require an insert dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter, and the same clamp 100 serves pipes of different diameters within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

The frame may carry a mounting boss 70 outside the annular guide 18 described below, as shown in FIG. 5. The mounting boss 70 supports a sensor, a tool, or a conduit that is to be held on the pipe 90 by the clamp 100. The mounting boss 70 is connected neither to the segmented cam ring 20 nor to any jaw carriage 30 and does not participate in the synchronization of the jaw carriages 30. Equipment carried at the mounting boss 70 therefore lies outside the drive path by which the jaws are advanced. The mounting boss 70 is an optional feature of the clamp 100 and may be omitted.

The segmented cam ring

FIG. 2 shows the segmented cam ring 20 of the clamp 100, drawn removed from the frame with its segments in the coupled condition. The segmented cam ring 20 comprises a first cam ring segment 22 and a second cam ring segment 24. The first cam ring segment 22 is carried by the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 is carried by the second frame half 12, so that each frame half carries one segment of the ring and each segment travels with its own frame half when the clamp 100 is opened.

The first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 meet at two places, one at the hinge end and one at the latch end. At the hinge end the two segments have complementary coupling faces 26, and at the latch end they have complementary coupling faces 28. The complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are circumferentially facing drive faces, each pair being shaped so that one segment can transmit circumferential force to the other through the joint. The faces are brought into engagement by the same motion that closes the frame halves: as the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are swung together about the hinge 14 and the latch 16 is engaged, the complementary coupling faces 26 close on one another at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 close on one another at the latch end.

Coupling the segments in this way solves a problem created by splitting the clamp. A clamp that must open from the side cannot carry a continuous drive ring across the split, and a divided drive must otherwise be operated separately in each half, with the result that the two halves advance their jaws by amounts that are not fixed relative to one another. Here the division of the ring is undone by the act of closing the clamp. In the closed condition the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 are coupled at both ends and rotate together in the annular guide as a coupled ring, and a circumferential input applied to either segment is carried around the whole ring. One input, applied at one point on one frame half, therefore reaches every jaw carriage 30 through a single kinematic element, and the relationship between the jaw carriages 30 is set by the geometry of the ring rather than by the way the clamp is operated. When the latch 16 is released and the frame halves are swung apart, the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 separate and each segment stays with its own frame half, so that the coupling is made and broken by the closing and opening of the frame halves.

The segmented cam ring 20 has three oblique slots 34, one for each jaw carriage 30. Each oblique slot 34 is inclined to the radial direction of the frame at the circumferential position of that slot, so that rotation of the coupled ring produces inward travel of its jaw carriage 30, the three oblique slots 34 being arranged so that the three jaw carriages 30 travel inwardly in synchronism. The inclination of the oblique slots 34 sets the ratio between the circumferential stroke of the coupled ring and the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

The segmented cam ring 20 further has a ring drive face 36, shown in FIG. 2 at the latch end of the ring, against which the latch acts as described below. The ring drive face 36 is presented at a position on the ring that the wedge of the latch can reach, and it lies at an inclination to the direction in which that wedge advances, so that advance of the wedge moves the segmented cam ring 20 circumferentially.

The jaw carriages

FIG. 3 is a fragmentary sectional view through one jaw carriage 30. The frame is channeled to form the annular guide 18, which receives the segmented cam ring 20. The annular guide 18 retains the first cam ring segment 22 on the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 on the second frame half 12, and permits the coupled ring to move circumferentially.

The frame is further formed with a radial guide 38 at the position of each jaw carriage 30. Each jaw carriage 30 is received in a respective radial guide 38 and is constrained by the radial guide 38 to move radially with respect to the frame. Each jaw carriage 30 carries a follower 32 that projects from the jaw carriage 30 into a respective one of the oblique slots 34 of the segmented cam ring 20. The follower 32 bears against the sides of the oblique slot 34.

The follower 32 is constrained in two ways at once. The radial guide 38 prevents the jaw carriage 30, and therefore the follower 32, from moving circumferentially, while the oblique slot 34 holds the follower 32 at a position along the slot, which is inclined to the radial direction, so that circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20 displaces the follower 32 radially. When the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the side of each oblique slot 34 bears on the corresponding follower 32 and drives it, and with it the jaw carriage 30, radially inward along the radial guide 38. Because all three followers 32 are engaged in oblique slots 34 of one coupled ring, the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism for as long as the ring turns. The jaw pads 40 therefore close on the pipe together.

At its inner end each jaw carriage 30 carries a jaw pad 40. The jaw pad 40 is pivotally mounted on the jaw carriage 30 and has a concave bearing face directed inwardly of the frame. Because the jaw pad 40 is free to pivot on the jaw carriage 30, the concave bearing face aligns itself with the outer surface of the pipe as it lands. The same concave bearing face therefore seats on pipes of different diameters, and no insert dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter is required.

A carriage return spring 44 acts between each jaw carriage 30 and the frame so as to urge that jaw carriage 30 radially outward. When the latch 16 is released and the drive from the latch to the ring drive face 36 is removed, the carriage return springs 44 push the jaw carriages 30 outward and the jaw pads 40 are retracted from the pipe, and the clamp 100 is left with its jaw carriages 30 retracted and ready for the next installation. Retraction of the jaw carriages 30 clears the jaw pads 40 from the pipe before the frame halves are swung apart.

The latch and the force-limiting drive train

FIG. 4 shows the latch 16 in fragmentary section. The latch 16 includes a latch housing 58 mounted on the frame at the latch end, a latch handle 50 pivotally mounted on the latch housing 58, a wedge 52 movable in the latch housing 58, and a force-limiting spring stack 54 in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52. The wedge 52 is positioned so that its inclined face bears on the ring drive face 36 of the segmented cam ring 20.

The latch 16 has two engaged positions. In a first position, the latch 16 holds the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 closed around the pipe 90 but does not clamp it: the frame is captive on the pipe 90 and cannot fall away, while the jaw carriages 30 remain retracted under their carriage return springs 44. In a second, over-center position, the wedge 52 drives the segmented cam ring 20 and the pipe 90 is clamped. Movement of the latch handle 50 from the first position to the second position advances the wedge 52 against the ring drive face 36. The inclined face of the wedge 52 converts that advance into circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the coupled ring turns through its limited stroke.

The force-limiting spring stack 54 answers the problem of what becomes of the operator's remaining handle travel. The jaw pads 40 land on the pipe 90 at some point in the stroke that depends on the diameter of the pipe 90, and the latch handle 50 has still to be carried into its over-center position. If the drive train from the latch handle 50 to the wedge 52 were rigid, that remaining travel would be taken up by whatever part of the assembly yielded first, in practice by driving one jaw farther into the pipe 90 than the others and loading it far more heavily. Additional travel of the latch handle 50 after all three jaw pads 40 have contacted the pipe 90 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than forcing one jaw carriage 30 farther inward than the others.

An indicator pin 56 is coupled to the force-limiting spring stack 54 and projects from the latch housing 58. As the force-limiting spring stack 54 compresses, the indicator pin 56 moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing 58, and the position of the indicator pin 56 with respect to that fixed edge shows the operator when the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered a predetermined compression range. The predetermined compression range is the range of stack compression that corresponds to the clamping force for which the clamp 100 is intended. The indicator pin 56 therefore reports clamp loading mechanically, and what it reports is the state of the force-limiting spring stack 54. It is not a measurement of the diameter of the pipe 90.

Operation

To install the clamp 100 on a pipe 90, the operator opens the latch 16 and swings the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 apart about the hinge 14. The first cam ring segment 22 stays with the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 stays with the second frame half 12, and the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are separated. The operator places the frame halves around the pipe 90 from the side and closes them about the hinge 14. Closing the frame halves brings the complementary coupling faces 26 into engagement at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 into engagement at the latch end, coupling the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 into the coupled ring within the annular guide 18.

The operator then moves the latch 16 to its first position, in which the frame is held around the pipe 90 without clamping. The operator moves the latch handle 50 to the second, over-center position. The wedge 52 is driven against the ring drive face 36, the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the sides of the three oblique slots 34 drive the three followers 32, and the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism until the pivoting jaw pads 40 seat on the pipe 90. The remaining travel of the latch handle 50 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54, and the operator watches the indicator pin 56 move relative to the fixed edge of the latch housing 58 and so sees that the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered the predetermined compression range. The latch 16 is left in the over-center position and the clamp 100 is loaded on the pipe 90.

To remove the clamp 100, the operator releases the latch 16. The latch handle 50 comes back over center, the wedge 52 retreats from the ring drive face 36, and the force-limiting spring stack 54 is unloaded. The carriage return springs 44 then push the jaw carriages 30 radially outward, so that the jaw pads 40 lift from the pipe 90. Only then are the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 swung apart about the hinge 14 and the clamp 100 taken off the pipe 90. The clamp 100 is undamaged by the cycle and may be installed again on the same pipe or on a pipe of a different diameter within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

Features described above in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another, except where the context makes the combination impossible. The embodiments described are illustrative of the disclosed clamp and are not exhaustive of it, and the scope of protection is defined by the claims that follow rather than by any particular embodiment described here.

# FIG. 1

Plan view of the assembled split pipe clamp, closed around a pipe, viewed along the axis of the pipe. Black line work on white, no shading, well inside the drawing area.

A circle at the centre of the drawing area is the pipe 90, seen end on.

A ring of substantial width surrounds the pipe 90, bounded by an inner circle spaced outward from the pipe 90 and an outer circle.

Two radial joint lines divide the ring into two semicircular bodies, one joint at the left and one at the right. The upper semicircular body is the first frame half 10 and the lower semicircular body is the second frame half 12.

At the left joint is the hinge 14, drawn schematically as a small circle centred on that joint line with a short knuckle block reaching to it from each frame end.

At the right joint is the latch 16, drawn schematically as a rectangular block lying outside the outer boundary of the ring and bridging both frame ends, with an elongated lever extending from the block outward and away from the ring.

Three jaw carriages 30 are spaced around the ring, one at the top, one at the lower left and one at the lower right. Each is drawn as a block that crosses the inner boundary of the ring and reaches radially inward toward the pipe 90. The topmost jaw carriage lies on the first frame half 10; the other two lie on the second frame half 12. The circumferential positions of the three jaw carriages 30, and their apportionment between the two frame halves, are shown schematically.

Each jaw carriage 30 carries at its inner end a separate member, joined to it at a small circle that is a pivot shown schematically. The inner face of that member is a shallow concave arc that meets the outer surface of the pipe 90. That member is the jaw pad 40.

A broken cutting-plane line runs along the radial centre line of the topmost jaw carriage 30, extending past the outer boundary of the ring at one end and past the jaw pad 40 at the other, with a short arrow at each end pointing to the same side, the viewing direction of FIG. 3. Each end of the line is designated by the view number of FIG. 3, placed outside the arrow at that end, so that the plane reads as line 3-3. That section designation is not a reference numeral and designates no part.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 100 split pipe clamp: target the outer boundary of the ring at its upper right.
- 10 first frame half: target well inside the upper semicircular body at its right.
- 12 second frame half: target well inside the lower semicircular body.
- 14 hinge: target the small circle at the left joint.
- 16 latch: target the rectangular block bridging the right joint.
- 30 jaw carriage: target well inside the block of the topmost jaw carriage.
- 40 jaw pad: target well inside the member at the inner end of the topmost jaw carriage.
- 90 pipe: target well inside the central circle.

# FIG. 1

Plan view of the assembled split pipe clamp, closed around a pipe, viewed along the axis of the pipe. Black line work on white, no shading, well inside the drawing area.

A circle at the centre of the drawing area is the pipe 90, seen end on.

A ring of substantial width surrounds the pipe 90, bounded by an inner circle spaced outward from the pipe 90 and an outer circle.

Two radial joint lines divide the ring into two semicircular bodies, one joint at the left and one at the right. The upper semicircular body is the first frame half 10 and the lower semicircular body is the second frame half 12.

At the left joint is the hinge 14, drawn schematically as a small circle centred on that joint line with a short knuckle block reaching to it from each frame end.

At the right joint is the latch 16, drawn schematically as a rectangular block lying outside the outer boundary of the ring and bridging both frame ends, with an elongated lever extending from the block outward and away from the ring.

Three jaw carriages 30 are spaced around the ring, one at the top, one at the lower left and one at the lower right. Each is drawn as a block that crosses the inner boundary of the ring and reaches radially inward toward the pipe 90. The topmost jaw carriage lies on the first frame half 10; the other two lie on the second frame half 12. The circumferential positions of the three jaw carriages 30, and their apportionment between the two frame halves, are shown schematically.

Each jaw carriage 30 carries at its inner end a separate member, joined to it at a small circle that is a pivot shown schematically. The inner face of that member is a shallow concave arc that meets the outer surface of the pipe 90. That member is the jaw pad 40.

A broken cutting-plane line runs along the radial centre line of the topmost jaw carriage 30, extending past the outer boundary of the ring at one end and past the jaw pad 40 at the other, with a short arrow at each end pointing to the same side, the viewing direction of FIG. 3. Each end of the line is designated by the view number of FIG. 3, placed outside the arrow at that end, so that the plane reads as line 3-3. The following description of embodiments refers to the accompanying drawings. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout. Terms of direction are used with respect to the frame of the clamp: the axis of the frame is the axis about which the frame is annular in the closed condition, "inward" and "radially inward" mean toward that axis, "outward" and "radially outward" mean away from it, and "circumferential" means about that axis. These terms describe relationships within the clamp and do not require the clamp to be used in any particular attitude.

Overall arrangement

FIG. 1 shows a split pipe clamp 100 in the closed condition around a pipe 90. The clamp 100 has a first frame half 10 and a second frame half 12. Each of the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 is semicircular, and the two frame halves together surround the pipe 90. The first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are joined at one end, referred to as the hinge end, by a hinge 14, and are releasably joined at the other end, referred to as the latch end, by a releasable latch 16. The hinge 14 permits the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 to be swung apart far enough for the clamp 100 to be passed sideways onto a pipe 90 that is already installed, so that the clamp 100 need not be threaded over a free end of the pipe 90. When the frame halves are brought together and the latch 16 is engaged, the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 define a frame that is annular about the axis of the clamp 100.

Three jaw carriages 30 are distributed around the frame in the closed condition, so that the three jaw carriages 30 approach the pipe 90 from three different directions. Each jaw carriage 30 moves radially with respect to the frame and carries at its inner end a jaw pad 40, which is described below in connection with FIG. 3. The jaw pads 40 carried at the inner ends of the three jaw carriages 30 bear on the pipe 90 when the clamp 100 is clamped. The clamp 100 does not require an insert dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter, and the same clamp 100 serves pipes of different diameters within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

The frame may carry a mounting boss 70 outside the annular guide 18 described below, as shown in FIG. 5. The mounting boss 70 supports a sensor, a tool, or a conduit that is to be held on the pipe 90 by the clamp 100. The mounting boss 70 is connected neither to the segmented cam ring 20 nor to any jaw carriage 30 and does not participate in the synchronization of the jaw carriages 30. Equipment carried at the mounting boss 70 therefore lies outside the drive path by which the jaws are advanced. The mounting boss 70 is an optional feature of the clamp 100 and may be omitted.

The segmented cam ring

FIG. 2 shows the segmented cam ring 20 of the clamp 100, drawn removed from the frame with its segments in the coupled condition. The segmented cam ring 20 comprises a first cam ring segment 22 and a second cam ring segment 24. The first cam ring segment 22 is carried by the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 is carried by the second frame half 12, so that each frame half carries one segment of the ring and each segment travels with its own frame half when the clamp 100 is opened.

The first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 meet at two places, one at the hinge end and one at the latch end. At the hinge end the two segments have complementary coupling faces 26, and at the latch end they have complementary coupling faces 28. The complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are circumferentially facing drive faces, each pair being shaped so that one segment can transmit circumferential force to the other through the joint. The faces are brought into engagement by the same motion that closes the frame halves: as the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are swung together about the hinge 14 and the latch 16 is engaged, the complementary coupling faces 26 close on one another at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 close on one another at the latch end.

Coupling the segments in this way solves a problem created by splitting the clamp. A clamp that must open from the side cannot carry a continuous drive ring across the split, and a divided drive must otherwise be operated separately in each half, with the result that the two halves advance their jaws by amounts that are not fixed relative to one another. Here the division of the ring is undone by the act of closing the clamp. In the closed condition the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 are coupled at both ends and rotate together in the annular guide as a coupled ring, and a circumferential input applied to either segment is carried around the whole ring. One input, applied at one point on one frame half, therefore reaches every jaw carriage 30 through a single kinematic element, and the relationship between the jaw carriages 30 is set by the geometry of the ring rather than by the way the clamp is operated. When the latch 16 is released and the frame halves are swung apart, the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 separate and each segment stays with its own frame half, so that the coupling is made and broken by the closing and opening of the frame halves.

The segmented cam ring 20 has three oblique slots 34, one for each jaw carriage 30. Each oblique slot 34 is inclined to the radial direction of the frame at the circumferential position of that slot, so that rotation of the coupled ring produces inward travel of its jaw carriage 30, the three oblique slots 34 being arranged so that the three jaw carriages 30 travel inwardly in synchronism. The inclination of the oblique slots 34 sets the ratio between the circumferential stroke of the coupled ring and the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

The segmented cam ring 20 further has a ring drive face 36, shown in FIG. 2 at the latch end of the ring, against which the latch acts as described below. The ring drive face 36 is presented at a position on the ring that the wedge of the latch can reach, and it lies at an inclination to the direction in which that wedge advances, so that advance of the wedge moves the segmented cam ring 20 circumferentially.

The jaw carriages

FIG. 3 is a fragmentary sectional view through one jaw carriage 30. The frame is channeled to form the annular guide 18, which receives the segmented cam ring 20. The annular guide 18 retains the first cam ring segment 22 on the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 on the second frame half 12, and permits the coupled ring to move circumferentially.

The frame is further formed with a radial guide 38 at the position of each jaw carriage 30. Each jaw carriage 30 is received in a respective radial guide 38 and is constrained by the radial guide 38 to move radially with respect to the frame. Each jaw carriage 30 carries a follower 32 that projects from the jaw carriage 30 into a respective one of the oblique slots 34 of the segmented cam ring 20. The follower 32 bears against the sides of the oblique slot 34.

The follower 32 is constrained in two ways at once. The radial guide 38 prevents the jaw carriage 30, and therefore the follower 32, from moving circumferentially, while the oblique slot 34 holds the follower 32 at a position along the slot, which is inclined to the radial direction, so that circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20 displaces the follower 32 radially. When the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the side of each oblique slot 34 bears on the corresponding follower 32 and drives it, and with it the jaw carriage 30, radially inward along the radial guide 38. Because all three followers 32 are engaged in oblique slots 34 of one coupled ring, the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism for as long as the ring turns. The jaw pads 40 therefore close on the pipe together.

At its inner end each jaw carriage 30 carries a jaw pad 40. The jaw pad 40 is pivotally mounted on the jaw carriage 30 and has a concave bearing face directed inwardly of the frame. Because the jaw pad 40 is free to pivot on the jaw carriage 30, the concave bearing face aligns itself with the outer surface of the pipe as it lands. The same concave bearing face therefore seats on pipes of different diameters, and no insert dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter is required.

A carriage return spring 44 acts between each jaw carriage 30 and the frame so as to urge that jaw carriage 30 radially outward. When the latch 16 is released and the drive from the latch to the ring drive face 36 is removed, the carriage return springs 44 push the jaw carriages 30 outward and the jaw pads 40 are retracted from the pipe, and the clamp 100 is left with its jaw carriages 30 retracted and ready for the next installation. Retraction of the jaw carriages 30 clears the jaw pads 40 from the pipe before the frame halves are swung apart.

The latch and the force-limiting drive train

FIG. 4 shows the latch 16 in fragmentary section. The latch 16 includes a latch housing 58 mounted on the frame at the latch end, a latch handle 50 pivotally mounted on the latch housing 58, a wedge 52 movable in the latch housing 58, and a force-limiting spring stack 54 in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52. The wedge 52 is positioned so that its inclined face bears on the ring drive face 36 of the segmented cam ring 20.

The latch 16 has two engaged positions. In a first position, the latch 16 holds the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 closed around the pipe 90 but does not clamp it: the frame is captive on the pipe 90 and cannot fall away, while the jaw carriages 30 remain retracted under their carriage return springs 44. In a second, over-center position, the wedge 52 drives the segmented cam ring 20 and the pipe 90 is clamped. Movement of the latch handle 50 from the first position to the second position advances the wedge 52 against the ring drive face 36. The inclined face of the wedge 52 converts that advance into circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the coupled ring turns through its limited stroke.

The force-limiting spring stack 54 answers the problem of what becomes of the operator's remaining handle travel. The jaw pads 40 land on the pipe 90 at some point in the stroke that depends on the diameter of the pipe 90, and the latch handle 50 has still to be carried into its over-center position. If the drive train from the latch handle 50 to the wedge 52 were rigid, that remaining travel would be taken up by whatever part of the assembly yielded first, in practice by driving one jaw farther into the pipe 90 than the others and loading it far more heavily. Additional travel of the latch handle 50 after all three jaw pads 40 have contacted the pipe 90 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than forcing one jaw carriage 30 farther inward than the others.

An indicator pin 56 is coupled to the force-limiting spring stack 54 and projects from the latch housing 58. As the force-limiting spring stack 54 compresses, the indicator pin 56 moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing 58, and the position of the indicator pin 56 with respect to that fixed edge shows the operator when the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered a predetermined compression range. The predetermined compression range is the range of stack compression that corresponds to the clamping force for which the clamp 100 is intended. The indicator pin 56 therefore reports clamp loading mechanically, and what it reports is the state of the force-limiting spring stack 54. It is not a measurement of the diameter of the pipe 90.

Operation

To install the clamp 100 on a pipe 90, the operator opens the latch 16 and swings the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 apart about the hinge 14. The first cam ring segment 22 stays with the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 stays with the second frame half 12, and the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are separated. The operator places the frame halves around the pipe 90 from the side and closes them about the hinge 14. Closing the frame halves brings the complementary coupling faces 26 into engagement at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 into engagement at the latch end, coupling the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 into the coupled ring within the annular guide 18.

The operator then moves the latch 16 to its first position, in which the frame is held around the pipe 90 without clamping. The operator moves the latch handle 50 to the second, over-center position. The wedge 52 is driven against the ring drive face 36, the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the sides of the three oblique slots 34 drive the three followers 32, and the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism until the pivoting jaw pads 40 seat on the pipe 90. The remaining travel of the latch handle 50 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54, and the operator watches the indicator pin 56 move relative to the fixed edge of the latch housing 58 and so sees that the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered the predetermined compression range. The latch 16 is left in the over-center position and the clamp 100 is loaded on the pipe 90.

To remove the clamp 100, the operator releases the latch 16. The latch handle 50 comes back over center, the wedge 52 retreats from the ring drive face 36, and the force-limiting spring stack 54 is unloaded. The carriage return springs 44 then push the jaw carriages 30 radially outward, so that the jaw pads 40 lift from the pipe 90. Only then are the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 swung apart about the hinge 14 and the clamp 100 taken off the pipe 90. The clamp 100 is undamaged by the cycle and may be installed again on the same pipe or on a pipe of a different diameter within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

Features described above in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another, except where the context makes the combination impossible. The embodiments described are illustrative of the disclosed clamp and are not exhaustive of it, and the scope of protection is defined by the claims that follow rather than by any particular embodiment described here.
