The following description of embodiments refers to the accompanying drawings. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout. Terms of direction are used with respect to the frame of the clamp: the axis of the frame is the axis about which the frame is annular in the closed condition, "inward" and "radially inward" mean toward that axis, "outward" and "radially outward" mean away from it, and "circumferential" means about that axis. These terms describe relationships within the clamp and do not require the clamp to be used in any particular attitude.

Overall arrangement

FIG. 1 shows a split pipe clamp 100 in the closed condition around a pipe 90. The clamp 100 has a first frame half 10 and a second frame half 12. Each of the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 is semicircular, and the two frame halves together surround the pipe 90. The first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are joined at one end, referred to as the hinge end, by a hinge 14, and are releasably joined at the other end, referred to as the latch end, by a releasable latch 16. The hinge 14 permits the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 to be swung apart far enough for the clamp 100 to be passed sideways onto a pipe 90 that is already installed, so that the clamp 100 need not be threaded over a free end of the pipe 90. When the frame halves are brought together and the latch 16 is engaged, the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 define a frame that is annular about the axis of the clamp 100.

Three jaw carriages 30 are distributed around the frame in the closed condition, so that the three jaw carriages 30 approach the pipe 90 from three different directions. Each jaw carriage 30 moves radially with respect to the frame and carries at its inner end a jaw pad 40, which is described below in connection with FIG. 3. The jaw pads 40 carried at the inner ends of the three jaw carriages 30 bear on the pipe 90 when the clamp 100 is clamped. The clamp 100 does not require a part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter, and the same clamp 100 serves pipes of different diameters within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

The frame may carry a mounting boss 70 outside the annular guide 18 described below, as shown in FIG. 5. The mounting boss 70 supports a sensor, a tool, or a conduit that is to be held on the pipe 90 by the clamp 100. The mounting boss 70 does not participate in the synchronization of the jaw carriages 30. Equipment carried at the mounting boss 70 therefore lies outside the drive path by which the jaws are advanced. The mounting boss 70 is an optional feature of the clamp 100 and may be omitted.

The segmented cam ring

FIG. 2 shows the segmented cam ring 20 of the clamp 100, drawn removed from the frame with its segments in the coupled condition. The segmented cam ring 20 comprises a first cam ring segment 22 and a second cam ring segment 24. The first cam ring segment 22 is carried by the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 is carried by the second frame half 12, so that each frame half carries one segment of the ring and each segment travels with its own frame half when the clamp 100 is opened.

The first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 meet at two places, one at the hinge end and one at the latch end. At the hinge end the two segments have complementary coupling faces 26, and at the latch end they have complementary coupling faces 28. The complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are circumferentially facing drive faces, each pair being shaped so that one segment can transmit circumferential force to the other through the joint. The faces are brought into engagement by the same motion that closes the frame halves: as the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are swung together about the hinge 14 and the latch 16 is engaged, the complementary coupling faces 26 close on one another at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 close on one another at the latch end.

Coupling the segments in this way solves a problem created by splitting the clamp. A clamp that must open from the side cannot carry a continuous drive ring across the split, and a divided drive must otherwise be operated separately in each half, with the result that the two halves advance their jaws by amounts that are not fixed relative to one another. Here the division of the ring is undone by the act of closing the clamp. In the closed condition the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 are coupled at both ends and rotate together in the annular guide as a coupled ring, and a circumferential input applied to either segment is carried around the whole ring. One input, applied at one point on one frame half, therefore reaches every jaw carriage 30 through a single kinematic element, and the relationship between the jaw carriages 30 is set by the geometry of the ring rather than by the way the clamp is operated. When the latch 16 is released and the frame halves are swung apart, the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 separate and each segment stays with its own frame half, so that the coupling is made and broken by the closing and opening of the frame halves.

The segmented cam ring 20 has three oblique slots 34, one for each jaw carriage 30. Each oblique slot 34 is inclined to the radial direction of the frame at the circumferential position of that slot, so that rotation of the coupled ring produces inward travel of its jaw carriage 30, the three oblique slots 34 being arranged so that the three jaw carriages 30 travel inwardly in synchronism. The inclination of the oblique slots 34 sets the ratio between the circumferential stroke of the coupled ring and the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

The segmented cam ring 20 further has a ring drive face 36, shown in FIG. 2 at the latch end of the ring, against which the latch acts as described below. The ring drive face 36 is presented at a position on the ring that the wedge of the latch can reach, and it lies at an inclination to the direction in which that wedge advances, so that advance of the wedge moves the segmented cam ring 20 circumferentially.

The jaw carriages

FIG. 3 is a fragmentary sectional view through one jaw carriage 30, taken along line 3-3 of FIG. 1. The frame is channeled to form the annular guide 18, which receives the segmented cam ring 20. The annular guide 18 retains the first cam ring segment 22 on the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 on the second frame half 12, and permits the coupled ring to move circumferentially.

The frame is further formed with a radial guide 38 at the position of each jaw carriage 30. Each jaw carriage 30 is received in a respective radial guide 38 and is constrained by the radial guide 38 to move radially with respect to the frame. Each jaw carriage 30 carries a follower 32 that projects from the jaw carriage 30 into a respective one of the oblique slots 34 of the segmented cam ring 20. The follower 32 bears against the sides of the oblique slot 34.

The follower 32 is constrained in two ways at once. The radial guide 38 prevents the jaw carriage 30, and therefore the follower 32, from moving circumferentially, while the oblique slot 34 holds the follower 32 at a position along the slot, which is inclined to the radial direction, so that circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20 displaces the follower 32 radially. When the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the side of each oblique slot 34 bears on the corresponding follower 32 and drives it, and with it the jaw carriage 30, radially inward along the radial guide 38. Because all three followers 32 are engaged in oblique slots 34 of one coupled ring, the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism for as long as the ring turns. The jaw pads 40 therefore close on the pipe together.

At its inner end each jaw carriage 30 carries a jaw pad 40. The jaw pad 40 is pivotally mounted on the jaw carriage 30 and has a concave bearing face directed inwardly of the frame. Because the jaw pad 40 is free to pivot on the jaw carriage 30, the concave bearing face aligns itself with the outer surface of the pipe as it lands. The same concave bearing face therefore seats on pipes of different diameters, and no insert dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter is required.

A carriage return spring 44 acts on each jaw carriage 30 so as to urge that jaw carriage 30 radially outward. When the latch 16 is released and the drive from the latch to the ring drive face 36 is removed, the carriage return springs 44 push the jaw carriages 30 outward and the jaw pads 40 are retracted from the pipe, and the clamp 100 is left with its jaw carriages 30 retracted and ready for the next installation. Retraction of the jaw carriages 30 clears the jaw pads 40 from the pipe before the frame halves are swung apart.

The latch and the force-limiting drive train

FIG. 4 shows the latch 16 in fragmentary section. The latch 16 includes a latch housing 58 at the latch end, a latch handle 50, a wedge 52, and a force-limiting spring stack 54 in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52. The latch housing 58 presents a fixed edge referred to below in connection with the indicator pin 56. The wedge 52 is positioned so that its inclined face bears on the ring drive face 36 of the segmented cam ring 20.

The latch 16 has two engaged positions. In a first position, the latch 16 holds the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 closed around the pipe 90 but does not clamp it: the frame is captive on the pipe 90 and cannot fall away, while the segmented cam ring 20 has not yet advanced the jaw carriages 30. In a second, over-center position, the wedge 52 drives the segmented cam ring 20 and the pipe 90 is clamped. Movement of the latch handle 50 from the first position to the second position advances the wedge 52 against the ring drive face 36. The inclined face of the wedge 52 converts that advance into circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the coupled ring turns through its limited stroke.

The force-limiting spring stack 54 answers the problem of what becomes of the operator's remaining handle travel. The jaw pads 40 land on the pipe 90 at some point in the stroke that depends on the diameter of the pipe 90, and the latch handle 50 has still to be carried into its over-center position. If the drive train from the latch handle 50 to the wedge 52 were rigid, that remaining travel would be taken up by whatever part of the assembly yielded first, in practice by driving one jaw farther into the pipe 90 than the others and loading it far more heavily. Additional travel of the latch handle 50 after all three jaw pads 40 have contacted the pipe 90 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than forcing one jaw carriage 30 farther inward than the others.

An indicator pin 56 is coupled to the force-limiting spring stack 54 and projects from the latch housing 58. As the force-limiting spring stack 54 compresses, the indicator pin 56 moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing 58, and the position of the indicator pin 56 with respect to that fixed edge shows the operator when the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered a predetermined compression range. The predetermined compression range is the range of stack compression that corresponds to the clamping force for which the clamp 100 is intended. The indicator pin 56 therefore reports clamp loading mechanically, and what it reports is the state of the force-limiting spring stack 54. It is not a measurement of the diameter of the pipe 90.

Operation

To install the clamp 100 on a pipe 90, the operator opens the latch 16 and swings the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 apart about the hinge 14. The first cam ring segment 22 stays with the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 stays with the second frame half 12, and the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are separated. The operator places the frame halves around the pipe 90 from the side and closes them about the hinge 14. Closing the frame halves brings the complementary coupling faces 26 into engagement at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 into engagement at the latch end, coupling the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 into the coupled ring within the annular guide 18.

The operator then moves the latch 16 to its first position, in which the frame is held around the pipe 90 without clamping. The operator moves the latch handle 50 to the second, over-center position. The wedge 52 is driven against the ring drive face 36, the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the sides of the three oblique slots 34 drive the three followers 32, and the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism until the pivoting jaw pads 40 seat on the pipe 90. The remaining travel of the latch handle 50 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54, and the operator watches the indicator pin 56 move relative to the fixed edge of the latch housing 58 and so sees that the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered the predetermined compression range. The latch 16 is left in the over-center position and the clamp 100 is loaded on the pipe 90.

To remove the clamp 100, the operator releases the latch 16. The latch handle 50 comes back over center, the wedge 52 retreats from the ring drive face 36, and the force-limiting spring stack 54 is unloaded. The carriage return springs 44 then push the jaw carriages 30 radially outward, so that the jaw pads 40 lift from the pipe 90. Only then are the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 swung apart about the hinge 14 and the clamp 100 taken off the pipe 90. The clamp 100 is undamaged by the cycle and may be installed again on the same pipe or on a pipe of a different diameter within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

Features described above in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another, except where the context makes the combination impossible. The embodiments described are illustrative of the disclosed clamp and are not exhaustive of it, and the scope of protection is defined by the claims that follow rather than by any particular embodiment described here.

A split pipe clamp is disclosed in which the element that advances the gripping jaws is divided with the clamp body but is made continuous again by the act of closing the clamp, so that one latch motion advances every jaw together.

In one aspect, a split pipe clamp comprises a first frame half and a second frame half joined at a hinge end by a hinge and releasably joined at a latch end by a latch. In a closed condition the two frame halves define a frame having an annular guide and three radial guides. Three jaw carriages are each slidable radially in a respective one of the radial guides, and each jaw carriage carries a jaw pad that is pivotally mounted on the jaw carriage and has a concave bearing face directed inwardly of the frame. A segmented cam ring is received in the annular guide and comprises a first cam ring segment carried by the first frame half and a second cam ring segment carried by the second frame half. The cam ring segments have complementary coupling faces at the hinge end and complementary coupling faces at the latch end, and those faces engage one another as the frame halves are closed, so that in the closed condition the two segments move in the annular guide as a coupled ring. Each jaw carriage has a follower received in a respective oblique slot of the segmented cam ring, each oblique slot being inclined to a radial direction of the frame so that rotation of the coupled ring through a stroke advances the three jaw carriages inwardly in synchronism. A wedge movable by the latch bears on a ring drive face of the segmented cam ring, so that movement of the latch rotates the coupled ring through the stroke, and a carriage return spring biases each jaw carriage outwardly so that releasing the latch retracts the jaws.

Because the coupled ring is a single kinematic element spanning both frame halves, the three jaw carriages are not driven independently. One latch motion, applied at one point on one frame half, is distributed by the coupled ring to every jaw carriage, and the jaw pads close on the pipe together. The pivoting concave jaw pads seat on the pipe without an insert dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter.

In a further aspect, the latch has a first position in which the frame halves are held around the pipe without clamping and a second, over-center position in which the wedge drives the cam ring and the pipe is clamped, and a force-limiting spring stack lies in the drive train between a latch handle and the wedge. Travel of the handle that remains after all three jaw pads have contacted the pipe compresses the force-limiting spring stack instead of advancing one jaw carriage farther than the others. An indicator pin moves relative to a fixed edge of a latch housing when the force-limiting spring stack enters a predetermined compression range, giving the operator a mechanical report of clamp loading that is produced by the state of the spring stack and not by the diameter of the pipe.

In a further aspect, the frame carries a mounting boss outside the annular guide for supporting a sensor, a tool, or a conduit, the mounting boss being connected neither to the segmented cam ring nor to any jaw carriage, so that equipment carried on the frame is outside the path by which the jaws are synchronized.

In a further aspect, a method of clamping a pipe comprises opening the latch, swinging the frame halves apart about the hinge, placing the frame halves around a pipe, closing the frame halves so that the complementary coupling faces engage and couple the cam ring segments, moving the latch to the first position, and moving the latch to the second, over-center position so that the wedge rotates the coupled ring and the followers advance the three jaw carriages inwardly in synchronism until the jaw pads seat on the pipe. Releasing the latch unloads the force-limiting spring stack and the carriage return springs retract the jaw carriages before the frame halves are opened.

a segmented cam ring received in the annular guide and comprising a first cam ring segment carried by the first frame half and a second cam ring segment carried by the second frame half, the first cam ring segment and the second cam ring segment having complementary coupling faces at the hinge end and complementary coupling faces at the latch end that engage one another as the first frame half and the second frame half are closed such that in the closed condition the first cam ring segment and the second cam ring segment rotate together in the annular guide as a coupled ring; three oblique slots in the segmented cam ring and a follower on each jaw carriage received in a respective one of the three oblique slots, each oblique slot being inclined to a radial direction of the frame such that rotation of the coupled ring through a stroke advances the three jaw carriages inwardly in synchronism; a wedge movable by the latch and positioned to bear on a ring drive face of the segmented cam ring; the latch comprising a latch handle and a force-limiting spring stack in a drive train between the latch handle and the wedge, the force-limiting spring stack being arranged such that travel of the latch handle after all three jaw pads have contacted a pipe received in the frame compresses the force-limiting spring stack rather than advancing one of the jaw carriages farther inwardly than the others; # FIG. 2

Plan view of the segmented cam ring alone, removed from the frame, its two segments coupled, viewed along the axis of the ring. Black line work on white, no shading, well inside the drawing area.

A flat annulus at the centre of the drawing area, bounded by inner and outer circular boundaries, is the segmented cam ring 20. The space inside it is empty.

Two joints, one at the left and one at the right, divide the annulus into two arcuate segments. The upper segment is the first cam ring segment 22 and the lower segment is the second cam ring segment 24.

At the left joint the ends of the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 meet along plain complementary surfaces facing circumferentially, the complementary coupling faces at the hinge end 26.

At the right joint the two segment ends meet in the same way, along plain complementary surfaces facing circumferentially, the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

Three elongated openings pass through the annulus, one near the top, one at the lower left and one at the lower right, spaced from one another and from both joints; those circumferential positions are shown schematically. Each is an oblique slot 34, a long narrow opening with rounded ends, lying within the width of the annulus and clearly inclined to the radius at its own position, so that one end is nearer the inner boundary and the other nearer the outer boundary. In each slot the end nearer the inner boundary lies counterclockwise of the end nearer the outer boundary, as viewed here, so that clockwise rotation of the ring, the sense in which the wedge drives it in FIG. 4, brings the inner portion of each slot to the circumferential position held by its outer portion.

Near the right joint, the outer boundary of the second cam ring segment 24 runs as a short straight surface slanting inward toward that joint, the ring drive face 36. The segment on which the ring drive face 36 is shown, and its position on the outer boundary, are shown schematically.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 20 segmented cam ring: target the outer boundary of the annulus in the upper right.
- 22 first cam ring segment: target well inside the upper segment, in its upper left.
- 24 second cam ring segment: target well inside the lower segment, at the bottom.
- 26 complementary coupling faces at the hinge end: target the surfaces meeting at the left joint.
- 28 complementary coupling faces at the latch end: target the meeting surfaces at the right joint.
- 34 oblique slot: target well inside the opening near the top.
- 36 ring drive face: target the slanting surface near the right joint.

# FIG. 4

Enlarged fragmentary section of the latch, taken at the latch end and viewed along the axis of the frame from the side opposite that of FIG. 1. Radially outward is toward the top, the circumferential direction runs left to right, and the right of the view lies toward the first frame half 10. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the flat plate spring seat, the latch housing and its cavity, the gap through which the latch handle 50 passes, the linkage by which it acts on the flat plate, and the coupling of the indicator pin 56 to the force-limiting spring stack 54.

At the lower left a plain hatched body in section holds a hatched arcuate band, the segmented cam ring 20, running from the left edge toward the middle, the frame being broken away above the band, exposing its upper side. Near its right end the upper side of the band runs as a short straight surface slanting downward to the right, the ring drive face 36.

To the right, a hatched enclosure, the latch housing 58, stands on the plain body, its left, right and top walls enclosing a cavity that opens downward above the right end of the band.

A block, the wedge 52, lies in the cavity between the left and right walls. Its lower left face slants at the same angle as the ring drive face 36 and bears on it, so downward movement drives the band to the left.

Above it, the force-limiting spring stack 54 is a zigzag spring line from the wedge 52 to a flat plate across the cavity.

An elongated lever, the latch handle 50, is pivoted to the latch housing 58 at a small circle at the upper right of the cavity. A short schematic arm reaches from that pivot down and to the left and presses down on the flat plate. From the pivot the lever runs up and to the right, out through a gap between the right end of the top wall and the upper end of the right wall, and ends inside the drawing area, leaning right past the upright in the over-center position.

A slender pin, the indicator pin 56, rises from the force-limiting spring stack 54 through a hole in the top wall of the latch housing 58 and stands above it.

Three jaw carriages 30 are distributed around the frame in the closed condition, so that the three jaw carriages 30 approach the pipe 90 from three different directions. Each jaw carriage 30 moves radially with respect to the frame and carries at its inner end a jaw pad 40, which is described below in connection with FIG. 3. The jaw pads 40 carried at the inner ends of the three jaw carriages 30 bear on the pipe 90 when the clamp 100 is clamped. The clamp 100 does not require a part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter, and the same clamp 100 serves pipes of different diameters within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.
The frame may carry a mounting boss 70 outside the annular guide 18 described below, as shown in FIG. 5. The mounting boss 70 supports a sensor, a tool, or a conduit that is to be held on the pipe 90 by the clamp 100. The mounting boss 70 does not participate in the synchronization of the jaw carriages 30. Equipment carried at the mounting boss 70 therefore lies outside the drive path by which the jaws are advanced. The mounting boss 70 is an optional feature of the clamp 100 and may be omitted.
A carriage return spring 44 acts on each jaw carriage 30 so as to urge that jaw carriage 30 radially outward. When the latch 16 is released and the drive from the latch to the ring drive face 36 is removed, the carriage return springs 44 push the jaw carriages 30 outward and the jaw pads 40 are retracted from the pipe, and the clamp 100 is left with its jaw carriages 30 retracted and ready for the next installation. Retraction of the jaw carriages 30 clears the jaw pads 40 from the pipe before the frame halves are swung apart.
FIG. 4 shows the latch 16 in fragmentary section. The latch 16 includes a latch housing 58 at the latch end, a latch handle 50, a wedge 52, and a force-limiting spring stack 54 in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52. The latch housing 58 presents a fixed edge referred to below in connection with the indicator pin 56. The wedge 52 is positioned so that its inclined face bears on the ring drive face 36 of the segmented cam ring 20.

Three jaw carriages 30 are distributed around the frame in the closed condition, so that the three jaw carriages 30 approach the pipe 90 from three different directions. Each jaw carriage 30 moves radially with respect to the frame and carries at its inner end a jaw pad 40, which is described below in connection with FIG. 3. The jaw pads 40 carried at the inner ends of the three jaw carriages 30 bear on the pipe 90 when the clamp 100 is clamped. The clamp 100 does not require a part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter, and the same clamp 100 serves pipes of different diameters within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.
The frame may carry a mounting boss 70 outside the annular guide 18 described below, as shown in FIG. 5. The mounting boss 70 supports a sensor, a tool, or a conduit that is to be held on the pipe 90 by the clamp 100. The mounting boss 70 does not participate in the synchronization of the jaw carriages 30. Equipment carried at the mounting boss 70 therefore lies outside the drive path by which the jaws are advanced. The mounting boss 70 is an optional feature of the clamp 100 and may be omitted.
A carriage return spring 44 acts on each jaw carriage 30 so as to urge that jaw carriage 30 radially outward. When the latch 16 is released and the drive from the latch to the ring drive face 36 is removed, the carriage return springs 44 push the jaw carriages 30 outward and the jaw pads 40 are retracted from the pipe, and the clamp 100 is left with its jaw carriages 30 retracted and ready for the next installation. Retraction of the jaw carriages 30 clears the jaw pads 40 from the pipe before the frame halves are swung apart.
FIG. 4 shows the latch 16 in fragmentary section. The latch 16 includes a latch housing 58 at the latch end, a latch handle 50, a wedge 52, and a force-limiting spring stack 54 in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52. The latch housing 58 presents a fixed edge referred to below in connection with the indicator pin 56. The wedge 52 is positioned so that its inclined face bears on the ring drive face 36 of the segmented cam ring 20.

input.summary: Fixed all six findings. (1) The latch paragraph in draft/08-detailed-description.md no longer asserts that the latch housing 58 is mounted on the frame, that the latch handle 50 is pivotally mounted on the housing, or that the wedge 52 moves inside the housing; it now recites the latch as including a latch housing 58 at the latch end, a latch handle 50, a wedge 52, and the force-limiting spring stack 54 in the drive train between handle and wedge, and states that the housing presents the fixed edge used later for the indicator pin 56, which is the only role the disclosure gives it. The wedge sentence bearing on the ring drive face 36 was kept, since driving a wedge against a drive face of the cam ring is disclosed. (2) The carriage return spring 44 now acts on each jaw carriage 30 to urge it radially outward, without naming the frame as the reaction member; the FIG. 3 brief was left as drawn, since it already marks the spring and its seats schematic. (3) The prior-art noun "insert" is out of claim 5, the summary, and the description, replaced by "a part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter" in each place; the Background keeps its own wording about liners and inserts. (4) Claims 8 and 10, the summary, and the description now use the inventor's functional statement, the mounting boss not participating in the synchronized advance of the jaw carriages, instead of the structural negative about connections to the cam ring and carriages. (5) The unnumbered flat plate is gone from figures/FIG-4.md: the force-limiting spring stack 54 now rises from the wedge 52 into the upper part of the cavity, the schematic arm of the latch handle 50 presses down on the upper end of that stack, the indicator pin 56 rises from the stack through a hole in the top wall, and the schematic list covers the housing and cavity, the handle gap, the handle-to-stack linkage, and the pin-to-stack coupling. The figure now shows only the disclosed force path of handle, spring stack, wedge, and nothing was added to the description, claims, or numeral table to accommodate it. (6) figures/FIG-2.md now states that the ring is viewed along its axis from the same side as FIG. 1, with the hinge end at the left and the latch end at the right, so the slot handedness and the clockwise drive sense it shares with FIG. 4 cannot be inverted by a mirrored rendering. Characters for the additions came out of rendering-only wording in FIG. 4: FIG-1.md is 2798, FIG-2.md 2766, FIG-3.md 2605, FIG-4.md 2783, FIG-5.md 1579. The numeral table is unchanged, no numeral was added or removed, and the drawing descriptions, description, claims, and briefs remain synchronized.
reasoning: The latch housing findings were about three separate structural assertions riding on one noun. The disclosure names the housing once, purely as the carrier of the fixed edge the indicator pin reads against, so mounting it on the frame, hanging the handle off it, and guiding the wedge inside it were all additions. The rewrite keeps every disclosed member of the drive train and its order, drops the mountings, and gives the housing the one job the inventor gave it. The second problem in the same clause disappears with it: the description defines the frame as existing only when the halves are closed, so a housing mounted on the frame had no host while the clamp was open, and a latch that releasably joins the halves has to be carried by one of them.

I left the FIG. 4 depiction of the housing standing on the frame body untouched, because the brief already lists the housing and its cavity as shown schematically and the finding located the defect in the description text. That keeps the depiction convention where it belongs, in the figure, and out of the specification.

On the carriage return spring, reacting against the frame is close to inherent, since the frame is the only body guiding the carriage, but the claim does not need it and the disclosure does not say it. Claim 1 recites only that each spring biases its carriage outwardly, so dropping the reaction member from the description costs no support and removes an assertion about where the spring seats.

The word 'insert' came from my own Background characterization of prior clamps, not from the inventor, and a negative limitation in claim 5 has to stand on its own affirmative support. Substituting 'part' keeps exactly the substance the disclosure gives, a pad that seats on pipes of different diameters without tool-specific tooling, while dropping a component noun borrowed from the art. I changed it in the same words in claim 5, the summary, and both places in the description so the claim language matches its support verbatim.

The mounting boss limitation had been converted from a function into a structure, and the two are not equivalent: a boss could be joined to the frame's ring channel and still take no part in advancing the jaws. Since this is a narrowing limitation in claims 8 and 10, I put back the inventor's own functional wording, which is at least as narrow in effect and is supported word for word. The summary now carries the claim phrase, so the claim has same-words support.

The flat plate was an element I had introduced to give the spring stack something to seat against, and it never earned a numeral or a line in the description. Rather than add it to the numeral table and the specification, which would have grown the application to fit a drawing, I removed it and let the sheet show the disclosed path only: handle presses the stack, stack presses the wedge, wedge drives the ring. The indicator pin still rises from the stack, so the pin reads stack compression against the fixed housing edge, which is what the description and claims 2, 3, 11, and 14 require.

The FIG. 2 viewing side mattered because handedness is only meaningful once the side is fixed. FIG. 4 declares a mirrored viewpoint, and FIG. 2 tied its slot obliquity to the drive sense in FIG. 4 without saying which side it was drawn from, so a renderer could mirror it and reverse the mechanism, turning inward jaw travel into outward. Naming the side and the ends closes that without changing any geometry: the hinge end stays at the left and the latch end at the right, exactly as FIG. 1 shows them.

The following description of embodiments refers to the accompanying drawings. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout. Terms of direction are used with respect to the frame of the clamp: the axis of the frame is the axis about which the frame is annular in the closed condition, "inward" and "radially inward" mean toward that axis, "outward" and "radially outward" mean away from it, and "circumferential" means about that axis. These terms describe relationships within the clamp and do not require the clamp to be used in any particular attitude.

Overall arrangement

FIG. 1 shows a split pipe clamp 100 in the closed condition around a pipe 90. The clamp 100 has a first frame half 10 and a second frame half 12. Each of the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 is semicircular, and the two frame halves together surround the pipe 90. The first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are joined at one end, referred to as the hinge end, by a hinge 14, and are releasably joined at the other end, referred to as the latch end, by a releasable latch 16. The hinge 14 permits the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 to be swung apart far enough for the clamp 100 to be passed sideways onto a pipe 90 that is already installed, so that the clamp 100 need not be threaded over a free end of the pipe 90. When the frame halves are brought together and the latch 16 is engaged, the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 define a frame that is annular about the axis of the clamp 100.

Three jaw carriages 30 are distributed around the frame in the closed condition, so that the three jaw carriages 30 approach the pipe 90 from three different directions. Each jaw carriage 30 moves radially with respect to the frame and carries at its inner end a jaw pad 40, which is described below in connection with FIG. 3. The jaw pads 40 carried at the inner ends of the three jaw carriages 30 bear on the pipe 90 when the clamp 100 is clamped. The clamp 100 does not require a part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter, and the same clamp 100 serves pipes of different diameters within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

The frame may carry a mounting boss 70 outside the annular guide 18 described below, as shown in FIG. 5. The mounting boss 70 supports a sensor, a tool, or a conduit that is to be held on the pipe 90 by the clamp 100. The mounting boss 70 does not participate in the synchronization of the jaw carriages 30. Equipment carried at the mounting boss 70 therefore lies outside the drive path by which the jaws are advanced. The mounting boss 70 is an optional feature of the clamp 100 and may be omitted.

The segmented cam ring

FIG. 2 shows the segmented cam ring 20 of the clamp 100, drawn removed from the frame with its segments in the coupled condition. The segmented cam ring 20 comprises a first cam ring segment 22 and a second cam ring segment 24. The first cam ring segment 22 is carried by the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 is carried by the second frame half 12, so that each frame half carries one segment of the ring and each segment travels with its own frame half when the clamp 100 is opened.

The first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 meet at two places, one at the hinge end and one at the latch end. At the hinge end the two segments have complementary coupling faces 26, and at the latch end they have complementary coupling faces 28. The complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are circumferentially facing drive faces, each pair being shaped so that one segment can transmit circumferential force to the other through the joint. The faces are brought into engagement by the same motion that closes the frame halves: as the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are swung together about the hinge 14 and the latch 16 is engaged, the complementary coupling faces 26 close on one another at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 close on one another at the latch end.

Coupling the segments in this way solves a problem created by splitting the clamp. A clamp that must open from the side cannot carry a continuous drive ring across the split, and a divided drive must otherwise be operated separately in each half, with the result that the two halves advance their jaws by amounts that are not fixed relative to one another. Here the division of the ring is undone by the act of closing the clamp. In the closed condition the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 are coupled at both ends and rotate together in the annular guide as a coupled ring, and a circumferential input applied to either segment is carried around the whole ring. One input, applied at one point on one frame half, therefore reaches every jaw carriage 30 through a single kinematic element, and the relationship between the jaw carriages 30 is set by the geometry of the ring rather than by the way the clamp is operated. When the latch 16 is released and the frame halves are swung apart, the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 separate and each segment stays with its own frame half, so that the coupling is made and broken by the closing and opening of the frame halves.

The segmented cam ring 20 has three oblique slots 34, one for each jaw carriage 30. Each oblique slot 34 is inclined to the radial direction of the frame at the circumferential position of that slot, so that rotation of the coupled ring produces inward travel of its jaw carriage 30, the three oblique slots 34 being arranged so that the three jaw carriages 30 travel inwardly in synchronism. The inclination of the oblique slots 34 sets the ratio between the circumferential stroke of the coupled ring and the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

The segmented cam ring 20 further has a ring drive face 36, shown in FIG. 2 at the latch end of the ring, against which the latch acts as described below. The ring drive face 36 is presented at a position on the ring that the wedge of the latch can reach, and it lies at an inclination to the direction in which that wedge advances, so that advance of the wedge moves the segmented cam ring 20 circumferentially.

The jaw carriages

FIG. 3 is a fragmentary sectional view through one jaw carriage 30, taken along line 3-3 of FIG. 1. The frame is channeled to form the annular guide 18, which receives the segmented cam ring 20. The annular guide 18 retains the first cam ring segment 22 on the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 on the second frame half 12, and permits the coupled ring to move circumferentially.

The frame is further formed with a radial guide 38 at the position of each jaw carriage 30. Each jaw carriage 30 is received in a respective radial guide 38 and is constrained by the radial guide 38 to move radially with respect to the frame. Each jaw carriage 30 carries a follower 32 that projects from the jaw carriage 30 into a respective one of the oblique slots 34 of the segmented cam ring 20. The follower 32 bears against the sides of the oblique slot 34.

The follower 32 is constrained in two ways at once. The radial guide 38 prevents the jaw carriage 30, and therefore the follower 32, from moving circumferentially, while the oblique slot 34 holds the follower 32 at a position along the slot, which is inclined to the radial direction, so that circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20 displaces the follower 32 radially. When the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the side of each oblique slot 34 bears on the corresponding follower 32 and drives it, and with it the jaw carriage 30, radially inward along the radial guide 38. Because all three followers 32 are engaged in oblique slots 34 of one coupled ring, the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism for as long as the ring turns. The jaw pads 40 therefore close on the pipe together.

At its inner end each jaw carriage 30 carries a jaw pad 40. The jaw pad 40 is pivotally mounted on the jaw carriage 30 and has a concave bearing face directed inwardly of the frame. Because the jaw pad 40 is free to pivot on the jaw carriage 30, the concave bearing face aligns itself with the outer surface of the pipe as it lands. The same concave bearing face therefore seats on pipes of different diameters, and no part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter is required.

A carriage return spring 44 acts on each jaw carriage 30 so as to urge that jaw carriage 30 radially outward. When the latch 16 is released and the drive from the latch to the ring drive face 36 is removed, the carriage return springs 44 push the jaw carriages 30 outward and the jaw pads 40 are retracted from the pipe, and the clamp 100 is left with its jaw carriages 30 retracted and ready for the next installation. Retraction of the jaw carriages 30 clears the jaw pads 40 from the pipe before the frame halves are swung apart.

The latch and the force-limiting drive train

FIG. 4 shows the latch 16 in fragmentary section. The latch 16 includes a latch housing 58 at the latch end, a latch handle 50, a wedge 52, and a force-limiting spring stack 54 in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52. The latch housing 58 presents a fixed edge referred to below in connection with the indicator pin 56. The wedge 52 is positioned so that its inclined face bears on the ring drive face 36 of the segmented cam ring 20.

The latch 16 has two engaged positions. In a first position, the latch 16 holds the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 closed around the pipe 90 but does not clamp it: the frame is captive on the pipe 90 and cannot fall away, while the segmented cam ring 20 has not yet advanced the jaw carriages 30. In a second, over-center position, the wedge 52 drives the segmented cam ring 20 and the pipe 90 is clamped. Movement of the latch handle 50 from the first position to the second position advances the wedge 52 against the ring drive face 36. The inclined face of the wedge 52 converts that advance into circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the coupled ring turns through its limited stroke.

The force-limiting spring stack 54 answers the problem of what becomes of the operator's remaining handle travel. The jaw pads 40 land on the pipe 90 at some point in the stroke that depends on the diameter of the pipe 90, and the latch handle 50 has still to be carried into its over-center position. If the drive train from the latch handle 50 to the wedge 52 were rigid, that remaining travel would be taken up by whatever part of the assembly yielded first, in practice by driving one jaw farther into the pipe 90 than the others and loading it far more heavily. Additional travel of the latch handle 50 after all three jaw pads 40 have contacted the pipe 90 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than forcing one jaw carriage 30 farther inward than the others.

An indicator pin 56 is coupled to the force-limiting spring stack 54 and projects from the latch housing 58. As the force-limiting spring stack 54 compresses, the indicator pin 56 moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing 58, and the position of the indicator pin 56 with respect to that fixed edge shows the operator when the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered a predetermined compression range. The predetermined compression range is the range of stack compression that corresponds to the clamping force for which the clamp 100 is intended. The indicator pin 56 therefore reports clamp loading mechanically, and what it reports is the state of the force-limiting spring stack 54. It is not a measurement of the diameter of the pipe 90.

Operation

To install the clamp 100 on a pipe 90, the operator opens the latch 16 and swings the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 apart about the hinge 14. The first cam ring segment 22 stays with the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 stays with the second frame half 12, and the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are separated. The operator places the frame halves around the pipe 90 from the side and closes them about the hinge 14. Closing the frame halves brings the complementary coupling faces 26 into engagement at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 into engagement at the latch end, coupling the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 into the coupled ring within the annular guide 18.

The operator then moves the latch 16 to its first position, in which the frame is held around the pipe 90 without clamping. The operator moves the latch handle 50 to the second, over-center position. The wedge 52 is driven against the ring drive face 36, the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the sides of the three oblique slots 34 drive the three followers 32, and the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism until the pivoting jaw pads 40 seat on the pipe 90. The remaining travel of the latch handle 50 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54, and the operator watches the indicator pin 56 move relative to the fixed edge of the latch housing 58 and so sees that the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered the predetermined compression range. The latch 16 is left in the over-center position and the clamp 100 is loaded on the pipe 90.

To remove the clamp 100, the operator releases the latch 16. The latch handle 50 comes back over center, the wedge 52 retreats from the ring drive face 36, and the force-limiting spring stack 54 is unloaded. The carriage return springs 44 then push the jaw carriages 30 radially outward, so that the jaw pads 40 lift from the pipe 90. Only then are the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 swung apart about the hinge 14 and the clamp 100 taken off the pipe 90. The clamp 100 is undamaged by the cycle and may be installed again on the same pipe or on a pipe of a different diameter within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

Features described above in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another, except where the context makes the combination impossible. The embodiments described are illustrative of the disclosed clamp and are not exhaustive of it, and the scope of protection is defined by the claims that follow rather than by any particular embodiment described here.

# FIG. 4

Enlarged fragmentary section of the latch, taken at the latch end and viewed along the axis of the frame from the side opposite that of FIG. 1. Radially outward is toward the top, the circumferential direction runs left to right, and the right of the view lies toward the first frame half 10. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the latch housing and its cavity, the gap through which the latch handle 50 passes, the linkage by which it acts on the force-limiting spring stack 54, and the coupling of the indicator pin 56 to that stack.

At the lower left a plain hatched body in section holds a hatched arcuate band, the segmented cam ring 20, running from the left edge toward the middle, the frame being broken away above the band, exposing its upper side. Near its right end the upper side of the band runs as a short straight surface slanting downward to the right, the ring drive face 36.

To the right, a hatched enclosure, the latch housing 58, stands on the plain body, its left, right and top walls enclosing a cavity that opens downward above the right end of the band.

A block, the wedge 52, lies in the cavity between the left and right walls. Its lower left face slants at the same angle as the ring drive face 36 and bears on it, so downward movement drives the band to the left.

Above it, the force-limiting spring stack 54 is a zigzag spring line rising from the wedge 52 into the upper part of the cavity.

An elongated lever, the latch handle 50, is pivoted to the latch housing 58 at a small circle at the upper right of the cavity. A short schematic arm reaches from that pivot down and to the left and presses down on the upper end of the force-limiting spring stack 54. From the pivot the lever runs up and to the right, out through a gap between the right end of the top wall and the upper end of the right wall, and ends inside the drawing area, leaning right past the upright in the over-center position.

A slender pin, the indicator pin 56, rises from the force-limiting spring stack 54 through a hole in the top wall of the latch housing 58.

- 20 segmented cam ring: target the hatching of the band.
- 36 ring drive face: target the slanting surface on the band.
- 50 latch handle: target well inside the lever.
- 52 wedge: target well inside the block in the cavity.
- 54 force-limiting spring stack: target the zigzag line.
- 56 indicator pin: target the pin above the top wall.
- 58 latch housing: target the hatching of the top wall.

input.summary: Fixed all three findings. (1) The sentence defining the claimed term "predetermined compression range" as the range of stack compression corresponding to an intended clamping force is deleted from draft/08-detailed-description.md. The paragraph now runs from the pin's movement against the fixed edge of the latch housing 58 straight to the supported statements that the indicator reports clamp loading mechanically, that what it reports is the state of the force-limiting spring stack 54, and that it is not a measurement of pipe diameter. Claims 2, 11, and 14 were not amended; they already recite the term in the inventor's own words. (2) figures/FIG-4.md no longer explains the missing radially outer wall as a break-away. The frame wall radially outside the band is now interrupted at the latch end, so that the upper side of the band is exposed and the wedge 52 can reach the ring drive face 36. That reconciles FIG. 4 with the groove bounded above and below in FIGS. 3 and 5 and with claim 6's retention limitation, and it keeps the access opening in the figure brief: I described the interrupted wall generically, without the canonical name or numeral of the annular guide 18, so FIG. 4 still lists eight numerals and the numeral table is untouched. The application text was not changed, since the description already keeps the drive face location neutral. (3) draft/07-drawings.md now identifies FIGS. 4 and 5 by reference to a view instead of by cutting planes that cannot be drawn: FIG. 4 is an enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end of the clamp of FIG. 1 with the latch shown in section in a plane parallel to the plane of FIG. 1 and viewed from the opposite side, and FIG. 5 is an enlarged fragmentary sectional view corresponding to a portion of FIG. 3, taken through a frame provided with the optional mounting boss. FIG. 3 keeps its line 3-3 indication on FIG. 1, and both figure briefs already matched these descriptions, so neither needed editing for the change. Characters for the FIG. 4 addition came out of rendering-only wording: FIG-1.md is 2798, FIG-2.md 2766, FIG-3.md 2605, FIG-4.md 2771, FIG-5.md 1579. The numeral table, claims, drawing descriptions, description, and all five briefs remain synchronized.
reasoning: The compression-range gloss was the one sentence in the draft that would have been read as claim construction. It defined a term appearing in three claims by reference to a design clamping force the inventor never mentions, which would have tied the claimed range to an undisclosed parameter and given an examiner or an opponent a definition to argue from. The inventor says only that the pin moves when the stack enters a predetermined compression range and that the indicator reports loading rather than diameter, and both of those statements are still on the page, so deleting the gloss removes the import without costing any support.

The FIG. 4 wall problem was a genuine conflict between three sheets rather than a wording slip. FIGS. 3 and 5 show frame material radially outside the ring, claim 6 recites that the annular guide retains each segment, and FIG. 4 sends the wedge radially inward through exactly that space. A break-away removes material from view only, so on a literal reading either the wall was there and the wedge could not reach the drive face, or the wedge reached it and the wall was gone. An interruption at the latch end resolves it in the direction the disclosure already entails, since the ring is retained in the annular guide and the latch nevertheless drives a wedge against a drive face of that ring.

I described the interrupted wall as the frame wall radially outside the band rather than naming the annular guide 18, deliberately. FIG. 4 already carries eight numerals, which is the ceiling for one sheet, and adding 18 would have meant either overcrowding the sheet or splitting the latch view. Describing the surrounding structure generically, without its canonical part name or numeral, keeps the geometry unambiguous while leaving the numeral discipline and the table exactly as they were.

For the sectional-view formality I took the route that does not manufacture a line that cannot exist. FIG. 4's plane is parallel to the plane of FIG. 1, so it projects to a point rather than a line there, and FIG. 5 is taken at the optional mounting boss, which FIG. 1 does not show and should not show, because the boss is expressly optional and FIG. 1 establishes the base embodiment. Identifying each by reference to a view, FIG. 4 to the latch end of FIG. 1 and FIG. 5 to a portion of FIG. 3, locates both without inventing an indication. FIG. 3, whose plane is perpendicular to FIG. 1, keeps its line 3-3.

Tying FIG. 5 to a portion of FIG. 3 also has a substantive benefit: both are sections through the frame in a plane containing a radial direction and the frame axis, and both show the annular guide with the cam ring in it, so the reader is told directly that FIG. 5 is that same section taken where the frame carries the boss. That is why the caption change needed no edit to either brief.

The trimming in FIG. 4 removed only renderer wording, never geometry: the band's endpoint qualifier, the mounting phrase for the housing, the exact ends of the walls bounding the handle gap, and repeated identifications of parts already named on the sheet. Every body, contact, opening, and path the reviewer verified as kinematically consistent, the wedge slant against the drive face, the downward wedge travel driving the band left, the handle-to-stack linkage, and the pin rising from the stack, is still specified.

input.prior_art_strategy: No citation was added, removed, or altered; prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references and input/brief.md records that no search was run, so the Background states the problem from the disclosure alone and cites nothing. Deleting the compression-range gloss strengthens the position on the indicator aspect: claims 2, 11, and 14 now stand on the inventor's own formulation, a pin that moves against a fixed edge of the latch housing when the stack enters a predetermined compression range and that reports loading rather than diameter, with no undisclosed design force in the specification for an opponent to read into the term. The features carrying the independent claims are unchanged and still explained as answers to stated technical problems: the coupling of the two cam ring segments by the act of closing the frame, which restores a single drive element across a split a side-opening clamp cannot otherwise bridge, and the force-limiting spring stack between latch handle and wedge, which absorbs travel a rigid train would dump into whichever jaw touched first. The corrected FIG. 4 also supports claim 6, since the ring is now shown retained in a guide whose outer wall is interrupted only where the wedge must reach the drive face. The art behind this draft is empty and may be incomplete; the claims should be retested against any later search, with the dependent ladder, the indicator pin and compression range, the two latch positions, the pivoting pads without size-specific tooling, the segments that separate with their own halves, and the mounting boss outside the drive path, as the retreat order.

Deleting the compression-range gloss strengthens the position on the indicator aspect: claims 2, 11, and 14 now stand on the inventor's own formulation, a pin that moves against a fixed edge of the latch housing when the stack enters a predetermined compression range and that reports loading rather than diameter, with no undisclosed design force in the specification for an opponent to read into the term. The features carrying the independent claims are unchanged and still explained as answers to stated technical problems: the coupling of the two cam ring segments by the act of closing the frame, which restores a single drive element across a split a side-opening clamp cannot otherwise bridge, and the force-limiting spring stack between latch handle and wedge, which absorbs travel a rigid train would dump into whichever jaw touched first. The corrected FIG. 4 also supports claim 6, since the ring is now shown retained in a guide whose outer wall is interrupted only where the wedge must reach the drive face. The art behind this draft is empty and may be incomplete; the claims should be retested against any later search, with the dependent ladder, the indicator pin and compression range, the two latch positions, the pivoting pads without size-specific tooling, the segments that separate with their own halves, and the mounting boss outside the drive path, as the retreat order.
structured_output.answer: All three findings are resolved. The description no longer defines the predetermined compression range in terms of an intended clamping force; the paragraph keeps only the inventor's statements that the pin moves against the fixed edge of the latch housing as the stack compresses, that it reports clamp loading mechanically, and that it is not a diameter measurement, so claims 2, 11, and 14 needed no amendment. FIG. 4 now shows the frame wall radially outside the cam ring interrupted at the latch end so the wedge can reach the ring drive face, which agrees with the retained-ring depiction in FIGS. 3 and 5 and with claim 6; I described that wall generically rather than naming the annular guide, so the sheet still carries eight numerals and the numeral table is unchanged. The Brief Description now locates FIG. 4 as a view of the latch end of FIG. 1 sectioned in a plane parallel to the plane of FIG. 1 and viewed from the opposite side, and FIG. 5 as a section corresponding to a portion of FIG. 3 taken through a frame provided with the optional mounting boss, so neither view relies on a cutting-plane line that cannot be drawn, while FIG. 3 keeps its line 3-3 on FIG. 1. Brief lengths are 2798, 2766, 2605, 2771, and 1579 characters, all within the limit.
